title: Nigeria Situation Report - September 2026
content:
In September 2026, Nigeria faced compounding climate, security, and public health crises. Severe seasonal flooding inundated internally displaced persons camps, destroyed farmland, and damaged critical water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure across conflict-affected Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe States, as well as parts of North-Central and Southern Nigeria. Meanwhile, attacks by non-state armed groups in the North-East and criminal banditry in the North-West and North-Central regions disrupted humanitarian operations and triggered further displacement.

The impacts are disproportionately affecting women and adolescent girls, creating urgent protection and reproductive health needs. In response, UNFPA provided 23,114 people with sexual and reproductive health services and 10,221 people with gender-based violence prevention, mitigation, and response services during September. Youth-focused empowerment initiatives also engaged 14,747 young people through a network of four dedicated youth-friendly spaces.

Despite these efforts, critical funding gaps threaten the continuity of life-saving humanitarian assistance. UNFPA requires US$11.9 million to implement its 2026 humanitarian response in Nigeria, but as of September, only 18 per cent of the required funding had been secured. Urgent additional funding is needed to sustain and scale up essential reproductive health and protection services for crisis-affected communities.

title: Epidemiological Update: Dengue and Chikungunya in the Americas Region - 20 October 2026
content: Given the increase in dengue cases observed in some countries of the Andean, Central American, and Caribbean subregions of the Americas Region, as well as the increase in chikungunya cases experienced between late 2025 and 2026, accompanied by the resurgence of chikungunya transmission in countries and territories of the Region where no viral circulation had been recorded for several years, the anticipated intensification of the El Niño phenomenon over the coming months, and the approaching peak season for dengue and chikungunya transmission in South America, the Pan American Health Organization/World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) urges Member States to maintain and strengthen epidemiological, virological, and entomological surveillance, as well as to strengthen diagnostic capacity, to ensure early detection and timely clinical management of cases, and to consolidate integrated vector management efforts, with the aim of limiting transmission and reducing morbidity and mortality associated with dengue, chikungunya, and other arboviral diseases.

title: Emergency Medical Teams’ response to Hurricane Dorian in The Bahamas (2019)
content:
Description

In September 2019, Hurricane Dorian devastated Abaco and Grand Bahama. It destroyed homes, clinics, and hospitals through winds, rain, and storm surge. Flooding left debris, loss of life, and disrupted power, water, and communications. Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) played a key role in supporting health services. The Ministry of Health, the Public Hospitals Authority, and the National Emergency Management Agency led the response with technical support from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). For the first time in the Caribbean, a Medical Information and Coordination Cell (CICOM) was activated within the Health Emergency Operations Center in Nassau. The CICOM managed requests for EMTs, validated incoming teams, and ensured that clinical data from the field were shared daily with national authorities. Seven EMTs deployed to The Bahamas. They delivered more than 9000 outpatient consultations, admitted 178 patients, and performed 134 surgeries. Type 1 teams offered essential outpatient care in shelters and damaged communities. A Type 2 team provided surgical and inpatient capacity, bridging gaps left by hospitals that had been damaged or closed. Their work was coordinated with Bahamian health services, ensuring referrals and continuity of care under austere conditions. The AAR gathered national counterparts, EMTs, and regional experts to examine the experience. The review identified best practices and challenges: customs clearance, inter-island transport, communication outages, and the need for clear transition once the acute phase ends. This report provides a legacy reference for strengthening preparedness and ensuring that EMT deployments in future emergencies are effective, efficient, and aligned with national coordination structures. It reinforces the importance of classified and self-sufficient EMTs, strong coordination through CICOM, and early planning for recovery.

title: UNHCR Syria Operational Update - September 2026
content:
Syria is experiencing large-scale refugee and IDP returns alongside persistent humanitarian vulnerability and reintegration needs.

While over 1.8 million refugees and 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) have returned since December 2024, 15.6 million people still require humanitarian assistance.

As return movements continue, access to documentation, housing, essential services, livelihoods and community support is critical to sustainable reintegration and Syria’s recovery.

In line with Syria’s National Recovery Priorities and the Government’s “No Tents, No Camps” vision, UNHCR supports return and reintegration while maintaining protection and humanitarian assistance for vulnerable populations.

title: Sudan Response: Humanitarian Situation and Operational Update | Renk County, Upper Nile State, South Sudan | January – June, 2026
content:
Operational Context

Between January and June 2026, Renk County remained a major entry point for people fleeing the conflict in Sudan (, with continued arrivals driven by insecurity, forced returns, deteriorating socioeconomic conditions, limited access to basic services, and declining humanitarian assistance.

Between January and June 2026, border monitoring conducted by UNHCR, IOM, and ACTED recorded 59,615 new arrivals comprising 19,237 households, of whom 60% were South Sudanese and 40% were Sudanese nationals. Women and children represented the majority of arrivals (80%), including 42% adult women, 28% children aged 0-11 years, and 10% adolescents aged 12-17 years.

To facilitate safe and organized movement from border entry points, 26,806 individuals (11,010 households) received Onward Transportation Assistance (OTA) from Joda to the Renk Transit Centre. Among them, 18,974 individuals (7,072 households) identified as Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) were prioritized for transportation due to heightened vulnerabilities, while 7,832 individuals (3,938 households) received support as non-PSNs. In addition, 4,828 refugees and returnees were assisted with onward transportation from Renk through Malakal to their final destinations.

The OTA assistance played a critical role in decongesting border reception center and the Renk Transit Centre, while ensuring timely access to registration, protection, health, nutrition, shelter, and other essential humanitarian services. The intervention contributed significantly to safeguarding the dignity, safety, and wellbeing of newly arrived refugees and returnees, while strengthening the overall humanitarian response and population management efforts in Renk County.

title: Upper Nile State, South Sudan: Renk Area-Based Durable Solutions Report (January–June) 2026
content:
Overview

The first half of 2026 marked an important transition period in Renk County, with humanitarian actors gradually complementing life-saving interventions with activities aimed at advancing durable solutions for refugees, returnees, and host communities. While the county continued to receive significant numbers of Sudanese refugees and South Sudanese returnees, resulting in sustained humanitarian needs, partners increasingly invested in initiatives that foster self-reliance, local integration, social cohesion, and equitable access to essential services.

Between January and June 2026, humanitarian partners, working closely with the Commission for Refugee Affairs (CRA), the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC), and relevant county-level ministries and departments including Education, Agriculture, Fisheries, Lands, Gender, Child and Social Welfare, Infrastructure, and Rural and Urban Water departments, strengthened efforts to support durable solutions. Key areas of focus included;

✓ Ensuring access to legal identity and civil documentation

✓ Promoting self-reliance through livelihoods, agriculture, and skills development;

✓ Strengthening community-based protection mechanisms

✓ Fostering social cohesion and peaceful coexistence among refugees, returnees, and host communities ✓ Expanding access to quality education and;

✓ Improving infrastructure and basic service delivery in the areas of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, and education.

These strategic investments were designed not only to address immediate humanitarian needs but also to support long-term recovery, resilience, and sustainable development. These interventions contributed to creating an enabling environment for refugees, returnees, and host communities to rebuild their lives and strengthen their socio-economic well-being across Renk County.

title: UNHCR Emergency Response: Earthquake in Panama – October 20 2026
content:
Situation

Ten days after the 7.5-magnitude earthquake that struck Panama's Azuero Peninsula, authorities continue assessing its full impact. According to the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC), 2,318 homes sustained total damage, 5,546 were partially damaged, and another 1,260 were affected to a lesser extent. Damage has also been reported to over 600 educational facilities and 120 health facilities. According to the Ministry of Social Development, 55 temporary shelters remain active and host 3,827 people. The number of injured remains at 27. However, media have also reported the subsequent death of a woman injured, as well as the death of an infant with pre-existing medical conditions, whose family had been staying in an informal shelter following the earthquake.

As of 19 October, the Institute of Geosciences reports 917 aftershocks. While seismic activity continues, experts report it is becoming less frequent over time, despite some stronger isolated events. Preliminary assessments also indicate the earthquake triggered about 2,300 landslides, and in the Isla Cañas area, authorities have identiﬁed a signiﬁcant ground fracture, with additional assessments ongoing to evaluate changes to the national topography.

Despite adverse weather conditions and a green alert issued in Veraguas and Los Santos Provinces, the government, local authorities, civil society organizations, and private sector actors have mobilized in solidarity, delivering donations and support to affected populations across the impacted areas.

title: UNICEF Eastern and Southern Africa Region Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1, 1 January-30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Eastern and Southern Africa continues to face overlapping, life-threatening shocks, including conflict, displacement, escalating malnutrition, recurrent cholera and measles outbreaks, climate-related droughts and floods, severe food insecurity, and fragile health systems.
  • UNICEF delivered integrated life-saving services to millions of people, including vaccination campaigns, treatment for severe wasting, safe water and sanitation support, nutrition screening among other interventions.
  • Public health emergencies remain a major regional concern, with cholera, mpox, measles, cVDPV2 and Ebola/Bundibugyo Virus Disease preparedness requiring sustained surveillance, infection prevention and control, community engagement, cross-border coordination and pre-positioned supplies.
  • Climate risks are intensifying across the region, with a heightened risk of El Niño-related shocks in 2026/27 expected to further compound food insecurity, child wasting, water scarcity, flooding and disease outbreaks, particularly in climate-vulnerable and displacement-affected communities.

REGIONAL OVERVIEW

SITUATION OVERVIEW AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

The humanitarian situation across Eastern and Southern Africa in the first half of 2026 has been marked by overlapping and compounding crises. Widespread disease outbreaks, including cholera, mpox and other epidemic threats, continue to place pressure on public health systems, while recurrent drought, floods and other climate- related shocks are deepening food insecurity, acute malnutrition and livelihood losses. Displacement linked to floods, conflict and fragile socio- economic conditions has left many households without adequate shelter, safe water, sanitation, education and protection services, with children and women bearing the greatest burden. Without urgent, coordinated and sustained support, humanitarian needs are expected to intensify, further worsening child health and nutrition outcomes and increasing exposure to protection risks, particularly in hard- to- reach and displacement- affected communities.

Forecasts indicate a heightened risk of El Niño- related shocks across the region during the 2026/27 season, potentially placing millions more people at risk of acute food insecurity while increasing flooding, drought and disease outbreak risks. Djibouti, Eritrea, Kenya, Malawi and Zambia are prioritizing anticipatory action frameworks, climate- resilient WASH infrastructure and pre- positioning of supplies ahead of the lean season. Continued Ebola/BVD transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo underscores the need to sustain preparedness across bordering and transit countries. UNICEF and partners will prioritize closing critical funding gaps for child protection, social protection and nutrition screening, while strengthening anticipatory, climate- resilient and cross- border systems to protect vulnerable children and communities region- wide.

title: UNICEF Panama Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 (Earthquake), 14-16 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • According to the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC), as of October 15, 5,821 homes have been evaluated, corresponding to 19,309 people, of which 3,696 remain in temporary accommodation. Among the population identified by SINAPROC, 475 newborns, 2,174 children and 1,030 adolescents were reported. The authorities continue damage assessments and assistance to affected families.
  • The evaluations continue to identify impacts on water, sanitation, education and protection services in rural and hard-to-reach communities in the provinces of Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas, where risk factors associated with displacement, interruption of basic services and access limitations persist.
  • UNICEF contributes to the government-led response, in coordination with UN agencies, funds and programmes, deploying efforts with donors and implementing partners to reach the most affected communities with psychosocial support, water, sanitation, health and learning spaces in the context of the emergency.
  • As part of the initial response, UNICEF distributed 415 hygiene kits to displaced people from Isla Cañas, including 325 kits for children aged 0-12 years and 90 kits for adolescents and adults, helping to reduce health risks and strengthen hygiene conditions in temporary shelters.
  • Needs continue to evolve as damage and impact assessments progress. UNICEF requires US$2.57 million to sustain and scale up the multisectoral response targeting children and their families in affected provinces, with an emphasis on protection, education, health and access to essential WASH services.

Humanitarian Situation and Needs

The 7.5 magnitude earthquake that struck Panama on October 9 continues to have significant impacts on families and essential services. Following the declaration of a state of emergency on October 10, national authorities continue damage assessments and humanitarian assistance to displaced families, while there are still needs for safe shelter and access to basic services in the affected areas. As of the date of the report, and according to official figures from SINAPROC, 19,309 people are affected by the earthquake. According to the preliminary breakdown by age and sex, 475 newborns, 2,174 children and 1,030 adolescents are identified. In turn, SINAPROC reports 3,696 people housed in temporary shelters, of which 2,569 are in Veraguas, followed by 644 people in Los Santos and 483 in other areas. That shows priority needs for protection, access to basic services and continuity of essential services for children. At the time of this report, two people have died as a result of the earthquake.

Infrastructure damage and access limitations persist in several of the impacted areas. In the province of Herrera, one community is reported to be cut off from communication and 32 landslides, while in areas of Veraguas there are still interruptions in drinking water, electricity and connectivity services.³ These conditions may limit the timely access of affected communities to humanitarian assistance and essential services, in addition to delaying assessment, rehabilitation and recovery efforts.
As government-led sectoral assessments progress, needs related to the restoration of water, sanitation and hygiene services, the recovery of safe learning spaces and the expansion of child protection services continue to be identified. The information remains subject to updating as authorities complete damage checks and early recovery and response efforts advance.

title: Jordan Operational Update - Jul-Sept 2026

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 01-15 October 2026
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that since the military coup on 01 February 2021 and 31 August 2026, at least 1,973 attacks on health care took place across Myanmar, with over 65% of attacks attributed to the Myanmar Armed Forces. Health facilities were damaged 519 times while 175 health workers were killed and 55 kidnapped.

At least 940 health workers were reportedly arrested or detained in 374 incidents across 17 regions and states during the reporting period. Detained staff were often beaten or threatened, while 14 health workers arrested by the MAF were reportedly killed. In the first year of the military coup, health workers were predominantly arrested on allegations of affiliation with the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM), for providing care to injured local defense forces (LDF), or for their leadership roles as caregivers within communities. Over time, the reasons for arrest shifted from health workers’ treatment of injured protesters to allegations that they were assisting or affiliated with opposing conflict parties.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 15 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In the Gaza Strip, Israeli airstrikes, shelling and gunfire continued to result in reported civilian casualties, while incursions, demolitions and reported shifts in the “Yellow Line” heightened concerns and risks of further displacement.
  • About 950,000 displaced people have been assessed as living in sites at medium to high risk of flooding, including over 400,000 at high risk. Available supplies could partially assist only 18 per cent of the 294,250 families requiring shelter assistance for the rainy season.
  • Daily cooked-meal production has declined by 12 per cent to approximately 614,000 amid funding constraints, while shortages of fuel, engine oil and essential supplies threaten the continuity of health and water services.
  • In the West Bank, over the past two weeks, five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settlers, with 74 per cent of injuries occurring in the context of settler attacks.
  • Over 160 olive harvest-related settler attacks resulted in casualties, property damage or both over the past two weeks. Since September, some 200 olive harvest-related settler attacks were documented.
  • Demolitions displaced 96 Palestinians over two weeks, including 69 in At Tur – the largest displacement in a single demolition incident in East Jerusalem since UN records began in 2009.

Gaza Strip

The reporting period is 29 September – 12 October 2026 unless otherwise specified.

Israeli airstrikes, shelling and gunfire continued across Gaza, reportedly causing civilian casualties, including among displaced people. Israeli incursions and demolitions were also reported near “Yellow Line.” On 10 October, Israeli authorities issued four evacuation orders and two shelter-in-place orders affecting humanitarian sites across three governorates; no damage was reported. On 11 October, Israeli forces reportedly moved the “Yellow Line” markers westward near Ash Shuja'iyyeh junction in Gaza city, raising concerns about further displacement in an area hosting displaced people. The UN Human Rights Office has verified 1,076 conflict-related deaths between the ceasefire announcement on 10 October 2025 and the end of July 2026, including 331 near the “Yellow Line.”

According to the Ministry of Health in Gaza, which operates under the de-facto authorities, 57 Palestinians were reported killed and 319 injured between 29 September and 12 October, bringing the total number of casualties since the ceasefire agreement to 1,493 fatalities and 5,299 injuries.

Humanitarian conditions remained critical amid widespread displacement, damaged infrastructure and shortages of essential supplies. Daily cooked-meal production declined by approximately 12 per cent compared with late September, while shortages of fuel, engine oil, spare parts and medicines threatened essential health and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services. Efforts to prepare for the rainy season became increasingly urgent for families in deteriorating shelters and unsafe buildings, but shortages of materials, machinery, and funding – alongside Israeli restrictions on access to suitable land – continued to constrain mitigation and relocation efforts.

Humanitarian cargo movements into Gaza continued to face operational and logistical challenges, including inspection and scanning procedures, limited handling capacity, and coordination requirements across multiple stages of the supply chain. According to the Logistics Cluster, between 29 September and 12 October, 937 trucks carrying humanitarian supplies were manifested and 807 offloaded across five corridors: Ashdod, Egypt, Jordan, Israel and the West Bank. Of those offloaded, 373 were routed through Ashdod, 206 through Egypt, 198 through Jordan, 18 through Israel and 12 through the West Bank. More intensive inspections and scanning procedures contributed to slower cargo movements from Egypt, while additional crossing capacity, improved coordination and more predictable clearance and handling arrangements remained critical to facilitating the timely entry of humanitarian assistance.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 01-15 October 2026
content:
Data by Insecurity Insight shows that since fighting started between the SAF and RSF in April 2023 and 30 September 2026, at least 802 attacks on health care took place across Sudan, with over 55% of attacks attributed to the RSF. Health facilities were damaged at least 229 times while 222 health workers were killed and 16 kidnapped.

At least 142 health workers were arrested or detained in 74 incidents across 14 states during the reporting period. Both the RSF and SAF carried out arrests, often accusing health workers of supporting opposing conflict parties. Staff were often beaten or threatened, while five health workers arrested by the RSF were reportedly killed. Around 30% of incidents occurred while health workers were on duty in health facilities or ambulances; others took place during commutes, at home, or in one case, while shopping at a market.

title: UNICEF Eastern and Southern Africa Region Humanitarian Situation Report No. 2 (Multi-country Great Lakes), 1 January-30 June 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Great Lakes subregion continues to face overlapping crises of conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks, leaving millions of vulnerable children and families in urgent need of assistance.
  • UNICEF and partners delivered lifesaving interventions across health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, education, and social protection, reaching about 400,000 people including 313,000 children of which 265,000 were under five1.
  • Persistent funding gaps, fragile systems, and limited district level capacity constrain scale up, while disability inclusion, and climate shocks remain under resourced challenges.
  • UNICEF is strengthening inclusive preparedness through surveillance, IPC/WASH, RCCE, MHPSS integration, disability inclusion, PSEA mechanisms, and cross border coordination to build resilience and accountability.

SUBREGIONAL OVERVIEW

SITUATION ANALYSIS AND HUMANITARIAN NEEDS

During the first half of 2026, the subregion faced overlapping crises of conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks. Burundi received large- scale refugee arrivals from DRC and the return of over 100,000 Burundian refugees from Tanzania, compounded by cholera, measles, and Mpox outbreaks; 1.28 million people, including 632,000 children require assistance. Rwanda activated its National Ebola Contingency Plan across 13 high- risk districts following the Bundibugyo strain outbreak in DRC and in Uganda, though no cases were confirmed locally. Tanzania managed a protracted refugee situation, recurrent flooding, and outbreaks of measles, Mpox, and circulating vaccine- derived poliovirus, with nearly 146,000 refugees — 57% children — dependent on humanitarian assistance. Uganda, hosting over two million refugees, simultaneously responded to Bundibugyo Virus Disease, measles (445 cases across 81 districts), anthrax, and CCHF, while 122,100 children in Karamoja faced acute malnutrition.

Forecasted El Niño- driven extreme weather threatens to worsen food insecurity, outbreaks, and malnutrition in the second half of 2026, making sustained investment in preparedness and cross- border coordination essential. Forecasts point to a high likelihood of El Niño- driven extreme weather across the subregion in the second half of 2026, including drought, flooding, and disruption to livelihoods and basic services. This is expected to compound existing disease outbreak risks and worsen acute malnutrition among already vulnerable children, particularly in Karamoja (Uganda) and refugee- hosting areas of Tanzania and Burundi. Continued Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease transmission in DRC and Uganda means preparedness efforts in Rwanda and Tanzania's high- risk regions must be sustained and, where possible, expanded to remaining high- risk districts. UNICEF and partners will prioritize closing funding gaps for disability inclusion, MHPSS, and child protection systems, while strengthening cross- border coordination mechanisms to ensure timely detection, response, and continuity of care for vulnerable children and families across the subregion.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #5 (19 October 2026)
content:
Djibouti | Somalia | Yemen

Highlights

▪ Displacement inside Yemen continued to rise sharply, reaching over 250,000 people between 1 August and 17 October1 , with Taiz hosting the largest share of those displaced. UNHCR is part of the inter-agency response under the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). Response and contingency planning is being adapted to evolving displacement trends, with revised displacement scenarios being prepared to guide assistance, strengthen preparedness and support the response to additional internal displacement and cross-border movements.

▪ As of 17 October 2026, 4,078 new arrivals from Yemen were recorded in the region, including 3,836 new arrivals in Djibouti and 242 in Somalia (which includes returnees and refugees), reflecting the continued search for safety by affected populations. Between 8 and 14 October, no new arrivals from Yemen to Djibouti were reported. Following the capsizing of a boat travelling from Djibouti to Yemen on the night of 8–9 October 2026, 139 bodies have been recovered, including 109 who have been identified. Burials have taken place in accordance with religious rites. 82 survivors have been identified and are receiving support based on their needs.

title: UNHCR-IOM Joint Annual Overview - Migrant and Refugee Movements through the Central Mediterranean Sea in 2025
content:
1. KEY FIGURES

▪ An estimated 100,777 recorded crossing attempts were observed from Libya, Tunisia and Algeria towards Italy and Malta in 2025, representing a 21% decrease compared with 2024. This aggregate includes arrivals in Italy and Malta, and people intercepted or rescued at sea and disembarked in Libya or Tunisia. It may include multiple attempts by the same person and does not include recorded deaths and disappearances at sea.

▪ Arrivals to Italy and Malta through the Central Mediterranean Sea reached 65,327 in 2025, representing a 4% increase compared to 2024.

▪ Reported disembarkations in 2025 decreased by 68% in Tunisia and increased by 8% in Libya compared to 2024.

▪ The main nationalities attempting to cross the Central Mediterranean Sea in 2025 were Bangladeshi (22%), Sudanese (12%), Egyptian (11%), Eritrean (9%) and Pakistani (5%) nationals.

▪ According to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project, 1,330 individuals were recorded as dead or missing while crossing the Central Mediterranean route in 2025. This represents a 24% decrease compared to 2024, when 1,754 dead or missing migrants were recorded.

title: Situation Report: September 2026 WHO Cox’s Bazar: Rohingya Emergency Response
content:
Overview

In September 2026, WHO and Health Sector partners continued delivering essential health services across Rohingya camps and host communities while addressing evolving public health risks. Disease surveillance remained robust, supporting the monitoring and response to priority diseases, including measles, dengue, cholera, and scabies. Dengue transmission showed a declining trend following the August peak, while immunization activities strengthened population immunity through routine vaccination and a successful preventive polio campaign. WHO supported Health Sector partners in sustaining emergency preparedness and response systems while strengthening health facility safety to improve readiness for public health threats. Persistent funding shortfalls remain a significant challenge, risking the continuity of health sector coordination, disease surveillance, emergency preparedness and response capacities, and the uninterrupted provision of essential health services.

title: World Vision Situation Report #3: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (17 October 2026)
content:
Synopsis:

Cambodia continues to experience the impacts of widespread flooding following prolonged heavy rainfall and seasonal weather disturbances. While floodwaters have begun to recede in several areas, affected families continue to face challenges, including food insecurity, damage to agricultural land, loss of income and disrupted livelihoods. Across World Vision’s operational areas, 171,448 people, including 33,669 children, have been affected.

World Vision International in Cambodia is implementing a 90-day humanitarian response across eight districts in Battambang and Banteay Meanchey provinces, providing food assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) support, child protection, nutrition and other essential assistance. To date, 1,227 households, representing 7,558 people, including 2,689 children, have received assistance, with particular attention to children and other vulnerable groups.

World Vision is working with government authorities, local communities and humanitarian partners to address the immediate needs of flood-affected families. The response prioritises access to essential supplies and services, the protection and well-being of vulnerable children, and support for families facing the ongoing impacts of flooding.

title: UNHCR Syria Factsheet - Livelihoods and Economic Inclusion - September 2026
content:
Syria is currently experiencing one of the largest return movements globally, with more than 1.8 million refugees and over 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) having returned, while millions more indicate they would consider returning if conditions improve.

Returnees in Syria face major barriers to livelihoods due to limited jobs, weak markets, and socio-economic challenges. As a result, many struggle to meet basic needs, making livelihoods support essential for sustainable reintegration.

UNHCR livelihoods and economic inclusion support is designed to contribute directly to UNHCR Syria’s overall strategy and overarching vision of enabling the safe, dignified, and voluntary return and reintegration of forcibly displaced persons by 2029.

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #218 - 19 October 2026
content:
Highlights

On 15 October, a refugee football team represented Romania at the UEFA Unity EURO Cup 2026 held in Florence, Italy, reaching the semi-finals of the European tournament organised in partnership with UNHCR. The tournament brought together 22 teams to celebrate inclusion through football. Romania’s team delivered an outstanding performance, winning five matches to secure a place in the semi-finals. The team was selected following the “Together on the Pitch” tournament held in Bucharest in June to mark World Refugee Day. The competition brought refugees from Ukraine and Afghanistan, authorities (GII and DGASMB) and civil society (CNRR) together, demonstrating how sport can build connections, foster mutual understanding and strengthen a sense of belonging. Romania’s participation, supported by the Romanian Football Federation and UNHCR, highlighted how football can break down barriers and promote inclusive communities.

title: South Sudan — Event Tracking Report #115 (01–30 September 2026)
content:
South Sudan is currently facing a severe humanitarian crisis characterized by extensive internal displacement. The underlying causes of these displacement dynamics are varied and include communal clashes, land disputes, insecurity, violence, and disasters. title: Afghanistan: Monthly Market Report Issue 76: September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

Markets remain functional, but higher global prices, regional uncertainty, trade disruptions and rising fuel costs continue to pressure domestic markets and household purchasing power.

MACROECONOMIC AND TRADE DEVELOPMENTS

Economic Growth and Household Welfare

Afghanistan’s economy continues to recover, supported by domestic demand and the return of large numbers of Afghans. However, rapid population growth limits improvements in per-capita income and living standards. Limited job creation, weak investment and women’s exclusion from labour force continue to constrain household incomes and broader economic potential. Widespread poverty, subsistence insecurity and limited access to basic services further weaken household resilience and the ability to absorb market shocks.

Trade Routes and Supply Network

Prolonged closures of key eastern and southern borders continue to disrupt established trade routes and alter Afghanistan’s traditional supply networks. Markets are increasingly relied on imports from Iran and Central Asia which requires longer delivery time and higher transport costs. These changes, combined with higher fuel prices, regional trade uncertainty and dependence on imported commodities, continue to put pressure on prices.

Exchange Rate

The Afghani appreciated by 1.2% in September to an average of AFN 64.6/USD, remaining 4.8% stronger yearon-year and 11% above its three-year average. Currency strength helps cushion imported inflation, but higher fuel costs, trade disruptions and elevated global prices limit the benefit.

Inflation (August 2026)

Headline inflation was 7.8% year-on-year in August, with food inflation at 8.0% and non-food inflation at 7.7%. Higher costs for food, housing, health and transport continue to weigh on household budgets.

Fuel and Logistics Costs

Diesel prices increased by 4.7% in September to AFN 80.3/litre, 14% above last year and 19% above the threeyear average, adding to transportation and market operating costs.

title: Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 21 (28 September - 04 October 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Central African Republic
content:
According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 4 October 2026, the country has reported 8,603 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including 4,148 confirmed deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate of 48.2 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 64 health zones across 7 provinces have reported at least 1 confirmed case. Ituri remains the epicentre, accounting for 75.0 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases nationwide.

Although transmission remains concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu, no new cases were reported in South Kivu, Bas- Uélé or South Ubangi during the reporting period, suggesting progress in limiting geographic expansion of the outbreak.

During the reporting period, the Ministry of Health reported 59 new confirmed cases and 34 confirmed deaths, including 23 community deaths. New cases were reported in North Kivu (33), Ituri (23), Haut-Uélé (2) and Tshopo (1). North Kivu accounted for 55.9 per cent of newly reported cases and continues to record a higher case fatality rate (58.1%) than the national average. Five patients recovered and were discharged during the reporting period

title: Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 22 (5 - 11 October 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Ethiopia
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 10 October 2026, the country had reported 8,978 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including 4,336 confirmed deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the start of the outbreak, 65 health zones across 7 provinces have reported at least 1 confirmed case. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for approximately 74 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases, while Ituri and North Kivu continue to account for most newly reported infections.

Encouraging improvements were observed in several epidemiological indicators during the reporting period. As of 10 October, the Ministry of Health reported only 64 new confirmed cases and 21 deaths, compared with 102 cases and 34 deaths reported one week earlier. Community deaths also declined to 13, while the national contact follow-up rate increased to 81 per cent.

Laboratory positivity declined from 25.9 per cent on 3 October to 14.4 per cent on 10 October, alongside declines in reported cases and deaths. However, only 143 of 232 validated suspected cases (61.6%) were transferred to treatment facilities, highlighting persistent challenges related to referral, treatment capacity and timely access to care. Community transmission remains active in Ituri, North Kivu and Haut-Uélé Provinces.

title: Islamic Republic of Iran: Humanitarian Update No. 09 | As of 30 September 2026
content:
This Humanitarian Update is produced by OCHA Regional Office for the Middle East and North Africa (ROMENA) on behalf of and in collaboration with UN agencies and humanitarian organisations. It covers the period from 1 to 30 September 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • In early September, strikes in four southern provinces reportedly killed 18 people and injured 142.
  • Household purchasing power deteriorated further amid rising food prices and currency depreciation.
  • School year started in person nationwide and temporarily online in Hormozgan Province.
  • The Ministry of Health reported supply shortages of 32 essential medicines, due to procurement challenges, import delays and transport disruptions.
  • Flooding reportedly damaged homes, infrastructure and farmland across Mazandaran, Gilan and Golestan provinces, killing one person, and leaving two missing. The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) provided assistance to 1,027 people.
  • Cash assistance reached 24,175 people in 6,166 households across five provinces, while an additional 618 highly vulnerable refugee households and 1,719 women and girls received targeted cash support to meet essential needs and protection-related expenses.

KEY FIGURES

3.4K+ Civilians killed (figure is for the period 28 February-14 September, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #11)

33K+ Civilians injured (figure is for the period 28 February-14 September, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #11)

149K+ Civilian units damaged (figure is for the period since 28 February as reported by the Iranian Red Crescent Society on 7 June 2026)

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The humanitarian response continued throughout September amid renewed hostilities early in the month in the southern provinces as well as flooding on 8-9 and 27-28 September in the northern provinces. On 1 September, damages to civilian buildings and critical infrastructure were reported in Sistan and Baluchestan, Hormozgan, Bushehr, Khuzestan and Kerman provinces, including Sirik Port, Jiroft Airport and the energy infrastructure in Assaluyeh. The Ministry of Health and Medical Education (MoHME) reported that 18 people were killed (including two women and one child) and 142 injured (including 61 women and 44 children), between 30 August and 2 September. Reports additionally indicated that a commercial vessel was impacted near Qeshm Island on 13 September and two fishing boats near Larak Island and Bandar Kargan on 14 September.

In northern Iran, heavy rainfall, storms and flooding reportedly damaged housing, public infrastructure and agricultural assets in Mazandaran and Gilan provinces on 8 and 9 September and in Golestan Province on 27 and 28 September. One person reportedly died and two went missing, while the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) provided emergency assistance to 1,027 people affected by these floods.

HUMANITARIAN IMPACT AND NEEDS

Health

Damage to health facilities and electricity infrastructure continued to disrupt essential health services and threaten cold-chain operations. Southern and southeastern provinces remained at risk of vector-borne and other communicable disease outbreaks, requiring strengthened surveillance and response capacity. The demand for mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) among healthcare workers continued to be high. On 22 September, MoHME reported supply shortages of 32 essential medicines, due to procurement challenges, import delays and transport disruptions. This has raised concerns over potential impacts on the availability of other medicines, diagnostic supplies and medical equipment, and the continuity of health service delivery.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

Communities in Hormozgan, Isfahan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces continued to face challenges in reliable access to safe drinking water due to damage sustained by water infrastructure and essential services during the July escalation. On 22 September, the Minister of Energy reported that since 28 February airstrikes had affected more than 2,000 water and electricity infrastructure sites nationwide. Priority needs include restoring access to safe water and expanding emergency water storage and treatment capacity.

Food Security

Food affordability deteriorated further amid high inflation, exchange-rate pressures and disruptions affecting the import of essential goods. Year-on-year food inflation reached 128.6 per cent in August (increasing by 0.5 per cent from July). The Iranian rial (IRR) continued to depreciate, with the exchange rate exceeding IRR 2.5 million per US dollar by 29 September, an 18 per cent decline in value relative to the previous month. The World Food Programme (WFP) reported in September that the costs for the standard food basket rose by 5.8 per cent in one month, reaching IRR 310.2 million (approximately US $173). Rising prices of nutrient-dense foods are increasing the risks of reduced dietary diversity. Priority needs include affordable, nutritious food and the protection of household purchasing power.

Protection

Protection risks continued to affect vulnerable groups, particularly women and girls facing challenges related to access to dignity items, menstrual hygiene supplies, and MHPSS. Refugees and other foreign nationals faced heightened protection risks as economic hardship intensified and documentation barriers, including the costs and administrative requirements associated with renewing residence documents, continued to limit access to food, housing, healthcare, education and legal stay. Priority needs included dignity items, MHPSS, regularization support, legal counselling, financial assistance, access to education and strengthened protection referral pathways.

Education

The 2026/27 academic year started on 23 September with in-person learning, except in Hormozgan Province, where all schools temporarily shifted to virtual and other non-face-to-face modalities for two weeks starting on 26 September. Several schools remained non-operational due to sustained damages or being used as collective shelters for temporarily relocated families. This has reduced the available learning space and increased pressure on functioning schools. Priority needs include rehabilitation of damaged and non-operational schools, expanding classroom capacity, supporting safe transport, and ensuring inclusive access to education among affected children.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

Low-income and vulnerable households continued to face difficulties meeting housing and basic needs. In Bandar Abbas (Hormozgan Province), 200 households remained temporarily sheltered in schools, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Priority needs include hygiene kits, food assistance, cash assistance and support for households in temporary accommodation.

Early Recovery

Conflict-related restrictions and damages continue to constrain fisheries in Hormozgan and Bushehr provinces. Affected fishing communities urgently need the restoration of fishing assets, facilities and post-harvest services to restart production, reduce losses and restore livelihoods.

RESPONSE

Health

The World Health Organization (WHO) delivered MHPSS services to more than 15,000 healthcare workers and donated 10,000 cholera rapid diagnostic tests to the Iranian Centre for Communicable Disease Control for use in Hormozgan, Khuzestan, Kerman and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces. The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) provided sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and MHPSS awareness-raising activities to 2,396 people (1,846 females and 550 males). Furthermore, 1,600 pregnant and lactating women received antenatal, postnatal, nutrition, and mental health awareness sessions through health providers. Among these beneficiary women, a total of 1,325 received cash assistance through the State Welfare Organization. UNFPA and MoHME also trained 248 social workers on cash and voucher assistance and basic SRH. The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) continued supporting inclusive public health services by financing health personnel through MoHME and advancing the procurement and delivery of essential medicines and medical equipment for facilities serving refugees and host communities. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) delivered five additional generators to MoHME as part of its ongoing support to essential health services and medical cold chains in 142 priority health facilities, bringing the total number of generators delivered to 46. In Kerman City, INTERSOS began rehabilitating two primary health facilities.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), in partnership with MoHME, installed 12 water tanks with a combined capacity of 105,000 litres, improving safe-water storage for more than 3,150 people and health facilities affected by intermittent or inadequate supply in Chabahar and Iranshahr counties (Sistan and Baluchestan Province). UNDP delivered 50 towable water tanks and 75 chlorination and disinfection units across Sistan and Baluchestan, Hormozgan and Isfahan provinces to strengthen emergency water-supply and treatment capacity. UNDP installed pumps and electrical cables at an affected pumping station in Chabahar, restoring the water-transmission system. UNHCR distributed more than 13,000 family hygiene kits to refugees and host communities across 10 provinces. Gaps in needs data, rising procurement costs, supply constraints and delays in the delivery of internationally sourced equipment continued to slow the implementation and assessment of WASH activities.

Food Security

WFP continued to deliver cash and food assistance to 35,611 highly vulnerable refugees across 20 settlements, including the delivery of bread and wheat flour for household baking.

Protection

UNFPA, through Relief International and local civil society organizations, provided integrated protection and MHPSS services in Hormozgan, Khuzestan and Tehran provinces. UNFPA reached 1,719 women and girls with cash assistance to purchase essential dignity and menstrual hygiene items and provided individual or group MHPSS services to 1,682 women and girls. Of those receiving MHPSS services, 267 also received cash assistance to help cover the costs of accessing five individual counselling sessions. A further 4,974 women and girls with disabilities across 11 provinces received menstrual-health awareness and cash assistance to address menstrual hygiene needs. UNHCR continued registration and verification of refugees and other foreign nationals and provided counselling, legal assistance, case management, MHPSS support and referrals.

Education

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) continued the rehabilitation and replacement of equipment for 42 schools across Kerman, Hormozgan and Tehran provinces, and delivered catch-up classes to 2,000 conflict-affected children in Tehran and Hormozgan provinces. NRC launched a learning and MHPSS programme at two school-based collective shelters for temporarily relocated families in Hormozgan Province targeting 200 children.

Early Recovery

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in coordination with the Ministry of Agriculture Jihad and the Iran Fisheries Organization started a project to support 300 affected fishing households in Hormozgan Province.

Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA)

WFP provided emergency cash assistance to 24,175 people in 6,166 households across Sistan and Baluchestan, Bushehr, Tehran, Hormozgan and Alborz provinces, targeting those affected by displacement, housing or livelihood losses, and conflict-related injury or death of a family member. UNHCR provided MPCA to 618 highly vulnerable refugee households to meet essential needs amid declining purchasing power.

title: Democratic Republic of Congo Flood 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRCD050), 16 October 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

01-05-2026

What happened, where and when?

On 7 April 2026, persistent heavy rainfall caused the Congo River to overflow its banks, resulting in severe flooding in Kindu City, Maniema Province. The communes of Alunguli, Kasuku and Mikelenge were among the most affected. The floods damaged and destroyed houses, contaminated water sources and sanitation facilities, disrupted livelihoods and displaced thousands of people. Approximately 62,000 people were affected, with more than 10,000 households impacted and over 10,416 people displaced, mainly seeking refuge with host families. The floods also affected agricultural fields, fishponds, local businesses, roads, schools and health infrastructure, increasing public health, protection and livelihood risks.

A few weeks later, on 1 May 2026, the city of Uvira in South Kivu Province was severely affected by heavy and persistent rainfall and the overflow of the Kalimabenge River, particularly in the densely populated and flood-prone neighbourhoods of Namianda and Kilibula in Kalundu commune. Rapid multisectoral assessments conducted between 1 and 5 May identied approximately 7,776 aected people (1,555 households). A total of 544 houses were damaged, including 13 completely destroyed and 172 partially destroyed, while at least 1,110 people were displaced and hosted by relatives or neighbouring families. Six deaths were also reported. The floods damaged or affected water and sanitation facilities, health structures, schools, roads, bridges, agricultural gardens and small businesses.

The two successive flooding events generated significant humanitarian needs across Maniema and South Kivu, particularly in shelter and household items, safe water and sanitation, health, protection and livelihoods. In response, the initial DREF operation launched following the Kindu oods was subsequently scaled up to include Uvira and other aected areas of South Kivu. The operation now targets 15,600 people (2,250 households), including 1,400 households in Kindu and 850 households in Uvira and other affected areas of South Kivu, through integrated interventions covering Health, WASH, Shelter/AME, Multipurpose Cash Assistance, PGI and CEA.

Following the floods that affected Kindu, Maniema, and Uvira, South Kivu, the DREF response has progressed from the initial emergency phase towards the delivery of essential assistance to affected households. In Uvira, the distribution of essential household items (AME) to the 850 targeted households has been completed. In Kindu, due to access challenges caused by poor road conditions, the Red Cross is currently receiving the essential household items (EHI), with distribution to the targeted households planned for the week of 28 September.

At present, affected households in both locations continue to face challenges related to damaged or destroyed Houses , access to safe water and sanitation, and displacement, including families staying with host households or living in precarious conditions. The remaining response activities therefore focus on nalizing the pending assistance in Kindu and completing the planned activities.

title: Sri Lanka Dengue Outbreak 2026 - DREF Operational Update (MDRLK024), 16 October 2026
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

02-06-2026

What happened, where and when?

Heavy rains, the southwest monsoon, and widespread flooding from mid-May 2026 led to a major dengue outbreak in Sri Lanka. Dengue cases increased from 25,082 in early May to 101,744 by October, representing almost a 600 per cent increase compared with the same period last year. The outbreak peaked in July 2026, when 29,964 cases were reported. This July peak was consistent with Sri Lanka’s usual post-monsoon pattern, when accumulated rainwater creates favourable breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes.

As of midnight on 6 October 2026, Sri Lanka’s National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU) had reported 101,744 dengue cases and 78 deaths nationwide, with a case fatality rate (CFR) of 0.076 per cent. The Western Province accounted for more than half of all reported cases, with 52,845 cases, mainly in Gampaha (21,520) and Colombo (19,879) districts. The Southern Province reported 14,463 cases (14.21 per cent), while the Central Province reported 9,580 cases (9.41 per cent), making them the next most affected regions. Dengue cases peaked in July at 29,964, followed by June with 21,533 cases and August with 10,155 cases, before declining significantly in September to 5,230 cases. As of epidemiological week 37, 37 Medical Officer of Health (MOH) areas remained classified as high-risk, with an average midnight census of 451. The NDCU identified seven provinces as high-risk, citing continued transmission associated with rainy conditions favourable to mosquito breeding.

Between August and the end of September, the geographic distribution of dengue cases shifted. Gampaha surpassed Colombo to become the most affected district, while the Western Province’s share of reported cases decreased slightly to approximately 52.6–52.8 per cent. Meanwhile, the Southern Province’s share increased to around 15.6–15.7 per cent, indicating a redistribution of cases rather than a uniform decline across the country. Overall, more than half of all dengue cases reported in 2026 were concentrated in the Western Province, consistent with historical patterns. Gampaha and Colombo districts continued to report the highest case numbers, underscoring the persistent challenge of vector control in densely populated areas. As of week 37, 36 Medical Officer of Health (MOH) areas remained classified as high-risk.

The decline in cases observed in August is likely associated with the rapid rollout of the national “Stop Dengue Now” programme. SLRCS supported this effort through the DREF, working closely with MOH and NDCU officials at both Head Office and district levels. These efforts increased community awareness and strengthened targeted surveillance in high-risk areas. The campaign covered 14 districts and 72 Medical Officer of Health divisions and included enforcement measures, such as issuing “red notices” to properties where mosquito breeding sites were identified.
A second seasonal increase related to the northeast monsoon remains possible. The 2026 case fatality rate of 0.076 per cent reflects a long-term downward trend. Over the past two decades, Sri Lanka has reduced its dengue CFR, and maintaining a low fatality rate with more than 100,000 reported cases reflects the continued capacity of the health system to manage severe dengue cases. The CFR of 0.076 per cent is based on 78 reported deaths among 101,744 reported cases.

Gampaha and Colombo remained the main transmission centres, largely due to high population density and urban infrastructure, while Kandy was the most affected district outside the Western Province. Other districts with continued transmission included Matara, Kalutara, Galle, and Ratnapura. A notable development occurred in mid-July, when a cluster of 71 cases, including five hospitalizations, was identified among University of Colombo students. The University of Moratuwa and the University of the Visual and Performing Arts temporarily closed their campuses, marking the first institutional clusters recorded during this outbreak.

title: Panama Earthquake 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRPA023)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

09-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

On October 9, 2026, at 12:56 p.m. (local time), a magnitude 7.7 Mw earthquake affected Panama. According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the epicenter was located approximately 12 km west-southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, Herrera province, at a depth of 12.6 km, generating strong seismic movements perceived in much of the national territory and in areas of neighboring countries (1). The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama initially reported the event with a magnitude of 7.2 and a depth of 20 km, approximately 45 km west of Tonosí, Los Santos province (8).

After the main earthquake, an intense seismic sequence was recorded, with numerous events of magnitude greater than 5.0. According to the records of the Institute of Geosciences, on October 9 there were movements of magnitude 6.9 east of Coiba and 6.6 northwest of Tonosí. On October 12, another movement of magnitude 6.4 was recorded northeast of Coiba, while seismic activity continued on October 13 (8). The persistence of the aftershocks has increased the concern of the population, generated uncertainty about the safety of the affected structures and hindered the work of assessing damage and the continuity of some essential services. Panamanian Red Cross teams reported episodes of fainting, emotional crises and convulsions in students from Bocas del Toro, as well as families who remained outdoors and in need of psychological first aid in different locations (4).

According to SINAPROC's Official Statement No. 12, dated October 14, 2026, damage assessments and needs analysis identified 4,045 affected families, equivalent to 13,623 people. Of these, 879 families reported total loss of their homes, 926 moderate damage, 1,577 partial damage, and 663 minor or minor damage. The damage also includes educational and health infrastructure, public buildings, roads, bridges, and water supply systems. Assessments continue in the affected provinces and the figures remain subject to verification.

The earthquake had a particular impact on coastal communities on the Azuero Peninsula. In Isla Cañas, Los Santos province, approximately 300 people were evacuated preventively during the first hours after the earthquake, according to initial reports from the Panamanian Red Cross (4). As of October 12, OCHA reported that 193 displaced people from Isla Cañas remained in three makeshift accommodation points in Cañas (5). Subsequently, SINAPROC's balance sheet of October 14 identified 13 shelters set up in Los Santos, with 644 people housed. At the national level, 45 shelters were reported with 3,696 people housed, evidencing the need for temporary accommodation and humanitarian assistance for families who cannot safely return to their homes (9).

The impact on health infrastructure has led to interruptions in the provision of services and preventive evacuations of patients. According to SINAPROC's Official Statement No. 12, as of October 14, 22 health centers in Veraguas, four hospitals in Los Santos, three hospitals in Herrera, and two hospitals in Coclé were affected, in addition to damage to health facilities in other provinces (9). At the Santo Tomás Hospital, more than 40 patients were preventively evacuated from the old maternity ward due to structural damage (3, 5). The Panamanian Red Cross reports also document hospital evacuations, patient transfers, and the provision of temporary care spaces (4). These effects represent risks for the continuity of health services, particularly for the elderly, patients with chronic diseases, and people with mobility difficulties or access to health facilities.

Access to drinking water has also been affected by damage to supply systems. SINAPROC reported the persistence of interruptions in the supply of water, electricity, and telecommunications in Veraguas, as well as damage to storage tanks and fissures in a water treatment plant in Chiriquí (9). These conditions can temporarily compromise families' access to safe water, especially in communities with access restrictions and interrupted services. As part of the response, as of October 12, authorities had reported the transfer of 240 tons of water to supply communities and hospitals (2).

As a response measure, the national authorities activated emergency coordination and response mechanisms to support damage and needs assessments in the affected areas. On October 10, 2026, the Government of Panama declared a State of National Emergency through Cabinet Resolution No. 108, with the purpose of facilitating resource mobilization and response actions (7). The Panamanian Red Cross mobilized its local committees and response teams to provide first aid, pre-hospital care, psychological first aid, support for hospital evacuations, and humanitarian assistance, in coordination with SINAPROC, the Ministry of Health, and other competent institutions (4).

Due to the magnitude of the event, its relatively shallow depth, and the persistence of aftershocks, many communities remain under observation while sectoral assessments are completed. Uncertainty about the stability of some structures, coupled with the risk of new seismic movements, has led to preventive evacuations and the temporary stay of families outside their homes. The damage to homes, health facilities, water supply systems, educational centers, and road infrastructure shows humanitarian needs related to temporary housing, access to basic services, assistance to cover essential needs, continuity of health care, and mental health and psychosocial support. The figures remain preliminary and may be modified as the assessments of the authorities and the Panamanian Red Cross progress (5, 9).

title: DTM Sudan Displacement and Return Snapshot - Update 10 (18 October 2026)
content:
The Sudan Displacement and Return Snapshot includes information on internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees, based on data from over 13,000 locations, 185 localities, and all 18 states in Sudan.

Main Findings

  • An estimated 8,585,611 internally displaced persons (IDPs) were recorded across all 18 states.
  • An estimated 5,273,334 returned individuals were recorded across nine states.
  • Eighty-two per cent of returnees moved back from internal displacement, while 18 per cent returned from abroad.
  • Approximately half of IDPs (56%) and returnees (50%) were children under 18 years old.

Key Trends

  • The number of IDPs decreased by 26 per cent compared to the highest-recorded displaced population, but increased slightly by one per cent compared to the previous month (<1%).
  • The number of returnees increased by two per cent compared to the previous month.

For further information, see the DTM Methodological Note and the DTM Sudan Interactive Dashboard.

title: West and Central Africa — Irregular Migration Routes to Europe (January - June 2026)
content:
This document presents the situation of irregular arrivals to Europe, from January 2021 to June 2026, and fatalities on migration routes to Europe, focusing on movements departing from West and Central Africa (WCA). Data on registered arrivals to Europe by sea and by land are based on quarterly data from national authorities and compiled by IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM). Data on migrant fatalities is collected daily by IOM’s Missing Migrants Project from the media, eyewitnesses, NGOs, UN agencies, and governments. As documenting migrant deaths and disappearances is challenging, these figures should be considered as minimum estimates.

Between 2021 and June 2026, more than 980,000 migrants arrived irregularly in Italy, Spain, Greece, Malta, and Cyprus by sea and land, of which 251,721 were nationals from West and Central Africa. During the first semester of 2026, the number of arrivals in Europe decreased by 15 per cent, compared to the same period in 2021 when 51,531 migrants arrived irregularly. Between January and June 2026, 6,629 nationals of West and Central Africa arrived in Europe, representing 15 per cent of all arrivals.

title: Situation Update No. 5: Escalation of hostilities and displacement across Yemen Update No. 5 | As of 15 October 2026 | Reporting period: 1 August – 15 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • A total of 231,991 people (38,664 households) have been displaced by conflict between 1 August and 14 October 2026. DTM figures, which also serve as the alert baseline for the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM), show that 99 per cent of this displacement was recorded from 31 August onwards, after hostilities intensified. Three quarters of the displaced fled from Ta’iz governorate. Ta’iz hosts 52 per cent of the displaced, followed by Lahj (23%), Aden (13%) and Abyan (5%).
  • Displacement continues as fighting moves inland and towards Ta’iz City. In early October, fighting in the Al-Turba area of Ta’iz displaced about 4,500 households in three days, and DTM recorded a further 44,202 newly displaced people (7,367 households) between 4 and 14 October. Fighting near existing sites is forcing already displaced families to flee again. With main roads closed, fewer families are able to reach Lahj and Aden, and further displacement towards Ta’iz City is likely if fighting continues.
  • Civilian casualties continue to rise, with children among the most affected. OHCHR verified 94 incidents during the reporting period that caused 233 civilian casualties: 55 people killed and 178 injured. Children account for more than a third of all casualties, with 27 children killed and 57 injured.
  • 152,222 IDPs (21,746 households) have been reached with first-line RRM assistance, equivalent to 56 per cent of displaced households. Partners have also provided emergency cash to 13,243 households, food assistance to 12,594 RRM-verified households and water, sanitation and hygiene support to 9,391 households. They have reached more than 38,500 IDPs with health services and screened 67,468 children and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls for malnutrition.
  • Assistance is not keeping pace with needs. Four in ten verified households have yet to receive emergency food assistance, and most of those reached have received only the first of three planned cycles. Fewer than one in ten households in need of shelter support have been reached, and about a quarter of those in need of WASH assistance. The displacement is deepening an already severe crisis: 84 per cent of verified displaced households are in districts classified in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency).
  • Ta’iz City is increasingly cut off, and essential services are under severe strain. Since early October, road closures have disrupted humanitarian and commercial supplies. Water production in the city has fallen by about half, fuel and cooking gas are scarce, food prices have risen by about 50 per cent, and partners have no food baskets left inside the city. Hospitals report medicines, oxygen and fuel close to depletion. Supplies held in Aden and Al-Turba cannot reach the city.
  • Displacement is raising the risk of disease spread, particularly cholera. Families are arriving in overcrowded sites amid an ongoing cholera outbreak, often in districts where water and sanitation services were already among the weakest in the country. Cholera alerts from displacement sites are increasing, and partners are expanding treatment centres, surveillance and safe water services.
  • Safe and sustained humanitarian access is urgently needed. Since 8 October, humanitarian partners have been unable to move between Ta’iz City and the southern districts. Insecurity, road closures and telecommunications outages continue to delay assistance and the registration of newly displaced families. Partners remain present and ready to scale up, but their ability to do so depends on safe access for supplies, patients and aid workers.

title: Monthly Report on the Implementation of Epidemic Intelligence in the Americas - Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) - August 2026
content:
I. Regional Epidemic Intelligence Activity

A. Detection of early warning flags

At the regional level, the Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) of the PAHO Health Emergencies Department (PHE) operates through the continuous epidemic intelligence phases, scanning multiple sources to identify Early warning flags (information indicating a potential acute public health risk) in the Americas Region.

Early warning flags are triaged to identify if these are signals requiring verification in close coordination with Member States3. Once verified, a signal becomes an event. PAHO conducts risk assessments and continuously monitors these events, including epidemiological and geospatial analysis, while facilitating information exchange with Member States and partners and producing actionable intelligence and technical support to guide timely public health decisions and response across the Americas.

Between 1 to 31 August 2026, a total of 403,850 reports of relevant information related to acute public health events in the Americas Region were scanned by PHE/HIM team. Of these, 154 were classified as early warning flags (Figure 1) and published in the public dashboard available at: https://shiny.paho-phe.org/ems/

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Lebanon Crisis (9 September - 8 October 2026)
content:
The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains volatile, with continued hostilities, reported violations of International Humanitarian Law and restricted humanitarian access, particularly in southern Lebanon. The ongoing movement restrictions along the “Yellow Line” continue to constrain humanitarian operations and impede the safe return of displaced populations. As of 29 September, approximately 330,000 people remained internally displaced, while ongoing insecurity, damaged infrastructure and limited access to essential services continue to hinder recovery.

Since the onset of the crisis, UNFPA has reached nearly 54,900 women and girls with sexual and reproductive health services and over 51,200 people with gender-based violence prevention and response activities. This includes supporting 5,000 women to access facility-based deliveries and distributing over 33,200 dignity kits to women and girls.

Severe funding shortages threaten the continuity of life-saving maternal health services, with financial support for institutional deliveries at risk of disruption as early as October. UNFPA continues to work with government authorities and partners to sustain essential reproductive health and protection services for displaced populations, returnees and vulnerable host communities.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 05 (as of 16 October 2026, 12:30)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • Following the magnitude 7.5 earthquake on 9 October, the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) reports 13,623 people affected, from 4,045 families. As of 16 October, it had assessed 5,807 homes, where 20,581 people live. Some 3,696 people remain in 46 shelters, mostly in Mariato (Veraguas), and many other families are staying with relatives or sleeping outdoors.
  • The Government has assisted 15,139 people from 4,485 families. Crews have started building the first homes in Las Tablas, Soná and Penonomé, and the Government will rebuild Tonosí Hospital and five health centres.
  • Classes remain suspended at public schools while the Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) inspects the 619 affected schools. Of these, 35 collapsed, affecting 3,031 students.
  • The bridge over the Oria River has reopened, but rain and landslides still limit access to some communities, and the sites housing displaced families still have gaps in water, sanitation and protection.
  • UN agencies and their partners have mobilized shelter items, mobile storage units and assistance with health, water and protection, among other areas, to back the Government-led response.

title: Humanitarian Response Forum (HRF) - Situation Report No. 2 – Floods in Cambodia (2026)
content:
As of 05 October 2026, flooding has affected 109,985 families across 10 provinces, with 9,027 families evacuated, 88,811 houses affected, 313 schools impacted, and over 209,867 hectares of agricultural land affected. While floodwaters are gradually receding in many areas, affected communities continue to face challenges related to damaged infrastructure, disrupted services, and impacts on livelihoods.

Key highlights include:

  • Flooding remains moderate in scale, with the monsoon season forecast to end in the third week of October.
  • Water levels at monitoring stations across Cambodia are currently below flood alarm levels and are expected to continue receding.
  • Localized heavy rainfall and flash flood risks remain possible, particularly in northwestern provinces.
  • The National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM), provincial authorities, and humanitarian partners continue to monitor the situation and support affected communities.
  • Ongoing response efforts include cash assistance, food and non-food item distributions, WASH support, education interventions, and health response activities in affected provinces.

title: occupied Palestinian territory (oPt) Situation Analysis: [28/9/2026] - [4/10/2026]
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire Humanitarian Situation Report Quarter 3, 1 July to 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of August 2026, an estimated 96,153 refugees and asylum seekers, including 45,544 children, have fled to northern Côte d’Ivoire due to the worsening security situation in Burkina Faso and Mali. Since the beginning of 2026, 13,367 new arrivals have been registered.
  • By epidemiological week 38 of 2026, Côte d’Ivoire had reported 26 confirmed yellow fever cases and 10 deaths across nine health districts in seven regions.
  • Côte d’Ivoire continues to face the mpox outbreak declared on 1 July 2024. To date, 1,160 suspected cases have been identified, including 216 reported in 2026. Of these, 276 cases have been confirmed across 48 health districts, with three deaths reported among the confirmed cases.
  • During the third quarter of 2026, UNICEF continued to work closely with the Government of Côte d’Ivoire to meet humanitarian needs, including through the following interventions:
    • 37,644 children under five were screened for wasting, of whom 652 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition received treatment.
    • 18,005 children were vaccinated against measles in the Tchologo and Bounkani regions, which host the majority of refugees and asylum seekers.
    • 2,862 people, including 1,407 children, gained access to safe drinking water.
    • With UNICEF support, 720 children were enrolled in community-based preschool programmes in the two northern regions affected by the refugee influx.
    • A total of 23 children received individual case management services to strengthen their protection and access to appropriate support services.

title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No. 7, 13 October 2026
content:
