title: Dooplaya District Situation Update: Challenges related to militarisation, displacement, air strikes, shelling, education, travel restrictions, drug issues, and livelihoods in Kaw T’Ree and Ra M’Tee Townships (January to May 2026)
content:
This Situation Update covers events occurring in Kaw T’Ree (Kawkareik) and Ra M’Tee (Myawaddy) townships, Dooplaya District, during the period between January and May 2026, including challenges related to militarisation, displacement, air strikes, shelling, education, travel restrictions, drug issues, and livelihoods. From January to March 2026, many displaced people from Maw Ma, Kaw Nweh, and Aaw Hpa Hpa Doh village tracts in Kaw T’Ree Township were unable to return to their villages because the Burma Army often carried out drone strikes, air strikes, and shelling. On 29 April 2026, Burma Army drone strikes killed two villagers and injured two others in Aa--- village, Kaw Nweh village tract. In Ra M’Tee Township, from January to March 2026, many villagers had to flee due to the escalation of fighting and air strikes. On 13 April 2026, the Burma Army dropped 500-pound bombs and fired 120 mm mortar shells into Ab--- village, Maw Hkee village tract, Ra M’Tee Township, burning almost all the houses. Villagers also faced challenges travelling to Kaw T’Ree Town, Kaw T’Ree Township, as they could not travel as usual and had to avoid the main road due to security risks. Regarding education in Kaw T’Ree and Ra M’Tee townships, some students were able to study in schools, while others had to study in displacement sites. Township leaders and police tried to ban drugs and provided drug awareness to the community, but drug use remained a problem in both townships.[1]

Military activities and displacement in Kaw T’Ree Township

From January to March 2026, the [Burma] military[2] continued operating in Kaw T’Ree (Kawkareik) Township, Dooplaya District, with their aircraft dropping bombs, and [their forces conducting] shelling. The Burma Army conducted shelling [approximately] once every two days, so the villagers who lived close to the main road [Asian Highway[3]] were unable to return to their villages [due to security risks]. Some villagers from the following villages had fled since the [2021] military coup[4]:

  • In Maw Ma village tract,[5] Kaw T’Ree Township: Ac--- village, Ad--- village, and Ae--- village.
  • In Kaw Nweh village tract, Kaw T’Ree Township: Af--- village, Ag--- village, Aa--- village, Ah--- village, and Ai--- village.
  • In Aaw Hpa Hpa Doh village tract, Kaw T’Ree Township: Aj--- village and Ak--- village.

As the fighting continued, more villagers had to flee in 2026. Villagers from the villages mentioned above were unable to return to their villages because the Burma Army carried out drone strikes, air strikes, and shelling [approximately] once every two or three days. In some villages, particularly Af--- village, most houses were damaged and burned by the air strikes and shelling. Only a few houses were left, and the village became the forest [Af--- village had become overgrown like a forest].

In the other villages, villagers were able to return temporarily to check their homes. However, they did not dare to stay or sleep in the village because armed conflict had occurred in the area. The villagers fled to villages that were located far from the main road.

On 29 April 2026, at 9:25 pm, a Burma Army drone dropped three 120 mm mortar shells into Bn--- village, Aaw Hpa Hpa Doh village tract, killing two villagers and injuring two others. Saw[6] A--- (10 years old) and Saw B--- (34 years old) were killed immediately. Saw C--- (8 years old) and Naw[7] D--- (3 years old) were injured. The two injured villagers were sent to a clinic, but I [the KHRG researcher] do not know which clinic. The place that the Burma Army bombed was not where fighting was taking place. Fighting had occurred in the past, but there had been no fighting for one to two months, so some villagers returned to check their houses [and were in the village when the attack occurred]. I [the KHRG researcher] received this information from a local villager. [Detailed information of the villager who provided the information is undisclosed for security reasons.]

Military activities and displacement in Ra M’Tee Township

In Ra M’Tee (Myawaddy) Township,[8] Dooplaya District, there are many armed groups, and fighting has intensified. Among those armed groups, some work with the Burma Army, some transport the Burma Army soldiers, and some do business. From January to March 2026, in Ra M’Tee Township, villagers living in areas where the Burma Army operated could not live peacefully in their villages. They always lived in fear because the Burma Army often carried out air strikes and shelling.

In Noh Poe village tract, Ra M’Tee Township, villagers from the following villages had to flee: Al--- village, Am--- village, An--- village, Ao--- village, Ap--- village, and Aq--- village. These villagers fled to mountainous areas, and some fled to other villages.

In P’Loo village tract, Ra M’Tee Township, villagers from the following villages had to flee: Ar--- village, As--- village, At--- village, Au--- village, Av--- village, Aw--- village, Ax--- village, Ay--- village, and Az--- village. The villagers fled to Ba--- [camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs)], P’Loo village tract, and some fled to Thailand.

[In 2026,] the Burma Army carried out drone strikes in Bb--- village and Ba--- village in P’Loo village tract. The villagers from these villages [including some who had previously fled to Ba--- village] had to flee to Bc--- and Bd--- villages in Thay Baw Boh village tract, Ra M’Tee Township, while some fled to other areas. According to a local villager in Bd--- village, more than 1,000 people fled to Bd--- village in March 2026.

Villagers from Ab--- village, Maw Hkee village tract, Ra M’Tee Township, had to flee [due to fighting and air strikes]. Villagers from Ab--- village fled on 1 April 2026, when the Karen army combined forces [Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA)[9] and People’s Defence Force (PDF)[10]] attacked Ghaw Lay strategic army camp. This army camp is located [distance censored for security] away from the village. The villagers were able to return to the village temporarily to check their houses.

On 13 April 2026, fighting intensified, and Burma Army aircraft dropped 500-pound bombs [on Ab--- village, which villagers believed was intentional,] while its forces fired 120 mm mortar shells into Ab--- village, burning almost all of the houses. Only a few houses were left. [Villagers believed that] the Burma Army may have targeted [Ab--- village] because they believed that [KNLA and PDF] leaders were staying there when the combined forces attacked [the Burma Army camp]. Actually, there were no soldiers staying in the village. However, occasionally soldiers passed through the village. [Later,] on 13 May 2026, it rained a lot, but some villagers from Ab--- village did not have a house, so they had to stay in huts and corn storage buildings.

Travel challenges in Kaw T’Ree Township

The villagers [from Bf--- and Bg--- villages in Kya Ka Wa village tract, Kaw T’Ree Township] had to go to Kaw T’Ree Town, Kaw T’Ree Township, to buy food. Some people [who had previously fled] had returned to stay in Kaw T’Ree Town, and some shops had reopened [after closing due to fighting, shelling, and air strikes]. Those who were not afraid went there to buy food. However, people still could not travel on the road as usual [due to security concerns]. If the villagers from Bf--- village and Bg--- village wanted to go to Kaw T’Ree Town to buy food, they had to avoid the main road and instead travel from Bh--- village in Ai Baing village tract, Kaw T’Ree Township, to Bi--- village in Hlaing Wa village tract, Kaw T’Ree Township, and then enter Kaw T’Ree Town. It was a bit easier for local people who understoond the situation to travel [to navigate travel restrictions].

Education challenges in Kaw T’Ree and Ra M’Tee Township

Regarding education, from 2025 to 2026, some students were able to study at school until the end of the school year. In some village tracts, students studied in displacement sites in the forest. Although there were many challenges, schools could [stay] open because the local authorities were well prepared to deal with the problems. Every school managed to complete the school year even though the students were afraid of aircraft.

There is a school in Bj--- IDP camp, Kaw T’Ree Township, for children to study at. In the past two years, this school received support from a nonprofit organisation [name censored for security] and the Karen Education and Culture Department (KECD).[11] The school principal, Naw E---, explained to KHRG that the school faced many challenges because it was a school for displaced villagers in Bj--- IDP camp. Displaced villagers in the camp relied on support from others. This year, in 2026 [as of May], the school had not received any support, so the students’ parents will have to put more effort into covering the costs themselves. Last year, in 2025, this school did not offer Grade 7. However, some students were facing challenges in finding another place to continue their studies, so the school decided to offer Grade 7 this year. In March 2026, there was funding available for the school through another organisation, but because the application was submitted late, the school did not receive the support. The school had already been built, but the chairs and other materials were still needed. The school also needed containers to store drinking water and water for the toilets.

Drug issues in Kaw T’Ree and Ra M’Tee Township

In Kaw T’Ree and Ra M’Tee townships, drug issues were not different from other townships. Township leaders and police tried to ban drugs, but they did not disappear. The police [Karen National Police Force (KNPF)[12]] also tried to provide drug awareness in the community, and organisations tried to provide awareness to young people, but people were still using drugs.

Livelihoods

In Ra M’Tee Township, nowadays [during the reporting period], there were many different livelihood activities. The main occupation of most local people was growing corn and beans. There was also some lowland farming and hill farming. However, some people may not have been able to do farming, hill farming, corn farming, and bean farming [due to security concerns]. People engaged in livelihood activities according to their individual abilities. There were many ways to make a living, including doing different kinds of business. These kinds of jobs may be for educated people.

title: UNHCR Tanzania Operational Update - September 2026
content:
As of 30 September 2026, Tanzania hosts 132,775 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from the DRC and Burundi. Of these, 91,480 live in Nyarugusu Camp, while 42,441 (mostly Burundian) refugees live in Dar es Salaam, urban areas, villages, and old settlements in Kigoma, Katavi, and Tabora regions.

In collaboration with the Government, UNHCR and partners have been receiving asylum seekers fleeing violent clashes in the DRC. In September 2026, a total of 97 new arrivals were received in Tanzania, bringing the total number of arrivals to 4,857 since renewed violence in eastern DRC in January 2025.

UNHCR continues to provide protection and assistance to the people we serve. Some services, including primary health care and education, are also extended to the host community. In addition, UNHCR seeks durable solutions for refugees.

title: WHO Sudan: Sudan Health Spotlight - September 2026
content:
Monthly highlights

• Cholera cases continued to decline overall, but transmission remains a concern, with suspected cases still being reported in some localities. Since 15 May 2026, a cumulative 3131 cases and 264 deaths have been reported, corresponding to an overall CFR of 8.0%.

• Oral cholera vaccination campaigns achieved high coverage in priority areas. The reactive campaign in Al Fula, An Nuhud and Wad Bandah vaccinated 675 295 people, while second-round campaigns reached 156 983 people in Kas and 83 100 people in Tawila. • WHO provided extended technical, operational and capacity-strengthening assistance to 17 stabilization centres across seven states, alongside treatment supplies, nutrition surveillance support and monitoring of services for displaced communities.

• The first high-level technical mission to Darfur, led by Dr Abdinasir Abubakar, WHO Representative in Sudan, together with the Health Cluster Coordinator and technical teams, visited four states across the region. The mission identified critical health needs and service gaps, providing evidence to inform priorities and strengthen the health response.

• Maintained effective early-warning surveillance and rapid outbreak-response capacities to enable timely detection and control of multiple disease outbreaks nationwide

title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 15 to 21 October 2026
content:
Review Summary:

• Heavy rains fell over Bay, Gedo, Mudug, Hiraan and parts of Somaliland during 6–12 October. Baidoa recorded 146.5 mm in 4 days, Bardheere 115.5 mm, Qansax Dheere 107.6 mm, Sheikh 100 mm and Hargeisa 86 mm in a single day.

• By 12 October, 16 stations had already exceeded their October normal, including Baidoa (220.0 mm, 163%), Bardheere (208.5 mm, 255%), Galkacyo (124.0 mm, 260%) and Hargeisa (86.0 mm, 318%).

• Satellite estimates (ARC2) show 100–500 mm over central and southern Somalia and the Somali region of Ethiopia since 1 October, more than four to six times the normal for the period.

• Jowhar crossed its moderate flood-risk level on 12 October and its high flood-risk level on 13 October. Dollow peaked 4 cm below moderate on 12 October before falling sharply.

• Communities in Galgaduud, Mudug, Sanaag and Dollow continued to report drought, heat and livestock losses during 1–7 October, while callers in Bay, Lower Shabelle and Kismayo reported good rain and crop planting.

Forecast Highlight:

• Light to moderate rains are expected over central and north-eastern Somalia. Moderate rainfall of 50–100 mm is forecast over most of Xarardheere and Burtinle districts and about half of Jariiban district, with localized heavy rainfall of 100–150 mm near the coast in Xarardheere Light rainfall of 10–30 mm is expected over Hiraan and Middle Shabelle

• Light rains are expected over most parts of the Juba River catchment whereas light to moderate rains are likely over Shabelle River catchment

• Jowhar remains above its high flood-risk level (5.36 m, 14 cm below bankfull). A new rise is moving downstream from Deefow (+0.76 m today) and Belet Weyne (+0.50 m today) and is expected to reach Jowhar during the week. Breakage flooding between Jowhar and Balcad is likely to continue

• The 10-day CHIRPS-GEFS forecast (14–24 October) indicates heavy rainfall of 100–150 mm over Bulo Burto, Jalalaqsi and Jowhar districts, an upside flood risk for Jowhar and Balcad towards 22–24 October

• Dry and hot conditions are forecast over most parts of Jubaland with very high maximum temperatures of 40–45°C over parts of Middle Juba, Lower Juba and Sablaale

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #7 (Reporting period: 3 – 11 October 2026 | Issued: 13 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

Situation

• The daily casualty toll has doubled. The HEOC recorded 2,007 new casualties between 3 and 11 October (1,684 injured, 323 killed), 223 a day against 114 in the previous period. That brings the total since 6 August to 7,173, including 1,282 deaths. Lahj is now the heaviest and deadliest front (553 casualties, 110 killed), followed by Taiz (518) and Marib (489). One in five casualties in Lahj and Marib died.

• Taiz city is being cut off and its hospitals are running out. Fighting has reached the urban districts where the main referral hospitals stand, and road closures are blocking resupply. Twelve hospitals have about four days of fuel and need 135,720 litres a month, oxygen falls 91 units a day short, 115 of 127 essential medicines are at a week’s stock or less, and 14 surgical consumables are at zero. 1,110 dialysis patients, 192 intensive care patients and 154 newborns in incubators depend on uninterrupted power and oxygen.

• Displacement has passed 200,000 people. IOM counts 201,217 displaced people in ten governorates, up from about 76,000 in mid-September. Taiz hosts 57%.

• Cholera continues to climb. Weekly suspected cases rose from 221 in week 36 to 683 in week 40, and 89% of rapid tests were positive. Culture-confirmed cases in the Al-Abr camps, where more than 4,000 displaced families need urgent health assistance, point to critical WASH gaps.

• Therapeutic food has run out. Seven West Coast facilities had no RUTF on 6 October, while screening of displaced children shows high acute malnutrition.

Response

• The response is now at Scenario 3 tempo and scale. MoPHP, WHO and Health Cluster partners have updated the Joint National Response Plan for Scenario 3, a comprehensive 90-day plan for October–December 2026 costed at US$ 31 million. It covers six response pillars: pre-hospital care and referral; surgical, critical and rehabilitative care; health for displaced populations; outbreak response; continuity of essential services; and coordination and enablers.

• Trauma and essential health supplies arrived in Aden. WHO received 233 TESK modules and 20 IEHK units (9.2 MT), which are being dispatched to targeted hospitals. The supplies can treat about 600 severe injuries and about 1,200 minor injuries and provide essential health care for up to 40,000 people, including displaced communities, for three months.

• Cholera response: . MSF and Save the Children are supporting the centre at Ibn Khaldoun Hospital in Lahj. WHO will be supporting 9 diarrhoea treatment centres in Abyan (4), Al-Dhale’e (3), Aden (1) and Taiz (1). Support covers operational costs, WASH, IV fluids, medicines and supplies for an initial month.

• Health services for displaced people: 18 Health Cluster partners have reached more than 36,700 displaced people in 35 districts of eight governorates. They work through 36 mobile teams and temporary health points and continue to support 47 fixed health facilities.

Gaps and key asks

• Negotiate humanitarian access to Taiz: secure safe, sustained access and alternative supply routes so that fuel, oxygen and medicines can reach Taiz hospitals and patients and health workers can move safely, to avert a humanitarian catastrophe.

• Strengthen pre-hospital care on the front lines: equip and staff the trauma stabilization points without partner support and procure and repair ambulances for safe referral.

• Sustain trauma and critical care in hospitals: resupply receiving hospitals in Lahj, Marib and Aden with trauma supplies, fuel and oxygen, and support specialized care teams to work 24/7.

• Contain cholera and reach displaced families: make the treatment centres operational, scale up WASH in IDP sites, add mobile capacity for Al-Abr and Taiz, and restore the therapeutic food pipeline.

• Fund the Joint Response Plan: WHO has secured US$ 3.8 million of the US$ 31 million needed, leaving a gap of US$ 27.2 million (88%). Flexible funding is urgently needed to sustain life-saving services over the next 90 days.

title: Pakistan Monsoon Floods 2025 - Operation Update #5 (MDRPK028)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

The 2025 monsoon season brought exceptionally heavy rainfall across Pakistan, triggering flash floods, riverine flooding, urban inundation, landslides and localized Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs), particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), Punjab, Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Sindh. As of 18 September 2025, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) reported that the floods affected approximately 6.9 million people nationwide and resulted in more than 1,000 deaths and over 1,000 injuries. Moreover, the floods caused widespread destruction of homes, public infrastructure, agricultural land and essential services. The NDMA reported that more than 229,000 houses, 2,800 kilometers of roads and 790 bridges were damaged, significantly disrupting livelihoods, access to markets, healthcare, education and basic services across affected provinces.

Over the past 12 months, floodwater has receded and most displaced families have returned to their areas of origin. As a result, humanitarian needs have evolved from immediate lifesaving assistance towards recovery and resilience-building interventions. However, many flood-affected households continue to face challenges in restoring livelihoods, repairing damaged homes, recovering agricultural production and accessing safe water and essential services. Findings from the Detailed Needs Assessment (DNA) conducted by PRCS and IFRC identified livelihoods recovery, health, WASH, shelter rehabilitation and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) as the key remaining priorities for the affected communities.

The recovery process, however, continues to be affected by the recurring impacts of climate-related hazards. Pakistan remains among the countries most vulnerable to climate-induced disasters, with increasing exposure to extreme rainfall events, floods, heatwaves, landslides and GLOFs. The ongoing 2026 monsoon season has again highlighted these risks, as several parts of the country experienced heavy rainfall, localized flooding and weather-related incidents during the season. The NDMA's seasonal outlook identified elevated risks of flash flooding, riverine flooding, landslides and GLOFs in vulnerable districts, particularly in the northern mountainous areas and along major river
systems.

According to NDMA's Disaster Vulnerability Scan for July to September 2026, Pakistan continues to face compound climate risks driven by extreme weather patterns, including glacier melt and recurring monsoon hazards, while exposed communities remain vulnerable due to damaged infrastructure, limited preparedness capacity and fragile livelihoods. While the scale of humanitarian needs has decreased compared to the peak of the emergency, recovery remains uneven, particularly among low-income households, women-headed households, Persons with Disabilities (PWDs), older persons and communities living in remote and hazard-prone areas. Continued investments in livelihood restoration, health services, resilient WASH systems, community preparedness and climate adaptation measures remain essential to reduce vulnerability and strengthen community resilience against future disasters.

title: Rwanda | Flood - Simplified Early Action Protocol: Activation (EAP No.: sEAP2025RW01, Operation No.: MDRRW026), 13 October 2026
content:
EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL ACTIVATION

Activation Overview

The simplified EAP focuses on the floods in the Rubavu and Nyabihu districts, in the Western Province of Rwanda. The pre-agree triggered if, within the rainy season, Meteo Rwanda’s Dekade forecasts indicate that the next 10-day total rainfall will exceed 90 mm.

According to Meteo Rwanda, a forecast dated 10 October predict rainfall amounts ranging between 85 and 105 mm are expected in Rubavu and Musanze Districts, several parts of Nyamasheke and Nyabihu Districts, western parts of Karongi and Gakenke Districts, western and northern parts of Rutsiro and Burera Districts as well as small portion of central parts of Rusizi District.

Since the preagree trigger is reached, the National Society will proceed with the implementation of early action activities that focus on supporting evacuation of at-risk communities, support community sandbagging, cash for shelter, for livelihoods and for evacuation, hygiene promotion and provision of water with water truck at evacuation centres and dissemination of early warning messages.

title: BGD: Epidemic - 10-2026 - Measles in Bangladesh #3 (2026-10-15)
content:
Description

Since 15 March 2026 to 14 October 2026, a cumulative total of 208,570 suspected measles cases have been reported nationwide. During the most recent 24-hour reporting period, 119 suspected cases were recorded. Given the current surge, suspected cases are being managed and treated as measles cases. Since mid-March, 22,840 laboratory-confirmed measles cases have been reported, while hospital surveillance data indicate 185,390 cumulative admissions for suspected measles. Measles-associated mortality also remains a major concern. Since 15 March, 1,073 suspected measles deaths have been reported nationally, including 104 confirmed measles deaths during the current reporting period. Dhaka Division continues to report the highest cumulative burden, with 87,200 suspected cases and 486 suspected deaths, while substantial case burdens have also been reported in Chattogram and Barishal. The outbreak has been driven in part by accumulated immunity gaps. Over several years, missed vaccinations and disruptions in vaccine supply have left a substantial number of children susceptible to measles. Infants under nine months, who are not yet eligible for routine measles immunisation, are particularly vulnerable. The accumulation of unvaccinated and under-immunised children over four to five years has created a large susceptible cohort, increasing the risk of sustained transmission and outbreaks across age groups. Since April 2026, Bangladesh has vaccinated nearly 20 million children through emergency and follow-up campaigns. However, significant immunity gaps remain, with some eligible children missed or left unvaccinated during previous vaccination drives. According to the latest EPI data, reported MR campaign coverage has reached 115.7% across the divisions and 115.4% in the City Corporations. Despite these reported coverage levels, measles transmission remains high. Hospital surveillance data recorded around 1,000 suspected measles admissions daily during the reporting period, peaking at 1,251 on 8 October 2026, highlighting the continued pressure on health facilities. In response to the continuing outbreak and remaining immunity gaps, the Ministry of Health launched a nationwide Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccination campaign on 26 September 2026, targeting approximately 3.4 million unvaccinated and missed children. The campaign is prioritising children who have missed routine immunisation and those at higher risk of severe illness and complications. Intensified efforts are being undertaken in high-risk and densely populated areas, particularly Dhaka and Cox’s Bazar. At least 95% vaccination coverage is required to maintain population-level immunity against measles, highlighting the continued need to identify and reach missed children despite the high reported campaign coverage. Increasing Pressure from Dengue: The measles outbreak is occurring alongside a rising dengue burden, creating an increasingly challenging situation for an already overstretched health system. Hospitals are managing more than 900 measles admissions per day, while increasing numbers of dengue patients are adding further pressure on hospital beds, healthcare workers, diagnostics, blood and other essential resources. Major public hospitals in Dhaka, which have managed large numbers of dengue patients during previous outbreaks, are already heavily burdened by measles cases. Any further increase in dengue admissions could intensify competition for limited resources and affect the continuity and quality of care for both measles and dengue patients. More than 100,000 people have reportedly been admitted to hospital with dengue in 2026. The concurrent measles and dengue outbreaks therefore pose a significant risk of further overwhelming health facilities, particularly in high-burden areas. Maintaining essential routine health services while responding to both outbreaks will require continued support to health facilities, particularly for case management, essential medical supplies, infection prevention and control, and referral services. Economic Impact on Affected Families: The impact of the measles outbreak extends beyond the health system and is placing a significant financial burden on affected households. Many patients, particularly those from outside Dhaka, continue to be referred to major hospitals in Dhaka for specialised or better-quality treatment. A large proportion of affected families are from lower- and middle-income households and depend on informal or daily wage-based employment. When children require prolonged hospitalisation away from their homes and places of work, families incur substantial additional costs for transport, food, accommodation, diagnostic tests and medicines that are not covered by the hospital. These indirect and out-of-pocket costs can be particularly difficult for households already facing financial constraints. The most recent cash assessment conducted by IFRC and BDRCS found that nine out of ten measles-affected families had to borrow money to cover medical expenses. Families spent an average of more than US$130 on treatment and related costs, while some families reported losing income or employment because caregivers had to remain away from work to accompany children during treatment. The combination of prolonged hospital stays, referral-related travel and loss of income is therefore increasing the economic vulnerability of affected households. While hospitals may cover core treatment costs, families continue to bear significant expenses associated with accessing and maintaining care. Key Gaps and Priority Needs: The current situation highlights several critical needs. These include continued efforts to identify and vaccinate missed and zero-dose children, strengthen routine immunisation and catch-up vaccination, and intensify vaccination and community engagement activities in high-risk areas. At the health-facility level, additional support is needed to manage the sustained measles caseload while preparing for a potential increase in dengue admissions. At the community and household level, affected families require support to cope with the indirect economic consequences of prolonged treatment and referral. Transport, food, diagnostic costs and other essential expenses can place families under significant financial stress and may lead to borrowing, loss of income or disruption of livelihoods. Multipurpose cash assistance and other appropriate forms of household support can help address these immediate economic impacts while reducing the risk of families resorting to negative coping mechanisms. With measles transmission continuing and dengue cases increasing simultaneously, strengthening both the health-system response and household-level support remains critical to prevent further deterioration of the situation and ensure that vulnerable families can access and continue essential care. BDRCS maintains active coordination with MoHFW, DGHS EPI Unit, IEDCR, WHO, UNICEF, ECHO, RRRC, and the Health Cluster/HCTT. As emergency DREF activities reach full completion, operational priorities are transitioning toward sustaining routine EPI catch-up support and reinforcing infection prevention standards in community health centers.

title: WFP Armenia Country Brief, October 2026 (Reporting period: September 2026)
content:
IN NUMBERS

USD 2.7 M required in the next six months (October 2026 – March 2027)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • The National School Meals Programme reached a key milestone with the launch of Yerevan’s first urban pilot and continued preparations for citywide expansion.
  • The Transformative Home-Grown School Feeding model is advancing sustainable school feeding systems in 87 schools through integrated investments in agriculture, renewable energy, and school capacities.
  • Through the Socio-Economic Integration of Refugees in Armenia (SEIRA) project, WFP is strengthening livelihoods, nutrition, and local food systems through climate-smart agriculture and wholegrain value chain development in Syunik.
  • WFP is supporting more inclusive social protection by completing a disability inclusion assessment and developing recommendations to improve accessibility for persons with disabilities.

title: WFP Djibouti Country Brief October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 3,700 refugees have arrived from Yemen since 10 September, increasing pressure on an already underfunded response. Food assistance has been suspended since August, and WFP requires USD 6.7 million to resume support and assist new arrivals.
  • WFP handed over the Humanitarian Logistics Base (HLB) to the Government of Djibouti, a milestone in the transition to national leadership of the country’s strategic logistics infrastructure. WFP will provide six months of technical support and capacity strengthening to ensure a seamless transition and continued operational readiness.
  • A delegation from the U.S. Bureau of Disaster and Humanitarian Response (DHR) visited Djibouti, including Markazi Refugee Village, to meet refugees, local authorities and partners. The visit coincided with a new U.S. contribution received in mid-September, which has enabled WFP to launch procurement and prepare the resumption of assistance to refugees.

title: WFP Ukraine Country Brief, October 2026 [EN/UK]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • WFP assisted an estimated 531,900 people across its activities in Ukraine in September, including 356,500 people provided with emergency food and cash assistance in frontline areas.
  • September saw a record-high number of high-speed jet powered drone attacks, dramatically reducing shelter warning and air defence reaction times.
  • Russian forces conducted a massive, combined attack targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure on 30 September.
  • Two WFP-supported schools were hit in attacks in late September in Sumy and Odesa regions, with no casualties reported.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Security Situation:

• September saw an intensification of attacks targeting energy infrastructure across Ukraine, as well as an unprecedented increase in the intensity of attacks targeting Kyiv city.

• This includes a record-high number of high-speed jet powered drone attacks, which has dramatically reduced shelter warning and air defence reaction times.

• At least three schools were hit in September, including two supported by WFP’s school meals programme in Sumy and Odesa regions.

• These attacks add itself to a pattern that increasingly targets civilian infrastructure, including medical centres, cultural and educational facilities, and humanitarian assets, including those of WFP.

• Kyiv city and its infrastructure is increasingly being targeted. September saw 193 air alarms, a 60 percent increase from August, with the city remaining under air raid alerts 34 percent of the time. WFP Staff Safety & Security:

• The deteriorating security situation is posing increasing risks to WFP staff across Ukraine.

• In Kyiv, attacks are now regularly impacting areas previously considered to be relatively safer, including the zone of central Kyiv where the WFP country office is located

title: Venezuela Earthquakes Situation Report #11 (October 15, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • On June 24, two earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 hit northern Venezuela less than one minute apart, impacting at least seven states—including the capital Caracas and the neighboring state of La Guaira.
  • Official figures have confirmed 6,509 fatalities, 6,462 people rescued and 226,696 people who have received hospital care following the quakes.
  • Priority needs include healthcare services, clean water, food, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), adequate sanitation and hygiene facilities, protection support and shelter.

Our Response

  • International Medical Corps has deployed three mobile medical units, which have provided 12,017 consultations since July 1.
  • On July 11, International Medical Corps opened an Emergency Medical Team Type 1 Fixed facility—a fully supplied, self-sufficient outpatient medical center—that has so far provided 8,716 consultations.
  • Our teams have delivered more than 1.8 million liters of safe water in displacement sites.
  • Our teams have provided 1,543 MHPSS consultations.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 89, as of 13 October 2026
content:

  • 69 latrines rehabilitated and four boreholes completed in Ouadda, Mouka and Gbali, Haute-Kotto.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

  • On 7 October, a humanitarian team and its partners travelling to Delembé to repair boreholes were robbed 35 km south of Birao. The assailants took cash, communication equipment, personal belongings and two motorcycles, and damaged the vehicle. Despite the incident, humanitarian operations in the area are continuing.

Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

  • Since 7 October, heavy rains and strong winds have caused significant damage in Bakouma and Nzako. According to preliminary data as of 11 October, 280 shelters were affected, 160 of them destroyed and 120 damaged. Some 1,400 people are affected. Affected households are being hosted by neighbouring families.

title: Cholera outbreak update, Minawao Refugee Camp (October 2026)
content:
Overview, current situation and key developments

The cholera outbreak in Minawao Refugee Camp remains active, although the number of new cases has declined from the peak recorded at the end of August. As of 11 October, 459 cumulative cases had been reported, of which 454 patients had recovered and one patient remained under observation, and four deaths had been recorded.

• The response is showing encouraging signs of containment, with very few new cases reported. One new case was recorded on 5 October. The decline follows intensified measures, including the camp- wide oral cholera vaccination campaign, closure of contaminated open wells, disinfection of households and public facilities, contact tracing and community sensitisation

title: Eastern Facade Factsheet 08 October 2026
content:
Cameroon’s Eastern Façade, covering the East,
Adamawa and North regions, hosts most of the country’s Central African Republic refugees, many displaced for more than a decade.

More than 80% live in host communities. Funding cuts and pressure on services are deepening vulnerabilities. At the same time, 87.3% of refugees say they wish to remain in Cameroon, making inclusion, access to national services and self-reliance urgent priorities.

UNHCR is shifting from emergency assistance to durable solutions, prioritising refugee inclusion in national systems, local development and self-reliance.
Peaceful coexistence largely prevails despite mounting pressure on basic services and a decline in humanitarian funding

title: Education Factsheet January - August 2026
content:
Cameroon has strong policies for refugee inclusion in education, but funding gaps are keeping children out of class. Less than one in four refugee children are enrolled; more than 152,000 remain out of school; and secondary education is almost out of reach in key refugee-hosting areas.
Predictable donor financing is urgently needed to turn policy commitments into safe classrooms, trained teachers and real learning opportunities — especially for girls, children with disabilities and adolescents at risk of being left behind

title: Health Factsheet January - August 2026
content:
UNHCR Cameroon is supporting a gradual shift from direct health service delivery towards sustainable refugee inclusion in national health systems. This approach strengthens Government ownership, expands refugees’ access to public services and aligns with the Global Compact on Refugees, Cameroon’s National Health Sector Strategy 2016–2027, and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

As national systems are increasingly taking the lead, targeted support remains critical to keep essential services for refugees with chronic and infectious diseases, pregnant women, malnourished children, referral patients and communities affected by public health emergencies.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 7 (15 October 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

title: Weekly Bulletin on Outbreak and other Emergencies: Week 40: 28 September to 05 October 2026
content:
This Weekly Bulletin focuses on public health emergencies occurring in the WHO African Region. This week’s articles cover:

  • Diphtheria, Senegal
  • Lassa Fever, Nigeria
  • Humanitarian situation, Tchad

For each of these events, a brief description, followed by public health measures implemented and an interpretation of the situation, is provided.

A table is provided at the end of the bulletin with information on all new and ongoing public health events currently being monitored in the region, as well as recent events that have been controlled and closed.

Major issues and challenges include

Senegal: Diphtheria has re-emerged as a significant public health concern in Senegal after more than two decades without reported cases. Since the first confirmed case in July, transmission has spread across multiple regions and health districts, with the highest burden reported in Kédougou, Diourbel, Dakar,
Louga and Thiès. Cases in densely populated Dakar and Touba, a major religious centre with substantial population movement, increase the risk of further spread. Transmission appears to be driven by immunity gaps, with cases among schoolaged children, adolescents and adults suggesting waning or missed booster protection, while unvaccinated and children with unknown vaccination status indicate gaps in routine immunization and documentation. The high case fatality, particularly among unvaccinated young children, raises concerns about delayed care-seeking, referral, access to diphtheria antitoxin and quality clinical care.
Limited clinical familiarity may further delay recognition and treatment.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #4 (12 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Displacement inside Yemen continued to rise sharply, reaching close to 213,000 people between 1 August and 10 October, with Taiz hosting the largest share of those displaced. UNHCR is part of the inter-agency response under the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). In light of the recent escalation, UNHCR requires US$25 million to support an estimated 231,000 people with protection services, including monitoring, legal assistance and support for people at heightened risk, cash assistance, shelter and core relief items (CRIs).
  • A total of 4,003 people have arrived in Eastern Africa from Yemen, including 3,807 refugees in Djibouti and more than 196 people in Somalia.
  • Reportedly, some 20,000 Ethiopians have also recently arrived from Ethiopia to Djibouti. UNHCR remains ready to support the national authorities in ensuring access to asylum and appropriate protection procedures for persons seeking international protection.
  • UNHCR is deeply saddened by the deaths of least 139 people, including multiple children, following the capsizing of a boat carrying more than 305 Ethiopians off the coast of Djibouti travelling to Yemen late last week. With more than 80 people still missing, the number of deaths may grow. Our teams are working with IOM and government partners on the ground to assess protection needs and are providing counseling for survivors.

title: NCDC Lassa Fever Situation Report Epi Week 40: 28th September – 4th October 2026
content:
Highlights

• In week 40, the number of new confirmed cases decreased from 13 reported in epi week 39 of 2026 to 3. These were reported in Bauchi and Benue States (Table 3).

• Cumulatively, 268 deaths have been reported with a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 23.6% which is higher than the CFR for the same period in 2025 (18.6%).

• In total for 2026, 24 States have recorded at least one confirmed case across 119 Local Government Areas (Figures 2 and 3).

• Eighty-eight percent (88%) of all confirmed Lassa fever cases were reported from 5 states (Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue) while twelve percent (12%) were reported from 19 states with confirmed Lassa fever cases. Of the 88% confirmed cases, Ondo reported 36%,
Bauchi 23%, Taraba 12%, Edo 11% and Benue 6%.

• The predominant age group affected is 21-30 years (Range: 1 to 93 years, Median Age: 30 years). The male-to-female ratio for confirmed cases is 1:0.9 (Figure 4).

• The number of suspected and confirmed cases increased compared to that reported for the same period in 2025.

• No new healthcare worker was affected in the reporting week 40.

• National Lassa fever multisectoral multi-partner Technical Working Group (TWG) continues supporting the coordination of activities at all levels.

title: Nepal - Gorkha–Budhigandaki Flash Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response Situation Report #03 (13 October 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
NDRRMA prepared this report using information received from the District Administration Office and the District and National Emergency Operation Centers. It summarizes search, rescue and relief operations following the Budhigandaki flood in Gorkha and Dhading districts.

SITUATION OVERVIEW (BASED ON TECHNICAL REPORT)

At approximately 04:20 on 11 October 2026 (25 Asoj 2083), a snow avalanche at about 6,000 m elevation and a major landslide involving glacier ice and debris at approximately 5,500 m occurred in the upper reaches of Ungdilung Khola, Chumnubri Rural Municipality–6, between Chamar Himal and Syerang Himal. The area contains relatively weak rocks of the Tibetan Tethys Himalaya.

Smaller landslides were observed both before and after the principal failure. The mixed flow of snow, water and debris traveled south down the steep Ungdilung valley, rising as much as 300 m along the valley sides. At about 2,000 m elevation, large quantities of debris accumulated at the narrow confluence of Ungdilung and Syar Khola, repeatedly blocking and releasing the water flow. Similar temporary blockage may also have occurred at the Syar Khola–Budhigandaki confluence. These processes produced multiple flood surges downstream.

The unusually large volume of debris from Ungdilung Khola appears to have contributed more to flood height than the water impounded in Syar Khola. Mud-laden flooding first reached Salleri at approximately 04:30. The largest surge, with an estimated height of 20–25 m, swept away the hydropower camp at Salleri at approximately 06:30. It damaged buildings, especially at Jagat, and infrastructure including permanent bridges at Soti Khola and across the Budhigandaki.

About one hour before the highest surge, the flow in Syar Khola had stopped. Field observations indicate that water had accumulated for approximately 1.5 km upstream. Smaller surges followed the main surge.

Compared with typical floods, the flow carried an unusually high proportion of fine soil relative to sand and rocks, giving it the characteristics of a viscous mudflow. This is consistent with the soil-rich layered rocks and debris at the source area. A preliminary estimate by the Department of Mines and Geology indicated that the landslide released energy equivalent to that of a magnitude 3.5 earthquake.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 04 (as of 14 October 2026, 14:30)
content:
KEY POINTS

• The 7.5-magnitude earthquake that struck on 9 October affected several provinces across the country, particularly Veraguas, Coclé, Herrera and Los Santos. The first death has been reported of a person who was hospitalised as a result of the earthquake.
• The earthquake caused extensive damage to homes, educational centres, health facilities and essential drinking water and transportation infrastructure, affecting access to basic services.
• The Government estimates more than 13,623 affected people. Several communities remain cut off due to the rains and landslides.
• On 10 October, the Government declared a state of emergency and deployed personnel and equipment to access affected communities by land, air and river.
• UN agencies are providing complementary support to the authority-led response. On 13 and 14 October, an interagency mission was conducted in Herrera and Los Santos.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 22, Data as of 11 October 2026
content:
Democratic Republic of the Congo

The BVD outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to evolve, expanding both geographically and in
terms of the numbers of cases and deaths. The Dakwa Health Zone in Bas-Uélé Province has become the latest affected
health zone, bringing the total number of impacted health zones to 65 across seven provinces since the start of the
outbreak. Transmission remains highly heterogeneous across these regions. Since External Situation Report #21, a total
of 463 additional confirmed cases and 233 confirmed deaths have been reported. This increases the cumulative total
to 9066 confirmed cases, including 4381 confirmed deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR) 48.3%] as of 11 October 2026.
Ituri remains the principal focus of the outbreak, though its relative contribution is declining; it is currently for 73.8%
of cumulative confirmed cases. Substantial transmission persist in Nord-Kivu and Haut-Uélé.

National incidence remains high and fluctuating, with no sustained downward trajectory evident. Following rapid
expansion through July and August, the epidemic has entered a more heterogeneous phase characterized by repeated
declines and rebounds. This pattern reflects asynchronous transmission across provinces and health zones; declining
activity in established Ituri hotspots is being offset by persistent or renewed activity elsewhere, particularly in Nord-
Kivu, while sporadic detections continue to extend the geographic footprint. The overall trend suggest a shifting and
geographically fragmented epidemic than sustained contraction.

title: UNHCR Emergency Response: Earthquake in Panama – October 13 2026
content:
Situation

On 9 October, Panama experienced one of the strongest earthquakes in its history. With a magnitude of 7.5, an epicentre on the Azuero Peninsula, and more than 400 aftershocks recorded to date, the earthquake affected several provinces, causing severe damage to homes and critical infrastructure in communities across Panama's countryside.

As of 12 October, authorities reported over 3,000 affected homes, damage to more than 650 schools, at least 27 people injured, and hundreds displaced, evacuated, and nearly 600 staying in 14 temporary shelters. Among those affected are refugee families, as well as other vulnerable populations. The full extent of the losses has not yet been quantified, but the Government declared a state of emergency to mobilize up to USD 100 million for response efforts. President Mulino reported that more than 6,000 people have been affected and that the government is implementing recovery measures, including a housing reconstruction programme.

Heavy rainfall, rising river levels and landslides in affected areas have hindered the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the assessment of the most urgent needs. Several communities remain inaccessible, with no access roads, safe drinking water or electricity.

UNHCR joined the Government of Panama-led response and has mobilized over 33 metric tons of core relief items (CRIs) to date, including family tents, blankets, mosquito nets, kitchen sets, a rub hall and other essential supplies. The Agency remains in contact with authorities and community leaders, supporting efforts to address the most urgent needs, particularly for the most vulnerable.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, October 15, 2026 – October 21, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño continues to strengthen. Long-term abnormal dryness and abnormal heat persist across areas of Africa, northern Central Asia, Central America, Hispaniola, and northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is forecast in the eastern Sahel and parts of Eastern Africa, while high risks of flooding with ongoing heavy rain in the horn of Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Large 90-day rainfall deficits have led to abnormal dryness across Chad and large parts of Eastern Africa. As a result, deteriorated vegetation conditions, driven by drought, have been observed over western Sudan, southern and southeastern South Sudan, northern Uganda, and parts of Ethiopia's northern, eastern, and central regions.
3) Central Mali and central/eastern Liberia and southern Cote D’Ivoire are under Abnormal Dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall over the past 30 and 90 days.
4) Recent heavy rainfall has caused flooding in southern Ethiopia and parts of Somalia with more heavy rains ongoing.
5) The forecast heavy rainfall elevates flood risk in Guinea-Conakry, Sierra Leone, and western Liberia, as well as western Kenya during the next week.
6) Abnormal heat is forecast in southern Chad, eastern CAR, southern Sudan, South Sudan, and northwestern Uganda, along with eastern South Africa, as well-above-average temperatures are expected to persist for 3 or more consecutive days in this region during the next week.

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Response Update (From Isolation to Assistance: UNICEF RRM - Lankien and Buong, Jonglei State), September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Sustained humanitarian operations in Lankien (Nyirol County) and Buong (Akobo West County) have largely not been possible since January 2026, owing to conflict, displacement, extreme remoteness and severe access constraints. Both counties are classified in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency), with some households facing IPC Phase 5 (Catastrophe) conditions.
  • Logistics support from the Logistics Cluster and UNHAS enabled the deployment of response teams and supplies to both locations, overcoming barriers that had limited humanitarian access for much of 2026.
  • Nutrition: 9,807 children aged 6–59 months were screened for acute malnutrition; 1,350 children were admitted to treatment for severe acute malnutrition and 2,290 referred for moderate acute malnutrition; 3,640 children received ready-to-use therapeutic food.
  • WASH: 12,956 people received critical WASH supplies and were reached with hygiene-promotion messaging, while 1,556 people gained access to safe emergency water supplies meeting the minimum standard of 7.5 litres per person per day.
  • Health: 228 outpatient consultations and 296 antenatal care consultations were provided in Buong; 325 women of reproductive age were vaccinated against tetanus and 138 children under 15 against polio.

title: UNICEF South Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 7, 31 August 2026
content:
Highlights

  • 445,611 people had been newly displaced by 30 August, with the majority recorded in Jonglei, Upper Nile and Lakes states, while more than 1.4 million refugees and returnees had arrived from Sudan, placing further pressure on host communities, and basic services.
  • Severe food insecurity and acute malnutrition persisted, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes expected to remain widespread through September. Global Acute Malnutrition rates remained critically high, including 36.2 percent in Guit, 28.8 percent in Akoka, 23.0 percent in Abyei and 21.6 percent in Pibor.
  • Despite declining cholera transmission nationally, 112,375 cumulative cases and 1,725 deaths had been reported by end August. Concurrently, worsening drought conditions reduced agricultural production, pasture regeneration and water availability, increasing concerns over poor harvests and further deterioration in food security.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal remained only 45 per cent funded, while humanitarian access incidents rose by 44 per cent compared with 2025.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 26 September – 2 October 2026
content:
Ukraine Conflict Monitor Update

Key trends

Russia intensified its strikes on civilians and critical infrastructure over the past week, with mass casualty incidents reported almost daily. Among the most deadly strikes, attacks in Kharkiv on 5 October, Pryluky on 7 October, and Kramatorsk on 8 October killed six, 22, and at least 32 civilians, respectively. Repeated mass casualty incidents point to a sustained threat to civilians and increase pressure on and danger to emergency responders across the country. Ukraine’s struggle to intercept faster, jet-powered Shahed drones compounds the threat as Russia has started intensifying strikes on civilian infrastructure ahead of winter. Although Russia has deployed fewer jet-powered drones on average per night so far in October than in September, it has increasingly dispersed them in smaller groups across the country, stretching Ukraine’s air defence and contributing to mass casualty incidents in multiple regions.
In Russia, Ukraine has expanded its strike campaign against Yandex data centers that host services ranging from online searches to transportation, entertainment, cloud services, and AI. A drone strike on 8 October disabled the company’s data center in Sasovo, while a subsequent attack on its largest facility in Kaluga disrupted services. The strikes were likely intended to counter Russia’s attack on Ukrainian data centers, weaken Russia’s technological capabilities, and increase economic pressure on Russia. Yandex was forced to operate its cloud infrastructure in emergency mode, indicating the scale of the damage. The disruption could have long-term consequences, as replacing high-tech hardware and restoring full capacity may take months, if it’s even possible at all.

title: WFP Eastern and Southern Africa Seasonal Outlook: Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office (ESARO) - October 2026
content:
Highlights

• Above-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures are favoured across much of Eastern Africa during October to December 2026. Southern Ethiopia, central and southern Somalia and Kenya show the strongest wet signal, increasing extreme rainfall and flood risks.

• Much of central and southern Southern Africa is expected to receive below-normal rainfall and experience above-average temperatures during the 2026/27 rainy season. Dry spells could disrupt planting and crop development. Wetter conditions are favoured in some northern areas and along much of the Angolan coast.

• Food insecurity is expected to rise across the region as a result of this outlook: in Southern Africa, drought is likely to reduce maize harvests, push up staple prices and deepen the October 2027 to March 2028 lean season, while in Eastern Africa flooding threatens displacement and crop and livestock losses from October 2026.

• Preparedness actions are critical to limit how far seasonal rainfall impacts translate into food insecurity. These include early warning and close seasonal monitoring, anticipatory action for drought and floods, prepositioning of stocks, and early response planning with governments and partners.

title: Myanmar monthly food price report - August 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • Rice prices increased substantially in August 2026, with the national average rising by 5.2 percent monthon-month and 14.9 percent year-on-year. Regional price disparities persisted, reflecting differences in production conditions, market access, and transportation costs. The country-wide increase in retail rice prices was reportedly associated with flood-related concerns, supply disruptions, and transportation difficulties.
  • Export crop prices showed mixed movements. Maize prices declined month-on-month but remained substantially above year-earlier levels, while black gram and pigeon pea prices also remained elevated year-on-year. Green gram prices declined while chickpea prices increased. Vegetable prices generally increased in August. Chili and onion prices rose sharply, supported by constrained supplies and continued export demand, while garlic prices increased following a seasonal pattern. Potato prices rose more moderately.
  • Most animal-sourced food prices remained substantially above year-earlier levels. Chicken, eggs, mutton, beef, and fish prices increased year-on-year, with mutton prices remaining at record highs. In contrast, pig prices declined both month-on-month and year-on-year amid reports of swine disease and weaker pork demand in Yangon. Reports of livestock disease affecting poultry, pigs, and cattle also raised broader animal health concerns.
  • The conflict in Iran has led to a partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a major transit route for global oil and fertilizer trade — while fighting has also escalated in the Red Sea, another key shipping corridor. Together, these disruptions are raising concerns for Myanmar's agrifood system, which depends heavily on fuel for transportation, irrigation, mechanization, and processing. Fertilizer prices also remain substantially above last year’s levels, possibly reducing the profitability of fertilizer use and leading to lower application rates and agricultural production.
  • Flooding intensified during August, particularly in major rice-producing areas of Ayeyarwady and Sagaing. Flooding reportedly inundated approximately 97,000 acres in Ayeyarwady and affected more than 10,000 acres of paddy and other cropland in Sagaing. Meanwhile, strengthening El Niño conditions could bring additional risks from irregular rainfall, higher temperatures, and drought, potentially affecting agricultural production and food supply.
  • The outlook for Myanmar food prices will remain influenced by export demand, border trade conditions, input costs, and weather-related risks. Concerns over pulses production in India could support demand for Myanmar’s black gram and pigeon pea, while softer Chinese demand for green gram remains a concern. Changes in Thailand’s maize import arrangements and continued volatility in border trade stations could also affect agricultural market flows and will be important to monitor in the coming months.
