title: WFP Lao People's Democratic Republic Country Brief, October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• The Ministry of Health signed public-private partnership agreements with two private millers to enable the production and distribution of fortified rice for government-led programmes. The partnerships also create opportunities for the private sector partners to expand production and commercialise fortified rice in the domestic market.

• WFP presented its new Country Strategic Plan (2027-2031) to Executive Board members and Member States during the Informal Executive Board Consultation. The strategy is expected to receive final approval at the Board’s second regular session in November.

• In September, WFP supported a government-led inter-agency rapid assessment across six flood affected provinces and began verifying and registering families for food assistance in Luang Namtha province.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• The Lao People's Democratic Republic is a landlocked, least developed country with a population of 7.8 million. As of 2024/2025, about 15 percent of the population lived below the national poverty line of USD 1.10 per day. Poverty has declined by over half in the past two decades. The 2024 Global Hunger Index rates the country's hunger as “moderate.”

• Climate change is a major challenge for rural populations, as the country is vulnerable due to its low adaptability and heavy dependence on climate-sensitive natural resources. Changing climate patterns, limited access to markets and varied livelihoods further worsen the situation in remote upland areas, where over 20 percent of households are food insecure (national average: 10 percent). Chronic malnutrition affects every third child under five, while micronutrient deficiencies are high and overnutrition is on the rise in urban areas.

• WFP has been present in Lao PDR since 1976, supporting national efforts to improve food security, nutrition, and resilience. It operates through a main office in Vientiane Capital and three field offices in Oudomxay, Xiengkhouang, and Champassak provinces.

title: VNM: Flood - 10-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #3 (2026-10-12)
content:
Description

According to local authorities, heavy rainfall on 10–11 October caused localized flooding, landslides and transport disruption in parts of Central Viet Nam, particularly Quang Tri, Da Nang and Lam Dong. One flood-related death was confirmed in Dan Hoa, Quang Tri. Floodwaters have generally receded, although some local roads and low-water crossings remain affected. In Da Nang, landslides affected two road sections in Nam Tra My, temporarily disrupting traffic. In Tra Giap, landslides affected three households, prompting local authorities to assist residents in moving away from dangerous areas. No casualties were reported in these incidents.

According to the National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting (NCHMF), localized heavy rainfall remains possible across Central Viet Nam, particularly from southern Quang Tri to Da Nang and in eastern areas from Quang Ngai to Dak Lak and Khanh Hoa. The forecast issued on 12 October indicated rainfall of 20–40 mm, locally exceeding 80 mm. Flash-flood and landslide warnings were issued for Da Nang, Quang Ngai and Dak Lak, with a further warning issued for parts of Dak Lak on 12 October.

River levels in North Central Viet Nam are generally receding. However, further heavy rainfall may trigger flash floods and landslides in vulnerable areas.

title: Serbia: Extreme Winter Condition and Floods - DREF Final Report (MDRRS016)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

09-01-2026

What happened, where and when?
Since 4 January, severe winter weather conditions, including heavy snowfall, strong winds and low temperatures, have affected several parts of Serbia, causing partial collapse of the electricity distribution network and widespread, prolonged power outages. These outages severely disrupted heating, water supply and access to essential services, particularly in rural and hard-to-reach areas. The situation further deteriorated on 7 January, when additional heavy snowfall coincided with a sharp drop in temperatures to severe sub-zero levels. The most affected municipalities included Loznica, Valjevo, Osečina, Ivanjica, Vladimirci, Krupanj, Lučani, Mali Zvornik and Majdanpek, where heavy snow accumulation caused restricted access to communities, disrupted transportation and prolonged electricity cuts due to damage to power infrastructure.

Additionally, as a consequence of heavy precipitation, rivers in Kosovo and Metohija began to overflow. Note: All references to Kosovo in the present document should be understood in the context of United Nations Security Council resolution 1244 (1999). On 7 January, the Ibar river overflowed, followed by the Sitnica river on 9 January, causing localized flooding in the municipalities of Kosovska Mitrovica, Zvečan, Kosovo Polje and Lipljan. Flooding affected residential areas, agricultural land and critical infrastructure, posing risks to livelihoods, health and safety of the population.

The Emergency Situations Sector of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Seriba announced a state of emergency due to snow in 11 municipalities (Loznica, Osečina, Prijepolje, Vladimirci, Mali Zvornik, Valjevo, Majdanpek, Krupanj, Sjenica, Lučani, Ivanjica) as a result of severe winter weather.

The State of emergency was declared in 11 municipalities:
Loznica 5/1/2026
Osečina 5/1/2026
Prijepolje 5/1/2026
Vladimirci 6/1/2026
Mali Zvornik 6/1/2026
Valjevo 8/1/2026
Majdnapek 8/1/2026
Krupanj 8/1/2026
Sjenica 9/1/2026
Lučani 10/1/2026
Ivanjica 10/1/2026

The state of emergency still remains in 10 municipalities. In response to immediate needs, the Red Cross of Serbia provided emergency assistance to over 400 households, including food and hygiene parcels, blankets, sleeping bags, drinking water, candles, and Primus stoves. However, the evolving situation, remaining unmet needs, and depletion of contingency stocks require continued support and reinforcement of operational capacities through DREF assistance.

title: THA: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #4 (2026-10-09)
content:
Description

According to DDPM report, as of 06:00 on 9 October 2026, flooding continued in 22 provinces, including Bangkok, affecting 109 districts, 927 subdistricts and 6,934 villages. According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), a total of 1,145,352 households (3,183,726 people) had been affected.

The flooding was caused by the influence of a monsoon trough, unstable weather conditions and accumulated water in low-lying areas along rivers. Flood levels were receding in several provinces, while water levels remained stable in others. Water levels were reported to be rising in Chachoengsao Province.

The highest reported impacts included Bangkok, with approximately 329,000 affected households; Pathum Thani, with 246,818; Samut Prakan, with 223,346; and Ayutthaya, with 61,365. DDPM reported fatalities in several affected provinces, including 19 in Prachin Buri, nine in Samut Prakan and five in Suphan Buri.

The Thai Meteorological Department forecasts unstable weather, thunderstorms, strong gusts and isolated heavy to very heavy rainfall across several regions during 9–13 October 2026. Continued rainfall may trigger flash floods, river overflows and landslides, particularly in low-lying and flood-prone areas. Authorities are advised to closely monitor the situation and prepare for potential further impacts.

title: Nepal - 25-28 September Heavy Rainfall Situation Report #1 (28 September 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
Brief Summary

A low-pressure system originating over the Bay of Bengal resulted in heavy to very heavy rainfall across various parts of Nepal from 25 to 28 September 2026. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research (CHWRR) initiated continuous monitoring and analysis of the development, movement, and potential impacts of the weather system from 23 September 2026 . Through the Flood Forecast Bulletin issued on 24 September 2026, advance information was disseminated regarding the potential risks of heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides.

On the same day, the Hon. Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation and the Hon. Minister for Home Affairs visited the Flood Forecasting Information Center and were briefed on the prevailing risk situation. To further strengthen preparedness and early warning measures, from 25 September 2026, the flood forecasting lead time for major rivers was extended from 3 days to 5 days, while the forecasting lead time for flash floods in smaller rivers and streams was increased from 24 hours to 48 hours.

title: UNHCR Facilitated Return of Syrian Refugees - Lebanon, 30 September 2026
content:
Since January 2025, 694,392 Syrians known to UNHCR have returned to Syria and consequently been inactivated from UNHCR's records. This includes refugees confirmed to have returned1 and those inactivated due to prolonged absence and loss of contact2 . Among the 694,392 Syrian returnees, 86% (597,552) returned spontaneously to Syria; this includes 11 % (65,500) who returned under duress in late 2024 and remained in Syria; 23% (140,000) identified by the General Security Office (GSO) while crossing through an Official Crossing Point (OCP) without a Repatriation Form; 6% (35,903) identified as returning due to force majeure after 2 March 2026; and 60% (356,149) who were inactivated due to prolonged absence or loss of contact, or whose return was confirmed by UNHCR through interviews with family members. The spontaneous departure figures reflected in the chart indicate the date of inactivation from UNHCR's database, rather than the date of departure, which explains the high number of inactivations in December 2025 following the completion of the presence verification.

By the end of September 2026, 14% of the 694,392 Syrians who had returned, representing 96,840 individuals, had been assisted by UNHCR: 79,548 under the voluntary repatriation programme and 17,292 under the Return due to Force Majeure (RFM) programme. The RFM programme was implemented between 1 April and 30 June 2026 in response to the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon to provide humanitarian assistance to refugees returning to Syria without a viable alternative for safety. Among those assisted under the RFM programme, 72% returned to their areas of origin in Syria, 19% were women, 59% were children. Almost all (96%) returned in complete families.

title: World Vision Situation Report #2: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (09 October 2026)
content:
Cambodia experienced significant flooding throughout September 2026 due to prolonged heavy rainfall and tropical weather disturbances, affecting 10 provinces, 53 districts and cities, 255 communes/sangkats, and approximately 73,922 households nationwide. The floods damaged homes, agricultural land, and public infrastructure, while continued rainfall poses ongoing risks to vulnerable communities, particularly in Battambang and Banteay Meanchey provinces.

In response, World Vision Cambodia launched a 90-day Flood Emergency Response Plan (October–December 2026) to address urgent humanitarian needs through an integrated multi-sectoral approach, including food assistance, nutrition, WASH, shelter and non-food items, protection, and education support. The response targets more than 20,000 people across the most affected areas.

To date, World Vision Cambodia has reached 3,169 people, including 1,798 children, and supported 898 households with emergency food and hygiene assistance valued at USD 35,922.73. The response has prioritized vulnerable groups such as young children, pregnant and lactating women, and persons with disabilities. Child protection awareness and community feedback mechanisms have also been integrated to ensure safe, accountable, and people-centered assistance.

Working closely with government authorities, local disaster management committees, humanitarian partners, volunteers, and youth, World Vision Cambodia continues to coordinate relief efforts while appealing for USD 800,000 to meet the growing needs of flood-affected communities across eight districts in Battambang and Banteay Meanchey.

title: Nepal Flood 2026 - DREF Operation Update #02 (MDRNP022)
content:
As of 2 October 2026, CHF 13.04 million in confirmed multilateral hard pledges recorded against the CHF 18 million IFRC Secretariat Emergency Appeal (approximately 72% per cent). Continued funding is required to sustain the response and scale up early recovery interventions.

On 26 August 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche occurred in the upper Lhende Khola watershed, around 20 km upstream of the Rasuwagadhi border point. The avalanche triggered a debris flow and severe flooding downstream along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. The flooding caused widespread erosion and sediment deposits and damaged settlements, agricultural land, productive assets and critical infrastructure. The most serious humanitarian impacts happened in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, although impacts were also reported further downstream along the river corridor.

The extent of infrastructure damage continues to affect access and recovery efforts. According to the Government-led Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA)3, around 69 km of road was damaged, including 55 km classified as completely damaged. The assessment also identified damage to 37 motorable bridges and 68 trail-bridge spans. Of the motorable bridges assessed, 33 were reported washed away. Damage to roads and bridges, as well as electricity, water-supply and communication networks, has disrupted essential services, economic activities and access to affected communities. Access remains difficult in some locations, particularly in Rasuwa, where relief supplies continue to be airlifted to communities that cannot be reached by road because of damaged roads and bridges.

According to the latest Government statistics4, dated 1 October 2026, 1,453 people had been reported dead, 5,179 remained reported missing, and 13,795 had been rescued. The number of people reported missing still requires further verification and reconciliation. In the context of the access barriers and the ongoing assessments, the Government RDNA also cautions that figures for deaths, missing people and rescues should not necessarily be treated as separate or mutually exclusive counts.

According to the Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) Situation Report5, displacement has decreased as families continue to leave collective accommodation, but considerable temporary shelter and recovery needs remain. NRCS reported that 1,107 people were staying in 21 holding centres across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading as of its latest update. In the very beginning, there were around 33 holding centers, which are gradually decreasing, depicting movement of people to alternate places. Thus, the number of people staying in these centres does not represent the full displaced population. Some affected families are staying with relatives or host families, while others have moved to different forms of temporary accommodation. The Government has also announced monthly cash support for displaced families choosing to live outside holding centres, providing NPR 15,000 (CHF 82) per month for households of up to four members and an additional NPR 2,000 (CHF 10.75) for each additional household member, for up to six months or until alternative accommodation is arranged. As displacement becomes more dispersed, continued household-level verification remains important to understand which families can safely return home and which will require temporary accommodation, reconstruction support or possible relocation. IFRC-supported ongoing emergency response efforts have distributed shelter items, including NFI sets, mattresses, blankets, etc., to approximately 9,905 people and the operation plans to prioritize emergencies and transition shelter going forward. The IFRC shelter coordination surge supports coordination among humanitarian partners in affected areas. Collectively, 51 actors have provided shelter and essential household items to around 23,000 people (5,900 households), against 25,709 people initially targeted in holding centres. Most households have since moved to temporary sites. By 2 October, basic services and access had largely been restored, except in some hard-to-reach areas of Rasuwa District.

More than a month after the disaster, the response is increasingly moving from immediate lifesaving assistance towards restoring essential services, temporary and transitional shelter and early recovery. This transition is already visible through household assessments, temporary site development and work to rehabilitate damaged water-supply systems, while emergency assistance continues in locations where access remains constrained. Humanitarian needs nevertheless remain, particularly among displaced families and communities that are difficult to reach. Unstable slopes, accumulated sediment, obstructed channels, continuing rainfall and the possibility of further flooding exacerbate the challenges for the affected people. Continuing rainfall is also affecting temporary shelter conditions and has already interrupted some shelter works, increasing the importance of adequate weather protection, sanitation, protection services and winterization as seasonal conditions change.

title: UNICEF Panama Situation Report No.1 (Earthquake), 9-10 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 9 October 2026, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck Panama, causing damage to homes, schools, health facilities, roads, bridges, and water supply infrastructure, particularly in Veraguas, Coclé, Los Santos and Herrera provinces. On 10 October, the government declared a state of emergency following the earthquake.
  • According to the National Emergency Operations Centre (COE), 27 people sustained minor injuries, with no fatalities or missing persons reported as of 10 October. The number of affected children and families remains unknown.
  • The Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) reported 419 affected educational facilities nationwide, raising concerns about school safety, access to water and sanitation, and continuity of learning.
  • The Ministry of Health (MINSA) reported 20 affected health facilities. Evacuations and temporary adjustments to patient care were reported, potentially affecting access to essential health services for children and families.
  • Damage to roads and bridges restricted access to several rural communities. Although water production has reportedly been restored at major treatment facilities, the situation in affected rural areas remains under assessment. Approximately 300 people were preventively evacuated from Isla Caña, while eight families were accommodated in a temporary shelter in Penonomé.
  • UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response and assessing priority needs affecting children and families. Initial efforts are focused on WASH, education, health and child protection, including assessing water and sanitation services in affected communities, schools, health facilities and temporary shelters. UNICEF is preparing to provide emergency supplies and support the rapid restoration of essential services, prioritizing isolated and displaced communities as needs are confirmed.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 314: Week 1 - October 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the 1st week of October, national average prices recorded generally modest week-on-week movements, while several key food commodities remained elevated compared with last year and their longer-term averages. Rice, wheat, cooking oil, sugar and salt prices remained above their corresponding annual levels, while elevated fuel and fertilizer prices continued to add pressure to transportation, production and supply-chain costs. Meanwhile weak labour availability and subdued purchasing power continued to constrain household access to food.

Food Categories:

National average food prices recorded limited week-on-week movements, although notable annual and longer-term price disparities persisted across commodities.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain prices increased marginally by 0.6% during the week, while high-price wheat flour remained unchanged and low-price wheat flour declined by 0.2%. Compared with last year, wheat grain and low-price wheat flour were both 10% higher, while high-price wheat flour was 6% higher.

• Rice: Rice prices declined during the week, with Palawi and Sholae falling by 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Despite these weekly declines, Palawi remained 17% and Sholae 31% above last year's levels, while both varieties remained substantially above their three-year averages, by 19% and 20%, respectively.

• Other Staples: Weekly movements in cooking oil, pulses, sugar, salt and bread remained limited. Cooking oil and sugar prices were 12% and 10% higher than last year, while salt was 4% higher. In contrast, pulses and bread remained 12% and 3% below their respective annual levels.

• Vegetables: Potato prices declined by 4.1% during the week, while onion fell by 3.1% and tomato by 0.2%. Despite the weekly decline, potato remained 25% above last year's level and 23% above its three-year average. In contrast, tomato and onion prices were 55% and 6% lower year-on-year, respectively.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): Purchasing power remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal unskilled labour ToT stood at 9.9 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 13% decline from last year and 12% below the three-year average. The continued deterioration indicates sustained pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 14% below last year and 21% below the three-year average. Unskilled labour wages also declined by 5% year-on-year, contributing to a 25% decline in the real unskilled labour ToT compared with last year and 30% below the three-year average.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 260 kg of low-price wheat flour, 12% below last year's level and 7% below the three-year average, indicating continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and Agricultural Inputs: DAP prices increased marginally by 0.3% during the week, while urea prices declined by 1.8%. Despite these limited weekly movements, DAP and urea remained 10% and 24% higher than last year, respectively. Improved seed and animal feed prices remained below last year, by 8% and 5%, respectively.

title: Nepal - Bhotekoshi-Trishuli Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Update (Reporting Period: 26 August – 3 October 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On 26 August 2026 (10 Bhadra 2083), a severe flash flood travelled through the Lhende Khola–Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. It was caused by an ice and rock avalanche, rather than monsoon rainfall. A hanging glacier and rocky mass covering approximately 2.0 km2 broke away at an altitude of about 5,200 metres on the northern side of Langtang Lirung in Rasuwa district and struck the Lhende Glacier at 3,800 metres. The resulting avalanche and subsequent flow down the Lhende Khola generated the flood. The impact produced a strong seismic signal of magnitude 5.2, recorded at 08:37.

Travelling at approximately 188 km/h from its source, the flood covered 20 km within seven to eight minutes and reached the Nepal–China border at Rasuwagadhi at 08:45. It destroyed the hydrological stations at Syafrubesi at 08:50 and Betrawati at 09:20.

title: Nepal - Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi Flood: Search, Rescue and Relief Response Situation Report #12 (13 September 2026) [EN/NE]
content:
Highlights

• The Government of Nepal has decided to provide immediate cash relief for temporary accommodation and livelihoods to families with completely destroyed and uninhabitable homes across 15 local levels in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading,
Tanahun, and Gorkha, with NPR 15,000 per month for families of up to four members and an additional NPR 2,000 per additional member, for up to six months, exclusively for those opting for self-arranged temporary accommodation instead of holding centers.

• The government has completed the preliminary damage and loss assessment, while the Post- Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) process is currently underway, based on which necessary resources will be secured to accelerate reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts.

• A total of 339 patients received treatment across 19 health facilities, of whom 271 have been discharged, 32 remain under treatment, 32 were referred to other hospitals, and 4 individuals passed away during treatment.

• According to respective districts information, 825 affected persons are currently taking shelter in 9 holding centers in Rasuwa District, 1,613 in 22 holding centers in Nuwakot District, and 94 in 2 holding centers in Dhading District. In total, 2,532 affected persons are currently taking shelter across 33 holding centers.

• In collaboration with the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction (DUDBC) and partner organizations, various prototype options for 1-room, 2-room, and 3/4-room emergency transitional shelters have been prepared and discussed.

• For the first time in Nepal following the Bhote Koshi floods, live monitoring of river conditions has been initiated under the leadership of the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research (CHWRR) by installing a CCTV camera in Timure, approximately 70 meters above the river level. Its live feed is connected to CHWRR’s 24/7 operated flood forecasting service.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 02 (as of 11 October 2026, 13:15)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • The University of Panama’s Institute of Geosciences (IGC-UP) has revised the magnitude of the 9 October earthquake to 7.6. The epicentre was 39 km north-west of Tonosí, at a depth of 4 km. The institute has since recorded more than 200 earthquakes, five of them magnitude 6.0 or above.
  • As of 6:30 p.m. on 10 October, the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) reported more than 820 damaged homes, 27 people with minor injuries and 29 affected health facilities across ten provinces and two Indigenous territories. The Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) reports 419 affected schools. No one has been reported missing.
  • Some 255 people are staying in two shelters in Mariato (Veraguas) and 12 in one in Penonomé (Coclé), and two more shelters are open in Boca de Quema (Los Santos). Authorities evacuated about 300 people from Isla de Cañas.
  • Tonosí has no water or electricity. The Pedasí–Tonosí road remains closed and the Ministry of Public Works (MOP) has shut the bridge over the Oria River, so only light vehicles can reach the town, via Macaracas and Llano de Piedra. Six communities in Los Santos and Herrera are still cut off.
  • MEDUCA has cancelled classes at all public and private schools on Monday 12 October. SINAPROC has called off the third national emergency drill, and a rain warning is in effect until 1:00 p.m. that day.

title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 01 (as of 10 October 2026, 13:15)
content:
KEY POINTS

  • On 9 October at 12:56 p.m., a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck 39 km north-west of Tonosí, in the south-central province of Los Santos, at a depth of 4 km, according to the University of Panama’s Institute of Geosciences (IGC-UP). Aftershocks are ongoing, with 56 aftershocks recorded up to 8:11 p.m. No deaths or missing people have been reported.
  • On 10 October, the Cabinet Council, convened by the President of Panama, declared a state of emergency following the earthquake.
  • The National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) reported at least 134 damaged homes, 27 people injured and 188 damaged schools nationwide as of 8:00 p.m.
  • Veraguas, Coclé, Los Santos and Herrera provinces account for most of the damage. In Veraguas, the townships (corregimientos) of Arena, Cacao and Quebro remain cut off, with power, water and Internet outages.
  • Some 300 people were evacuated from Isla Cañas (Los Santos) due to rising sea levels, and eight families are staying in a shelter set up in Penonomé (Coclé).
  • The Ministry of Health (MINSA) reported non-structural damage to 17 health facilities: 6 hospitals, 8 health centres and 3 MINSA-CAPSI (Innovative Primary Health Care Centres). Hospitals in Los Santos, Chiriquí and Herrera provinces and the Panama City metropolitan area were evacuated, and the Hospital del Oriente Chiricano was fully evacuated (209 people).
  • The Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) suspended classes nationwide and reported 188 affected schools. Those with infrastructure damage include 22 in the Ngäbe-Buglé Indigenous comarca (a semi-autonomous territory), 15 in Chiriquí, 5 in Panamá Centro, 4 in Los Santos and 3 in Panamá Este. At the Alberto Zúñiga School (Coclé), 15 students suffered minor injuries.
  • The National Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (IDAAN) reported that the Chilibre water treatment plant is operating at full capacity and that supply is gradually recovering.

title: International Rescue Committee (IRC) Protection Analysis Report (Mid-Year Review, January-June 2026 ) [EN/UK]
content:
The first half of 2026 saw the protection environment in Ukraine deteriorate further, shaped by three converging pressures: intensified attacks on civilian infrastructure, a winter energy crisis that disrupted essential services during the coldest season in over a decade, and the progressive exhaustion of coping capacity among a population deep into protracted displacement.

This report presents IRC protection monitoring findings from 1,828 household respondents surveyed in Mykolaivska, Sumska, Kharkivska, Zaporizka and Dnipropetrovska oblasts across the first half of 2026, complemented by 133 key informant interviews with community representatives, service providers and local authorities across the same geographies. Findings were triangulated with secondary data from humanitarian partners, cluster reporting and open-source monitoring, and read alongside IRC service-delivery data, to contextualise trends and corroborate protection risks.

title: Conflict Response in Baidoa, Somalia: Situation Report #1 (October 9, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • The conflict in Baidoa, Somalia, has resulted in significant damage to civilian infrastructure and public buildings while displacing residents and increasing humanitarian needs across the district.
  • The deteriorating security situation has disrupted access to essential services, including healthcare, and increased the number of displaced people seeking assistance.

OUR FOOTPRINT

  • International Medical Corps has operated in Somalia since 1990, providing a wide range of humanitarian and health services, including primary and secondary healthcare, health workforce training, health education, emergency response, mental health and psychosocial support, nutrition, protection, community empowerment, and water, sanitation and hygiene services.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps is working with relevant authorities, clusters and humanitarian partners to support a coordinated response and sustain essential services for affected communities. We have launched a targeted three-month emergency response in Baidoa to support conflict-affected and displaced communities amid escalating humanitarian needs, providing emergency hospital support, primary healthcare and nutrition services through two primary health units and limited rehabilitation of critical infrastructure, prioritizing vulnerable populations such as women and children.

title: Protection Cluster: West Bank Operational Update | 1 June - 31 August 2026
content:
Protection Developments – Escalating Settler Violence and Displacement

Between June and August 2026, the operating environment in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, deteriorated further amid a worsening security situation and additional measures by Israeli authorities that constrained humanitarian access and operations.
During the reporting period, OHCHR verified the killing of 27 Palestinians in the West Bank, including eight boys. Of these, 20 were killed by Israeli forces (IF), two by Israeli settlers, and five by either IF or Israeli settlers. In addition, two Israelis, including one civilian and one IF member, were killed in settler attacks followed by clashes with Palestinians.
Settler violence continued to intensify in scale, geographic spread, and severity, with repeated attacks occurring amid persistent impunity and insufficient protection for affected Palestinian communities. OCHA recorded 229 settler attacks resulting in casualties and/or property damage in June 2026, 221 in July, and 198 in August, up from 148 in January 2026, reflecting a sustained upward trend. Annual incidents have exceeded 1,000 since 2023 and reached 1,836 in 2025. In many cases, attacks reportedly occurred in the presence of IF, which are increasingly seen failing to prevent, facilitating, or participating in such violence.

A related trend was the expansion of settler attacks beyond areas qualified as “C” under the Oslo Accords, alongside the growth of settler farm outposts, which reportedly controlled about 18% of West Bank land as of July 2026. According to the CSO Yesh Din, the share of attacks occurring in Areas “A” and “B” increased from 32% in 2025 to 63% in January-June 2026. This surge contributed to increased casualties, property damage and livelihood losses, movement restrictions, limited access to services, heightened displacement risks, shrinking safe spaces for Palestinians, and increasingly constrained humanitarian operations.

In one particularly grave incident, on 24 July 2026, approximately 60 settlers, several of them armed, entered the village of Tell, southwest of Nablus in Area “B”, reportedly as part of an unauthorized hike, triggering clashes involving Palestinians, armed settlers, and IF. Four Palestinian men from the same family and two Israelis, one of them an off duty IF soldier, were killed. The incident was followed by what appeared to be extensive collective punishment measures, including the temporary detention of approximately 100 Palestinian men. In the following days, settlers carried out coordinated attacks across Qalqilya and Nablus in apparent retaliation, resulting in Palestinian injuries, extensive property damage, and movement restrictions that impeded access to essential services. According to the CSO Peace Now, settlers had established five outposts near Tell in reprisal by the end of July.

A similar incident occurred on 21 August 2026 in Sa'ir, Hebron (also in Area “B”), when at least 50 settlers participating in a reported unauthorized hike entered the village armed with firearms, batons, sharp objects, slings, and Molotov cocktails. They attacked homes and residents, resulting in the shooting and killing of a 16-year-old boy and critically injuring several others, including a 71-year-old man.

A related emerging pattern involved the forcible displacement of Palestinian families from homes in residential areas on the outskirts of Palestinian villages in Area “B”, following sustained harassment and intimidation by Israeli settlers. In several cases, families reportedly endured prolonged sieges of their homes, including repeated attacks and obstruction of access to essential services and supplies, making daily life untenable and ultimately forcing them to leave. Their properties were subsequently occupied by settlers.

One such incident occurred on 22 July 2026, when two Palestinian families comprising seven people, including three children, were displaced from their home northeast of Jalud, Nablus, following months of settler violence and harassment. After a nearby outpost was established in April, the families reportedly faced repeated attacks, had their vehicle burned, were denied access to food and medicine, and experienced disruptions to water and electricity services. Settlers reportedly occupied the two homes immediately after the families left.

A similar case occurred in Area B near Qusra, Nablus Governorate. On 9 August 2026, settlers from a nearby outpost blocked access roads to three Palestinian homes and erected a tent between them, effectively trapping approximately 15 Palestinians, including children, inside. Although Israeli forces later removed the tent, deployed to the area and declared it a closed military zone, residents continued to face severe movement restrictions as of the end of August, with limited access to food, water and other essential supplies. Settler harassment and intimidation continued, while visits to the affected homes required prior coordination with the Israeli military.

Against this backdrop, protection partners faced growing challenges in addressing protection risks and maintaining services to affected communities. Reports indicated increased harassment and attacks against humanitarian actors, which, together with the designation of some affected areas as closed military zones, further restricted humanitarian space.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 16-30 September 2026
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that since the military coup on 01 February 2021 and 31 August 2026, at least 1,973 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across Myanmar:

  • health facilities were damaged 519 times
  • 175 health workers were killed, 940 arrested and 55 kidnapped

Since January 2025, incidents involving damage to or destruction of temporary or makeshift health facilities in Myanmar have increased sharply, from four incidents between February 2021 and December 2024 to 33 between January 2025 and August 2026. In total, 89% of the reported incidents were attributed to Myanmar Armed Forces (MAF) aircraft and drone strikes. Temporary or makeshift health facilities in Sagaing Region were particularly affected, with incidents also frequently reported in Kachin and Mandalay.

16-30 September 2026

title: UNRWA Situation Report #236 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • Over 106,000 children attended in-person learning in UNRWA Temporary Learning Spaces (TLS) during the first weeks of the 2026/2027 school year, marking an important milestone in efforts to expand access to learning across the Gaza Strip. At the same time, demand for in-person learning continues to outpace available capacity, and efforts are ongoing to identify additional learning spaces and expand existing TLS. Learning activities continue in challenging conditions in many locations, and significant investment is required to improve learning environments, undertake repairs, rehabilitate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) facilities, and produce essential education furniture. UNRWA estimates that several million dollars are needed to address these requirements and support safe, inclusive, and conducive learning conditions for children across UNRWA schools and temporary learning spaces.
  • Over the past months, with the support of partners, UNRWA teams have produced more than 6,000 pieces of furniture for UNRWA TLS and health centres, including desks, chairs, tables, cupboards, and benches, helping expand learning capacity despite severe resource constraints.
  • Military activity remained concentrated along and around the Israeli-controlled military zone, known as the "Yellow Line", continuing to expose civilians to significant protection risks. UNRWA recorded several incidents affecting its installations and displaced persons sheltering within them. In the Middle Area, quadcopter fire prompted the precautionary relocation of displaced persons within an UNRWA school. In separate incidents in Jabalia, two displaced persons sheltering in UNRWA schools, including a seven-year-old child, were reportedly injured by gunfire while sleeping inside the shelters.
  • As winter approaches, as reported by the Site Management and Shelter Clusters, an estimated 235,000 people are sheltering in around 400 flood-prone displacement sites, while more than 44,000 people continue to live in unsafe buildings at heightened risk of collapse during winter. Combined, these figures represent over 13 per cent of Gaza's population exposed to heightened winter-related risks. On 28 September, the UN Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov warned the UN Security Council that “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items continue to impede the scale-up of the humanitarian response, including preparations” for the rainy season. As co-lead of the Site Management Cluster, UNRWA continues to coordinate and support winter preparedness and risk-reduction efforts through site-level risk assessments, prioritisation of high-risk locations, and coordination of targeted mitigation measures, including flood-risk reduction, access improvements, debris removal, site and shelter reinforcement, and community engagement.

Key points

The Gaza Strip

Fatalities and injuries

  • Between 7 October 2023 and 2 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the Health Cluster, 74,228 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 175,188 were injured. This includes 1,445 fatalities and 5,227 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 2 October 2026.
  • UNRWA has recorded 394 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 83 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2], as of 6 October.

Health crisis

  • The worsening fuel and engine oil shortage is increasingly disrupting health services across the Gaza Strip. The UN warned that reduced fuel support to hospitals, driven by funding shortfalls and high procurement costs, could affect most hospitals and lead to cuts in primary and secondary healthcare services.
  • In September, six UNRWA health centres also experienced temporary disruptions due to generator overload, highlighting the growing operational impact of the shortage of fuel, lubricant oil, and spare parts on the delivery of healthcare.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs

  • According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in early July, 90 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene – an increase from 84 per cent the previous month.

Shelter needs

  • According to the Shelter Cluster’s classification, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks.

Operational implications and humanitarian response

  • Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with over 4,000 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, health, and other services to Palestine Refugees.
  • All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[3] that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact between Israeli officials and UNRWA. Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including the Gaza Strip, since the end of January 2025.
  • Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

  • According to OCHA, between 7 October 2023 and 6 October 2026, 1,138 Palestinians – at least 250 of them children – were killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Ninety-one of them have been killed since the beginning of 2026.
  • Israeli forces again renewed the military closure orders covering Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams camps in the northern West Bank until 30 November, deepening the near-total restrictions on accessing the camps. Some 34,000 Palestine Refugees remain forcibly displaced as a result of the ongoing operation “Iron Wall”, which started in January 2025.
  • Movement and access restrictions imposed by Israeli forces across the occupied West Bank were tightened during this period, coinciding with the Jewish holiday of Sukkot and in anticipation of the third anniversary of the attacks of 7 October 2023. The Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967 released a statement on 2 October condemning the impact of checkpoints on Palestinian life.
  • Tendering for the construction of the E1 Israeli settlement plan located east of Jerusalem was postponed by the office of the Israeli Attorney General until after the upcoming Israeli elections. The E1 settlement project stands to displace multiple Palestine Refugee communities and would severely undermine the territorial contiguity of the occupied West Bank.
  • During this period, two Palestinians were killed in connection with settler violence incidents, which also resulted in damage to Palestinian property and agricultural assets across the occupied West Bank. The official start of the annual olive harvest season is scheduled for 15 October, with an increase in settler violence and harassment anticipated.

title: UNICEF Burundi Humanitarian Situation Report No. 24, 1-30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

· UNICEF strengthened Ebola preparedness through investments in surveillance, RCCE, WASH and health system readiness.

· Refugee returns continued, reducing the Busuma population to approximately 37,000 people.

· Access to safe water in Busuma tripled, increasing from 5.8 to 17.5 litres per person per day.

· More than 34,000 people, including 29,000 children, accessed mental health and psychosocial support services.

· Measles and cholera outbreaks persisted, underscoring the need for sustained preparedness and response efforts.

· Severe funding gaps in education, child protection and social protection threaten children's access to learning, protection and resilience services, increasing risks of school dropout, violence, distress and harmful coping strategies.

Situation Overview & Humanitarian Needs

In September 2026, Burundi continued to face humanitarian pressures driven by refugee movements, public health risks and climate-related threats. Government and humanitarian partners strengthened preparedness for the Ebola risk from neighbouring DRC through enhanced coordination, surveillance and community readiness.

Population movements remained significant. The number of Congolese refugees in Busuma declined to approximately 37,000 people, following the continuation of voluntary returns to DRC. By mid-September, 18,232 refugees had benefited from facilitated returns, while additional households expressed interest in returning voluntarily. Around 21,000 refugees remained in Musenyi, and over 3,000 asylum seekers were hosted in Cishemere, where UNHCR was preparing the launch of voluntary returns in October. Humanitarian partners also updated the inter-agency refugee response plan to support the transition from emergency response towards protection and durable solutions. The repatriation of Burundian refugees from Tanzania was nearing completion, with 98,617 returnees recorded in 2026. Public health risks remained elevated, with continued Ebola preparedness efforts supported by UNICEF's US$3.39 million contribution to the national plan.

As of 30 September 2026, cholera transmission persisted in affected districts, while the measles outbreak affecting eight health districts had reached 1,661 suspected cases

Meanwhile, preparedness for the forecasted El Niño 2026-2027 was intensified to anticipate potential risks of flooding, displacement, disease outbreaks and food insecurity.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.13: Measles in the Region of the Americas (8 October 2026)
content:
Summary of the Situation

Between epidemiological week (EW)1 and EW 39 of 2026 (which ended on 3 October2026), the Region of the Americas reported 55,792 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 4.8-fold increase compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (34,355), Mexico (13,595), the United States (3,887), Peru (2,553), and Canada (1,121) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 77 deaths has been reported, including 50 in Guatemala, 23 in Mexico, 2 in the United States of America, one in Peru and one in Bolivia (1). Notably, the deaths reported in the United States of America and Peru are the first deaths reported by these countries in 2026.

During EW 37 andEW 38 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 687 new confirmed cases of measles in seven countries and territories, representing a 35% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 35–36; 1,059 new cases, including 350 retrospectively reported since the last Regional Situation Report) (Figure 1). Of the 687 new confirmed cases reported during EW 37–38, the United States accounted for 293, followed by Guatemala 200, Peru with 155, Mexico with 34, and Bolivia with 3, while Canada and Brazil reported one case each.

Despite declining transmission in some countries of the Americas, with Rt estimates below 1, persistent lowlevel transmission may continue through sporadic and hard-to-detect chains of infection. This "drop-by-drop" transmission pattern can sustain virus circulation for more than 12 months, delaying outbreak closure and increasing the risk of re-establishment of endemic transmission, which could ultimately jeopardize a country's measles-free status.

title: Cuba | Hurricane Melissa - Operation Update #5 (MDRCU013)
content:
Description of the crisis

Nearly one year after Hurricane Melissa, its effects continue to shape humanitarian conditions in eastern Cuba, compounded by an energy and fuel crisis that deepened further between May and August 2026. Melissa made landfall in eastern Cuba on 29 October 2025 as a Category 3 hurricane with sustained winds of 125 mph (195 km/h) causing severe flooding, landslides, and significant storm-surge impacts across the provinces of Granma, Santiago de Cuba, Holguín, and Guantanamo. Close to 2.2 million people were affected, with no fatalities reported (OCHA, 2025a).

More than 215,000 homes were damaged or destroyed, affecting an estimated 645,000 people, half of whom are considered vulnerable. Of the 642 healthcare institutions that sustained damage, all are now operational and essential services have been restored across the affected provinces, although repairs to address the remaining hurricane related damage are ongoing (PAHO/WHO, 2026a). Around 450,000 people lacked access to safe water in the immediate aftermath (OCHA, 2025c). Livelihoods were also heavily impacted: at least 158,000 hectares of crops were damaged or destroyed – including grains, cassava, plantains, and coffee – alongside significant losses to fishing vessels and livestock (OCHA, 2025b; IOM, 2025).

Recovery has been particularly challenging due to pre-existing structural vulnerabilities and the cumulative effects of prior disasters, including Hurricanes Oscar and Rafael in 2024, from which many communities had not yet fully recovered (IFRC, 2025).

The situation has been further aggravated since end of 2025 by concurrent outbreaks of dengue, oropouche, and chikungunya, declared by Cuba's Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP), severe energy and fuel constraints and supply chain disruption due to external factors that have limited the access to essential services and items throughout 2026.

Cuba is also experiencing severe energy and fuel constraints that have become a dominant compounding factor across all sectors. Since January 2026, disruptions in petroleum product imports – linked to broader geopolitical dynamics and international market conditions – have sharply reduced fuel availability nationwide (ACAPS, 2026). The national electricity grid experienced repeated nationwide collapses, including two failures within one week in March, three within nine days in July and another major grid failure in early August (Reuters, 2026a). By August, electricity generation covered less than one third of national demand, compared with 45 per cent in January, and some areas experienced outages of more than 30 hours (OCHA, 2026).

The effects of these energy and fuel constraints are wide-ranging and cross-cutting. With more than 80 per cent of Cuba's water pumping infrastructure electricity-dependent, prolonged blackouts are severely affecting access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (IFRC, 2026). In August, around 3.5 million people were affected by water-supply disruptions (OCHA, 2026). Close to one million people depend on water tanker trucks, many of which face operational limitations due to reduced fuel availability (OCHA, 2026). Solid waste collection has been significantly reduced in many areas, heightening public health risks. The health system continued to face severe pressure. By May, more than 100,000 patients were awaiting delayed surgical procedures, including approximately 12,000 children. As of March 2026, all 46 blood banks were experiencing operational constraints; while interruptions to electricity dependent services placed 2,888 dialysis patients at heightened risk (OCHA/UNCT, 2026). More than 32,000 pregnant women also faced increased risks due to limited access to diagnostic services, transportation for obstetric emergencies and reliable electricity for maternal and neonatal care. Routine immunisation services remained operational but were under growing pressure from cold-chain disruptions, transport constraints and supply shortages (United Nations System in Cuba, 2026; PAHO/WHO, 2026). In August, cold-chain disruptions put the routine immunisation of nearly 70,000 children at risk (OCHA, 2026).

In the social sphere, reduced access to food, essential services, and income has deepened existing vulnerabilities. In addition, household diets in 2026 were often inadequate in energy intake and insufficiently healthy or diverse, amid persistent inflation, reduced purchasing power, fuel shortages and reduced availability of domestic and imported food (WFP, 2026). In July, year-on-year inflation in the formal market reached 20.7 per cent, with food prices up 26.4 per cent (ONEI, 2026). These dynamics reflect the convergence of compounding pressures: the energy and fuel constraints, the ongoing recovery needs in communities affected by Hurricane Melissa, and the persistent deteriorating health situation together place Cuban communities – particularly in the eastern provinces and those recently affected by arboviruses and hepatitis A outbreaks – at heightened and escalating risk.

title: Argentina: Pluvial/Flash Flood - DREF Final Report (MDRAR024)
content:
Description of the Event

Affected districts: Campana and Zárate, Buenos Aires, May 2025.

Date of event

17-05-2025

What happened, where and when?

On 15 May 2025, intense rainfall began in the Metropolitan Area of Buenos Aires (AMBA) and the northern part of the Province of Buenos Aires. Between 16 and 17 May, exceptional cumulative precipitation was recorded — with estimated values ranging between 150 and 300 millimetres within 24 hours, according to official sources — leading to flash flooding, widespread waterlogging, disruption of transport routes (including National Route No. 9 near Zárate), water ingress into homes, and population evacuations.

The National Meteorological Service issued a red alert for rainfall in the northern part of the province. The most severe impacts were concentrated in the partidos of Campana and Zárate, with significant effects in neighborhoods such as San Cayetano and San Felipe, as well as in other localities along the province’s northern corridor.

Following the event, conditions began to improve gradually from 18 May onwards, with water levels progressively receding in several areas. However, waterlogging persisted in parts of Zárate for several days, necessitating the continuation of temporary shelter arrangements and ongoing clean-up and recovery actions.

In total, over 4.300 families were displaced as a result of the event. However, due to the terrain characteristics, water receded within a few days, leading to a gradual decline in the number of evacuees, who returned to their homes between 19 and 29 May.

Scope and Scale

The Province of Buenos Aires has experienced recurrent flooding events, particularly in the Areco River basin and the north-eastern corridor, which includes localities such as Zárate, San Antonio de Areco, Exaltación de la Cruz, Baradero and Salto. These events have shown increased frequency and intensity in recent years, in line with patterns associated with climate change, which heighten the recurrence of intense and prolonged rainfall.

The event that occurred between 15 and 17 May 2025 exceeded the response capacity of local systems, primarily affecting the partidos of Campana and Zárate.

In Campana, more than 37,600 people were affected, with more than 4,000 families relocated to eight centres. In neighborhoods such as San Cayetano and San Felipe, water levels exceeded 1.5 metres inside homes. Educational activities were suspended for between 10 and 20 days, depending on the area, and multiple health centres, public services and industries sustained significant damage.

In Zárate, approximately 48,000 people were affected, and more than 300 families were relocated, with waterlogging persisting for several days following the event. Disruptions to basic services, such as electricity and drinking water, affected a large proportion of the population.

At the regional level, it is estimated that more than 250,000 people in the AMBA region and the northern part of the province experienced direct or indirect impacts. At least one death was confirmed following the floods, and missing persons were reported who were subsequently found. Basic services began to be progressively restored within the first ten days, while the full recovery of damaged infrastructure extended to approximately two months after the event.

The impact of the event significantly affected daily life, livelihoods and the well-being of the population, particularly among highly vulnerable groups. Those most affected included people living in low-lying and flood-prone areas, with precarious housing or limited access to basic services, as well as informal workers who depend on daily income.

Among the groups identified as having heightened vulnerability are older persons, children, persons with disabilities and low-income households, who face greater challenges in evacuating, restoring their livelihoods and accessing health services and assistance.

Furthermore, communities previously affected by similar events exhibit limited coping capacity, increasing their exposure to recurrent impacts.

title: Brazil: Floods DREF Final Report (MDRBR012)
content:
Description of the Event

Areas affected in Minas Gerais. February, 2026.

Date of event

26-02-2026

What happened, where and when?

In February 2026, the Zona da Mata region in Minas Gerais, Brazil, suffered one of the most severe socio-environmental disasters in its recent history due to extreme rainfall. In 12 hours, accumulated precipitation reached up to 220 milimetres, representing four times the expected monthly average for the region. This phenomenon triggered flash floods and massive landslides in densely populated urban areas, primarily affecting the municipalities of Juiz de Fora and Ubá. Although the rains were seasonal, this specific event generated an exceptionally high humanitarian impact concentrated in the aforementioned zones, affecting approximately 5,510 individuals, all of whom were subsequently displaced from their homes. The disaster was officially classified as the fourth deadliest rainfall-related disaster in Brazil over the last decade, resulting in 74 confirmed deaths and leaving one person missing, whose body was ultimately recovered by 17 March.

Geographically, the impact was concentrated within specific municipal boundaries. Juiz de Fora (population 540,000) lies in the south-east of the state, near the border with Rio de Janeiro state, on the Paraibuna River, a tributary of the Paraíba do Sul. It is 272 kilometres from Belo Horizonte, the state capital. Ubá (population 103,000), also in the Zona da Mata, is 290 kilometres from Belo Horizonte. Regarding the historical context of exposure, Minas Gerais had frequently faced recurrent flooding, though the prevalence of such events was historically higher in Juiz de Fora than in Ubá. Since the year 2000, the region had recorded at least 19 relevant hydrometeorological events evenly distributed over time, with a clear predominance of pluvial flooding. Within this vulnerable context, the recent disaster pushed population risks to critical levels; in Juiz de Fora alone, an estimated 129,000 people were living in areas classified under high geological and hydrological risk. Consequently, survivors experienced severe psychosocial consequences, reporting acute anxiety, sleep disorders, and a complete loss of their sense of security after floodwaters reached heights of 1.5 metres in urban centers.

The damage inflicted upon infrastructure and public services networks was substantial, heavily compromising immediate local response capabilities.

  • The damage to homes was the most severe and difficult to address. In Matias Barbosa, many families lost the temporary homes they were renting and cannot afford alternative housing due to high rental costs. Some remain in damaged properties as they have no other option. Although the return to their homes in Guaraní municipality was faster, damp and unsanitary conditions persist.
  • In terms of the impact on health services, in Juiz de Fora, 11 Basic Health Units (UBS) were forced to close due to direct flooding of severe structural risks. The Emergency Hospital (Hospital de Pronto Socorro - HPS), the primary regional reference center, suffered severe flooding in its basement, which directly compromised critical care services. Other essential facilities, such as the Terezinha de Jesus Maternity Hospital and local oncology centers, also reported significant structural damage. Furthermore, the process of returning to homes that have not been properly sanitized posed health risks. Cleaning efforts relied heavily on community initiatives and limited support from local governments, and there was no evidence of any post-disaster epidemiological assessments having been carried out.

As a consequence of total soil saturation and the partial collapse of sanitation infrastructure, severe epidemiological risks were identified for the subsequent recovery phase. Public health assessments indicated an elevated risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, particularly leptospirosis, hepatitis A, and acute diarrhoeal diseases. Stagnant waters left by the receding floods created ideal conditions for the proliferation of disease-carrying mosquito vectors, compounding risks in a broader national context where chikungunya outbreaks were already active in several Brazilian states. This situation was further aggravated by the fact that Juiz de Fora served as the regional healthcare hub for the entire southeastern zone of Minas Gerais, meaning the impairment of its health network caused a severe patient overflow into the hospitals of neighboring cities.

Although it has received limited institutional attention, the emotional impact has been significant. Communities reported trauma, a recurring fear of further flooding, the loss of belongings and ongoing psychological effects, yet there were no specific psychosocial programmes in place.

  • In terms of the impact on educational services, these were completely suspended across the area, and at least 15 schools were repurposed to serve as temporary shelters for displaced families who had lost their homes.
  • Regarding the impact on the mobility system, transport networks collapsed as widespread road blockages and landslides isolated entire neighbourhoods, severely hindering the mobilization of emergency supplies and the critical transfer of patients toward high-complexity healthcare facilities. The destruction of access roads in rural areas prolonged the disruption to the education system.
  • In terms of the impact on the livelihoods of the local population, the flood affected informal workers as well as businesses and formal sector employees, leading to loss of income, business closures, and unemployment. Juiz de Fora’s economic dependence amplified the impacts in Matias Barbosa municipality.

title: UNICEF Djibouti Humanitarian Flash Update No. 3 (Refugee influx from Yemen), 7 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • As of 7 October 2026, according to the Prefecture of Obock, 3,807 people have arrived in Djibouti from Yemen, including refugees identified in host families in Obock. 50% are children (around 1,900), and 15 per cent are children under five. Arrivals continue : 78 new arrivals were recorded between 28 September and 2 October.
  • Acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) cases have been reported in Markazi village. 35 cases have been reported and children under 15 account for 74% of cases.
  • The Ministry of Health leads the AWD response, and UNICEF is supporting case management, supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) and hygiene promotion.
  • UNICEF is supporting safe water and sanitation in Markazi, including water trucking, 6 water points management and 43 emergency latrines, as well as support to the national office for water and sanitation to increase water production in Obock.
  • Acute malnutrition among targeted screened children is very high. Of 267 children aged 6–59 months screened, 69 had severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 97 had moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). As screening focused on children at higher risk, these results are not representative of the refugee population, but they call for urgent scale-up of treatment and infant feeding support.
  • Child protection caseload is growing. Nine unaccompanied and separated children have been identified and referred to UNICEF. The UNICEF-supported child-friendly space has provides services to 330 children since 16 September.
  • UNICEF requires 3 million United States dollars (USD) to respond to the needs of children and families over six months.

title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 4, 23 July-23 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • The outbreak continues to expand geographically. Laboratory-confirmed cholera cases are reported in twenty-one health districts across the Far North and North regions, while four additional districts in the Far North remain under investigation for suspected cases.
  • UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response through Health, WASH, Social and Behaviour Change, Accountability to Affected Populations, Child Protection, Nutrition, Youth Engagement and coordination.
  • The response is 48 per cent funded. A US$660,800 gap remains, with particularly significant needs in Health, Nutrition and Child Protection/MHPSS.

Overview

Cholera transmission continues to expand across the Far North and North regions. Population movements and active transmission in neighbouring areas increase the risk of further spread. Immediate priorities include stronger surveillance, timely case management, targeted WASH interventions, risk communication and preparedness in affected and high-risk districts.

As of 23 September 2026, the Far North region has reported 2,753 cholera cases and 77 deaths (CFR: 2.8%), with active transmission persisting in several health districts, notably Mada, Kolofata, Mokolo, Mora and Makary. The implementation of two rounds of reactive Oral Cholera Vaccination (OCV) campaigns in seven high-risk districts (Fotokol, Kousseri, Mada, Makary, Mora, Kolofata and Mokolo) has likely contributed to reducing the spread and severity of the outbreak. However, the worsening humanitarian situation, including population displacement from Logone-et-Chari division due to insecurity, is placing additional pressure on host communities in Waza and the urban health districts of Maroua I, Maroua II and Maroua III. This influx of displaced populations is increasing vulnerability to cholera transmission through overcrowding and heightened pressure on already constrained health and WASH services.

In the North Region, 37 cases and 6 deaths have been reported (CFR: 16.22%). Guider reported the highest number of cases. Although the caseload remains low, the high case fatality rate may indicate delays in detection and referral or limited access to quality case management.

Continued surveillance, WASH interventions, risk communication and community engagement and cross-border coordination remain critical to prevent further spread and reduce mortality

title: Yemen Emergency Response Situation Report #4 (October 8, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • 197,906 people from 29,519 families have been displaced across 10 governorates, approximately a 10% increase from the last report.
  • Eighteen of 19 International Medical Corps-supported health facilities remain operational across the west coast despite continuing access constraints.

OUR FOOTPRINT

  • Across Yemen, International Medical Corps supports 63 health facilities, with an estimated coverage of 3.3 million people across seven governorates: Aden, Al Dhale’e, Al Hodeidah, Ibb, Lahj, Sana’a and Taiz.
  • Our lifesaving multi-sectoral assistance prioritizes active conflict zones and high-risk environments. In 2025, we helped more than 400,000 people.

OUR RESPONSE

  • A mobile medical team that we support has provided 475 medical consultations, screened 106 children under 5 and 38 pregnant and lactating women for acute malnutrition, provided immunization services to 31 women and 36 children, and conducted 50 antenatal care consultations.
  • Our supported facilities have provided 11,835 medical consultations to people on the west coast.
  • We have provided 26 metric tons of essential medicines and medical supplies to six health facilities in Aden and Lahj that will help sustain critical health, emergency obstetric and referral services amid increasing needs and ongoing supply constraints.

title: Nigeria: Conflict - LTS Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #117 - Reporting period: September 2026
content:
Led by the World Food Programme (WFP), the Logistics & Telecommunications Sector (LTS)1 was activated in North-East Nigeria in November 2016 in response to the protection crisis. LTS (telecoms area) Nigeria Situation Reports are issued monthly.

Summary Points

• LTS Telecoms facilitated internet connectivity services for 1,070 users from 144 humanitarian organizations across northeast Nigeria. Throughout September, the team maintained and strengthened connectivity services across multiple locations, resolving network disruptions, restoring services following facility renovations, and improving network reliability, resilience, and security to support humanitarian operations.

• LTS Telecoms provided onsite connectivity support for the Inter-Sector Training on Data Systems for the Borno State Government. Through the deployment of a CrisisNet kit and in collaboration with humanitarian partners, the support enabled reliable internet access and effective coordination among participating stakeholders.

• LTS Telecoms strengthened security communications services across deep-field locations in northeast Nigeria. Infrastructure upgrades, including the deployment of lithium batteries at five operational sites, preventive maintenance, and VHF coverage testing, improved the reliability and continuity of critical telecommunications services supporting humanitarian responders.

Situation overview

Insecurity continues to constrain humanitarian operations across Borno State, particularly in Dikwa, Bama, Banki, Gwoza, Monguno, Damasak, and Ngala. Ongoing security incidents, including the persistent threat of improvised explosive devices (IEDs), together with planned camp closures in Gwoza, continue to drive population movements and complicate humanitarian access. Despite these challenges, humanitarian partners remain engaged in delivering assistance to displaced populations and hard-to-reach communities.

The humanitarian situation in northeast Nigeria remains critical, with cholera outbreaks, acute malnutrition, food insecurity, and continued displacement driving humanitarian needs across the region.

title: Attacks on Health Care in the occupied Palestinian territory (01-15 September 2026)
content:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that between 07 October 2023 and 15 September 2026, at least 3,486 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across the occupied Palestinian territory. 94% of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

In the West Bank, where 1,020 attacks on health care were recorded, 13 health workers were killed and 198 arrested while ambulances and health workers were prevented from providing vital medical care to people in need over over 600 times.

Attacks on health care in the West Bank increased between September 2025 and August 2026, rising from an average of around 14 incidents per month during the first six months of the reporting period to around 35 in July. Many incidents involved disruption of health care delivery, including delays or obstruction of ambulances. These incidents occurred alongside checkpoint closures, roadblocks and other movement restrictions, further limiting patients’ ability to reach health facilities.

View the incidents on our interactive map. Download the data. Updated every Monday and includes information on weapons use, perpetrators and effects. For data enquiries, please get in touch. Data is continuously updated and numbers may change if/ when further information is made available. See here for methodology.

Documented incidents

16-30 September 2026

The incidents below have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open source verification protocol.
