title: THA: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #3 (2026-10-06)
content:
Description

Thailand has experienced heavy rainfall since mid-September 2026, resulting in widespread flooding across the country. From 16 September to 6 October 2026, flooding was reported across 50 provinces, affecting 1,474,981 households (4,188,452 people), with 31 deaths reported. As of 6 October, flooding remains ongoing in 27 provinces and Bangkok, affecting 1,149,285 households (3,143,962 people).

The situation remains particularly concerning in parts of the Central and Eastern regions, where water levels are increasing in several provinces. Continued rainfall and increased water discharge from major reservoirs and the Chao Phraya Dam may further increase flood risks in low-lying and riverside areas.

Bangkok: Approximately 329,000 households / 700,000 people were affected by flooding, with 4 deaths reported. The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration, DDPM, Drainage and Sewerage Department, district offices, military units, police, local authorities and volunteers are supporting response activities. Actions include traffic management, accelerated drainage and establishment of 233 temporary shelters. Water levels are decreasing.

Weather forecast

The Thai Meteorological Department forecasts unstable weather from 6–7 October, with thunderstorms, strong wind gusts and heavy to very heavy rainfall in parts of northern, central, eastern and southern Thailand, including Bangkok and surrounding areas. Heavy rainfall is expected to increase again in the Eastern and Central regions, Bangkok and the South from 9–13 October. Flash floods, runoff and waterlogging remain possible, particularly in low-lying areas and near waterways. In the Chao Phraya basin, increased dam discharge of 2,200–2,500 m³/second could raise water levels by approximately 0.4–0.7 metres, requiring continued close monitoring and preparedness.

title: Somalia: Monthly Humanitarian Update, September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Hunger and malnutrition are persisting in Somalia, driven by climatic shocks, conflict, disease outbreaks, displacement and reduced assistance, according to new findings.
  • The analysis projects that 5.4 million people will face crisis levels of hunger or worse in October to December, including 1.5 million facing emergency levels of hunger or worse.
  • An estimated 1.92 million under-five children will require treatment for acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027, including 433,000 with severe acute malnutrition.
  • Humanitarian partners, authorities and local actors are accelerating preparedness measures as forecasts indicate significant flooding in October to December.
  • An estimated 3.4 million people could be exposed to flood risks during October to December, especially in Hiraan, Middle Juba and Lower Juba regions.

title: UNFPA Somalia: Situation Report (July - September 2026)
content:
Somalia’s humanitarian crisis remains severe. Drought impacts in northern and central regions have left approximately 1.9 million people acutely food insecure. Worsening food insecurity and malnutrition are heightening risks for pregnant and breastfeeding women, including pregnancy-related complications and adverse maternal and newborn outcomes. Ongoing disease outbreaks of acute watery diarrhoea, cholera, measles and diphtheria are further compounding high levels of malnutrition and placing additional pressure on already overstretched health services.

In early September, renewed clashes in Baidoa displaced an additional 14,832 people, of which women, children and older people accounted for 79 per cent. Displacement and economic hardship are increasing protection risks for women and girls as well as disrupting access to sexual and reproductive health services and referral pathways.

Between July to September, UNFPA has reached more than 55,000 people with life-saving sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence, and adolescent and youth-focused services. As the humanitarian risk profile shifted towards anticipated flooding, UNFPA also strengthened anticipatory action, leveraging its programme presence in 12 flood-exposed districts to support the continuity of essential services.

Funding constraints continue to limit the scale and sustainability of the response in Somalia, with only 25 per cent of the US$27 million required by UNFPA secured to date. Additional flexible funding is urgently needed to maintain essential sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence services, sustain the availability of reproductive health commodities, and strengthen preparedness in areas at risk of flooding.

title: South Sudan Health Cluster Bulletin, August September 2026
content:
URGENT PRIORITIES AND ASKS FOR DONORS AND PARTNERS

• Mount an immediate multisectoral response in Lafon County and Imehejek Administrative Area (Eastern Equatoria), where field teams verified 73 deaths (49 in Lafon, including 27 children under five; 24 in Imehejek) linked to acute malnutrition, malaria, acute watery diarrhoea, unsafe water and delayed access to care; 660 of 2,191 children screened were acutely malnourished, and MAM treatment is nonfunctional in Imehejek after WFP support withdrew.

• Scale up health, nutrition and WASH support across the five Warrap State counties assessed in the 7–15 September IRNA (Gogrial East, Gogrial West, Tonj North, Tonj South, Tonj East), where 210,000 people (~35,000 households) are in need, GAM among under-fives screened reached 34.5% with four sites (Majak Juer, Athieng Puol, Kanaf, Chueicok) past the IPC Phase 5 threshold, and only 27 of 84 boreholes (32%) are functional.

• Close the last-mile gaps in BVD readiness identified by the second-round sub-national assessment: safe and dignified burial (34.8%), operations/logistics (38.5%) and essential health-service continuity (41.7%, down 12.5 points since the previous assessment) remain the weakest pillars, and Budi, Ibba, Kapoeta South and Tambura need critical-function closure before dependable deployment; Western Equatoria urgency has increased after DRC's Dungu Health Zone (Haut-Uélé) confirmed its first case on 18 September.

• Respond to the new measles outbreaks confirmed in Tonj North (Warrap) and Aweil South (NBG) and complete the Pariang reactive campaign (7% coverage as of late September); investigations continue in Rubkona, Aweil East/Centre, Magwi and Wau.

• Restore surveillance and health services after the 24 September Duk Padiet conflict (Jonglei), which

• Secure the funding needed to prevent an end-September/October service cliff: Coalition for Humanity's SSHF-USG (Mayendit) and Cholera Emergency Response (Leer) projects, Concern Worldwide's USG-SSHFfunded facilities across Guit/Leer/Panyijiar, and GOAL's SSHF-US-funded Twic sites and BHA-US-funded Ulang nutrition sites all close within days of each other (see Partners Response Update chapter).

title: UNHCR Romania Ukraine Refugee Situation Weekly Update #216 - 5 October 2026
content:
Highlight

On 1 October, UNHCR re-established its partnership with Estuar, an NGO specialized in mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Until the end of 2026, the partnership with Estuar will provide psychosocial and emotional support to 50 refugees from Ukraine living in Bucharest and Prahova county, selected according to identified needs and vulnerability criteria. Support will include some 400 individual counselling and psychological support sessions, information, orientation and referrals to specialized services, as well as initial and follow-up assessments to monitor beneficiaries’ progress. The partnership will also include the capacity building of 11 Estuar staff and MHPSS capacity building and self-care support for 20 staff from civil society organizations working with refugees through training on burnout prevention and staff wellbeing, crisis intervention and psychological first aid and support. UNHCR is also increasing support to it partners the Romanian National Council for Refugees (CNRR) and the Centre for Comparative Migration Studies (CSCM), using savings generated in other areas. This will help sustain and expand essential services, ensuring that refugees can continue to access timely and appropriate assistance.

UNHCR held meetings with Mr. Mircea-Dorin Crețu, Prefect of Sibiu county, county administration officials, Ms. Astrid Cora Fodor, Mayor of Sibiu, and Mr. Gheorghe Roman, Mayor of Mediaș to discuss the situation and inclusion of refugees from Ukraine and other countries who have found safety in Romania. UNHCR expressed its appreciation for the welcome extended by local authorities and communities and for their continued efforts to support the inclusion of refugees to access employment, education, language learning, and other essential services, enabling them to rebuild their lives in safety and dignity and become active members of their host communities. The UNHCR Representative, Mr. Pablo Zapata, and the UNHCR team provided an update on the refugee situation and presented UNHCR’s work to protect and support refugees across the country. UNHCR also met with its three grant partners in Sibiu County: the community-based organization Phoneo, including for a participatory assessment with Ukrainian refugee women, and the refugee-led organizations Arab Cultural Centre and ACUM, where a participatory assessment was conducted with older refugee women. UNHCR looks forward to continuing its close cooperation with local authorities to promote refugee inclusion and ensure that people seeking protection can access the support they need to build a safe and dignified future.

title: Nigeria Flood Operation: DREF Operational Update (MDRNG045)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

14-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Nigeria entered the 2026 rainy season with significant flood exposure, prompting the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), with IFRC support, to activate an Imminent DREF in July 2026. The operation focused on early warning, community preparedness, evacuation planning, risk communication and community level mitigation in areas identified as vulnerable to flooding. As the season progressed, forecast risk materialized into flooding across several parts of the country, resulting in displacement, damage to homes and assets, disruption of livelihoods and access to essential services, and increasing humanitarian needs.

Between 10 and 16 September 2026, NRCS conducted a multi sectoral assessment across 14 states, covering 3,944 respondents. The assessment estimated that 54,540 people had been affected, including 19,823 displaced people (36.3%). Ondo recorded the highest proportion of affected people who were displaced at 72.4%. The findings confirmed that the impact extended beyond displacement, with significant damage to shelter and household assets, disruption of food access and livelihoods, and gaps in WASH, health and psychosocial support.

The situation has continued to evolve. As of 18 September, the NRCS Emergency Operations Reporting (EOR) dashboard recorded 73,247 people affected and 31,175 displaced, based on 52 incident reports from 11 states and 32 LGAS, with 38 deaths, 1,968 injuries and 53,382 people reported in need. These figures are not combined with the assessment results because the two datasets have different coverage and methodologies. The EOR provides the latest operational picture, while the assessment provides household level evidence for response planning.

The geographic footprint has also expanded beyond the locations initially prioritized under the Imminent DREF. National coordination was strengthened through NEMA's activation of the National Emergency Operations Centre (NEOC) on 4 August 2026. In addition, NIHSA's National Flood Advisory NFA 2026 262, issued on 19 September and valid through 25 September, identified 15 states at high riverine flood risk, including several within the proposed response footprint. This indicates that the hazard remains active and further flooding is possible.

Against this progression from forecast risk to confirmed humanitarian impacts and continuing flood risk, NRCS proposes to scale up the Imminent DREF to a Response DREF. The initial operation established early action and preparedness capacity. The response phase will address the most severe unmet needs while maintaining early warning, preparedness and risk reduction measures in areas that remain exposed.

The proposed Response DREF will cover 10 states: Akwa Ibom, Anambra, Bayelsa, Benue, Cross River, Delta, Edo, Lagos, Ondo and Ogun, providing direct assistance to 3,000 households over six months and indirect support to approximately 73,000 people through early warning, community engagement, preparedness, WASH and public health risk communication, and targeted flood risk reduction.

title: Nigeria Weekly Report: Week of 25 September – 1 October 2026
content:
BOTTOM LINE

154 operational incidents and 116 fatalities across 32 states and the FCT. The secondhighest incident count of the past eight weeks and about 20% above the seven-week average (128). ISWAP's internal rift in Kukawa did not reduce operational reach: the group ran coordinated attacks in Adamawa, destroyed a school and clinic in Yobe, and mounted four road and public-space attacks in Borno on Independence Day. 29 September was the busiest day (30 incidents) and 30 September the deadliest (31 fatalities).

Three incidents directly hit humanitarian operations: RUTF looted at an INGO distribution site in Konduga (Borno); gunfire on an NGO vehicle at a bandit checkpoint on the Marafa–Maru road (Zamfara); and ISWAP's destruction of the Dokshi health facility with abduction of its head (Yobe).

title: Venezuela Emergency Response, Situation Report #5 (June 24 – 1 October)
content:
This Situation Report summarises CESVI’s first 100 days of response to the magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026, with a focus on La Guaira, Miranda and Distrito Capital, covering the period to 1 October. It outlines the results achieved and the transition towards early recovery.

Highlights

  • CESVI reached 2,568 households, approximately 10,100 people. Of these households, 99% had received no previous assistance.
  • The response combines essential supplies, shelter support and protection with expanding WASH activities. Five fixed and two mobile child-friendly spaces are operational, while preparations are under way to provide household water filters and launch seven water treatment plants.
  • CESVI is progressively expanding its restricted electronic voucher model, formally authorised by the relevant authorities, enabling families to choose essential items according to their priorities while supporting local businesses. Targeted in-kind assistance continues where markets remain disrupted or inaccessible.

The report identifies priorities for sustained, coordinated support to meet remaining needs and strengthen community recovery. English and Spanish versions are included.

title: Dooplaya District Incident Report: Burma Army air strike killed three villagers, injured two others, including a child, and caused destruction in Noh T'Kaw Township (May 2026)
content: This Incident Report describes events occurring in Noh T’Kaw (Kyainseikgyi) Township, Dooplaya District, in May 2026. On 24 May 2026, a Burma Army fighter jet dropped two 500-pound bombs in Aa--- village, Noh Tar Ghaw village tract, Noh T’Kaw Township. As a result, three women were killed, two villagers were injured, including a 16-year-old girl, and three houses, one restaurant, and one car were damaged. After the air strike, the villagers were panicked and fled temporarily to a place where they felt safer. The villagers were also worried about opening the village tract school, and some parents sent their children to schools in Thailand.

title: DRC - Concept of Operations - Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) Outbreak, October 2026
content:
Context

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially declared an Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak on 15 May 2026, following laboratory confirmation of the Bundibugyo strain in Ituri Province.

As of 26 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak remains concentrated in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with sustained transmission across multiple provinces and 8,067 confirmed cases and 3,901 deaths reported. The outbreak has expanded to 63 affected health zones across seven provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, and Sud-Ubangi. Uganda was officially declared the end of outbreak in late August 2026 following completion of the 42-day surveillance period with no onward transmission detected. While regional preparedness measures remain in place, the outbreak continues to pose a significant public health risk in eastern DRC, particularly in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé, where active transmission persists. Insecurity, population movements, displacement, difficult terrain, and limited access to health services continue to complicate response efforts and increase the risk of further spread within affected communities.

The World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Ebola outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May 2026 due to the risk of international spread and the need for a coordinated international response.

The outbreak poses a significant risk of further transmission both within the DRC and across neighbouring countries, particularly Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic, and South Sudan. Population movements and regional connectivity may further facilitate the spread of the disease to other major urban centres, including Butembo and Kisangani. At present, no vaccine is available for the Bundibugyo strain.
This marks the seventeenth Ebola outbreak recorded in the DRC. In response, the Minister of Health in DRC has called for the mobilisation of technical and financial partners to support the national response plan.

Compounding the public health crisis, eastern DRC remains severely affected by ongoing insecurity, population displacement, limited infrastructure, and access constraints. Recent developments in North and South Kivu have resulted in new population movements, including both displacement and returns to areas where basic services and security conditions remain fragile. Elsewhere, including in Maniema and Tanganyika provinces, ongoing instability continues to heighten humanitarian needs and increase protection risks, particularly for women and children, including exposure to gender-based violence.

title: World Vision Situation Report #1: Humanitarian Response to Flooding (03 October 2026)
content:

In World Vision Cambodia’s operational areas, 2,535 households, including 3,066 children among 7,919 affected people, have been directly impacted, with flooding also disrupting livelihoods, education and access to safe water and sanitation.

Working alongside local authorities and partners, we aim to protect the most vulnerable children and families and support their recovery with dignity and hope.

content:

title: Syria: Health Sector Bulletin - September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Core monthly subjects:

Service continuity became the central operational issue: the transition of health services from fragmented humanitarian and NGO arrangements toward national management, particularly in the northeast and in areas where NGO support was ending. Fuel costs, transport, staffing, medicine supply, equipment maintenance and referral access had become the clearest sources of operational pressure. Northeast transition risk centered on staffing, authority, referral pathways, ambulance movement, supplies and road access rather than a complete breakdown of services. Fuel pressure affected generators, ambulances, staff transport, water pumping and trucking, cold chain, medical logistics and household access to care. Essential medicines, dialysis consumables, diagnostics, oxygen, oncology and equipment maintenance remained high-priority continuity risks.

Trauma, EMS and referral readiness remained critical: Explosive ordnance and ammunition incidents, serious road crashes, localized violence and referral constraints repeatedly kept trauma readiness at or near the top of the priority lists. There is a need for facility-level surge readiness rather than an assumption that national capacity can absorb localized shocks. Maintain ambulance, blood, surgical, burn, ICU and alternate referral capacity in exposed areas. Referral networks are particularly vulnerable where insecurity, road restrictions, fuel costs and limited receiving capacity overlap. Explosive-risk management remains a health-sector issue because casualty events can rapidly overwhelm individual facilities.

Public-health surveillance stayed in a high-vigilance posture: Vaccination, measles and polio surveillance were critical and shifted toward campaign verification, missed-child identification and catch-up activity. Later updates continued to prioritize measles case finding and vaccination, while waterborne disease, acute watery diarrhoea, foodborne illness and hepatitis A remained medium-high vulnerabilities requiring investigation if local clusters appeared. Key VPD triggers: rash-fever clusters, missed or zero-dose child pockets, cold-chain interruption, AFP alerts and school or returnee-community clustering. Key WASH triggers: linked severe diarrhoeal cases, unsafe shared water, interrupted pumping or chlorination, or a localized jaundice/hepatitis cluster. Malnutrition remained a chronic high-pressure issue, especially where food costs, diarrhoeal disease and nutrition-supply interruptions overlap.

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 20 (21 - 27 September 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Central African Republic
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 27 September 2026, the country had reported 8,116 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including 3,924 deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 63 health zones across 7 provinces have reported at least 1 confirmed case. Transmission remains concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu Provinces, with Ituri accounting for 76.2 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases nationwide, underscoring its continued role as the epicentre of the outbreak.

Although the daily number of new confirmed cases has declined from earlier peaks observed during the outbreak, transmission continues across multiple provinces, and the outbreak remains a significant public health threat. On 27 September, the Ministry of Health reported 49 new confirmed cases and 23 confirmed deaths, including 18 community deaths. Transmission remains concentrated in Ituri (27), North Kivu (18) and Haut-Uélé (4).

The continued occurrence of community deaths and ongoing transmission across multiple provinces points to persistent challenges in early detection, referral, contact follow-up and timely access to care. As of 27 September, the national contact follow-up rate stood at 75.9 per cent, underscoring the need for sustained investment in disease surveillance, case investigation and response capacities.

The outbreak continues to evolve within a complex humanitarian and mobility context. Population movements associated with trade, livelihoods, displacement, health-seeking behaviour and family ties continue within outbreak-affected areas and across international borders. Continued transmission in eastern DRC reinforces the importance of preparedness measures in neighbouring countries connected through established mobility corridors, including disease surveillance, population mobility monitoring, referral systems, infection, prevention and control (IPC) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE).

Preparedness activities across affected and at-risk countries continue to be informed by findings from population mobility mapping (PMM), flow monitoring, preparedness assessments and cross-border risk analyses. These approaches support evidencebased prioritization of preparedness investments, including disease surveillance, referral systems, RCCE and operational readiness measures at points of entry (PoEs), border communities, displacement settings and other high-risk locations.

In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) system-wide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM continues to support outbreak response activities across affected and at-risk countries. Response and readiness activities remain ongoing in DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, while preparedness efforts continue in Angola, the Central African Republic (CAR), Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia to strengthen disease surveillance, operational readiness, community engagement and cross-border coordination capacities.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) Earthquake Response Situation Report #31 (24 to 30 September 2026)
content:
The Report #31 provides an update on IOM's response to the earthquakes that struck Venezuela on 24 June 2026. According to the latest official information, 107 transitory camps remain operational with a capacity for 25,212 people, of whom 23,901 remain accommodated. During the reporting period, IOM continued managing and co-managing four planned camps in La Guaira, strengthened inter-agency coordination and expanded support across shelter, WASH, health, protection and early recovery sectors.

Highlights

IOM expanded Health and MHPSS service coverage in planned camps and affected communities through mobile outreach, hospital-based care and deployed health teams in La Guaira and Miranda. More than 700 health and mental health consultations were delivered during the reporting period, strengthening access to primary healthcare, sexual and reproductive health services, chronic disease follow-up and specialized referrals.

IOM strengthened camp management and early recovery efforts through population registry updates, demographic verification exercises and follow-up on housing solutions. Progress was also made in the housing repair pilot in César Nieves, where technical assessments were completed for the first 20 prioritized houses to support future recovery interventions.

IOM reinforced its protection response through the deployment of specialized mobile teams in all planned camps. Through its partners, IOM reached 126 people with protection services, provided 84 legal counselling sessions, managed 32 new cases and facilitated 64 referrals to competent institutions, while strengthening access to documentation, child protection activities and prevention measures for women and girls.

IOM Activities

IOM continued managing the José María Vargas Sports Complex planned camp and co-managing César Nieves, Campo de Golf and Mare Abajo II together with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Activities included monitoring shelter conditions, updating population records, supporting relocation and housing solution processes, strengthening community information mechanisms and coordinating with national, state and local authorities.

As part of its early recovery and relief response, IOM distributed 225 non-food item kits to 225 families in the communities of Boca de Yaracuy and El Cambur. Between 25 July and 30 September, IOM distributed 9,679 collapsible jerry cans and 5,846 hygiene items. Since the onset of the response, more than 11,173 plastic tarpaulins, 6,813 kitchen sets, 6,146 toolkits and 4,563 solar lamps have been distributed to affected households.

In the WASH sector, IOM continued monitoring water supply, drainage systems and sanitation infrastructure in planned camps. During the reporting period, hygiene kit distributions were coordinated, water quality monitoring continued and 90,000 litres of water were delivered to affected camps and communities. In Mare Abajo II, IOM monitored the functionality of 47 portable toilets, 44 handwashing stations and 13 laundry points.

In health and mental health, IOM, Ven Da Tu Mano and humanitarian partners expanded service delivery through mobile medical teams in La Guaira and Miranda, interventions at the José María Vargas Sports Complex and services provided through the César Nieves Field Hospital. At the same time, IOM strengthened community-based protection activities, referral mechanisms, legal assistance, access to documentation, inter-agency coordination and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) actions, including staff training and partner capacity assessments.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue monitoring shelter conditions, population movements, relocation processes and housing solutions across planned camps. The Organization will also continue implementing the housing repair pilot in César Nieves, strengthen preparedness measures in transitory camps and complete ongoing population verification and registration activities.

IOM will maintain Health and MHPSS services, expand the deployment of emergency medical teams according to identified needs, continue monitoring WASH services and chronic health conditions, reinforce protection and documentation support activities, and further strengthen coordination with authorities, humanitarian partners and sectoral coordination mechanisms to ensure continuity of assistance.

title: Monthly Report on the Implementation of Epidemic Intelligence in the Americas - Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) - July 2026
content:
I. Regional Epidemic Intelligence Activity

A. Detection of early warning flags

At the regional level, the Health Emergency Information and Risk Assessment Unit (HIM) of the PAHO Health Emergencies Department (PHE) operates through the continuous epidemic intelligence phases, scanning multiple sources to identify Early warning flags1 (information indicating a potential acute public health risk) in the Americas Region.

Early warning flags are triaged to identify if these are signals requiring verification in close coordination with Member States. Once verified, a signal becomes an event. PAHO conducts risk assessments and continuously monitors these events, including epidemiological and geospatial analysis, while facilitating information exchange with Member States and partners and producing actionable intelligence and technical support to guide timely public health decisions and response across the Americas.

title: Kler Lwee Htoo District Incident Report: A Burma Army landmine injured two displaced villagers in Moo Township (March 2026) [EN/Karen/MY]
content:
Excerpt

Part 3 – Complete Description of the Incident

Describe the Incident(s) in complete detail.

The villagers who live in Moo special area, Moo (Mone) Township, Kler Lwee Htoo (Nyaunglebin) District had to experience displacement and relocation because the Burma military regime conducted indiscriminate shelling and air strikes during January 2026. Maung H--- was also one of the displaced villagers from Ba--- village, Lay Tone village tract, Moo special area, who displaced in Bc--- village, Mya P’Go village tract, Moo special area.

On 4 March 2026, some of the displaced villagers from Ba--- village went back to check on their houses and take their properties that they left in the village. Maung H--- was asked for help to carry the properties, so he accompanied those villagers to help his friends. Four villagers, including Maung H---, went back, and when they arrived at Ba--- village’s entrance at 6:40 am, Maung H--- stepped on a landmine, and it exploded. Due to the explosion, both of Maung H---’s legs were hit and injured by mine fragments, and another villager [unknown name] was also hit by the fragments and sustained minor injuries on his bladder and one of his eyes.

Prior to the incident [in early January 2026], an unknown battalion of the Burma military regime had entered the village for a short time, before leaving again. After they went back, the local army, PDF [People’s Defence Force][10] and KNLA [Karen National Liberation Army][11] soldiers, checked the area, and they found the Burma military regime had planted a lot of landmines. They removed [some of] the landmines, but [some of] these were not gone yet. However, [the PDF and KNLA] allowed the villagers to go back because the villagers wanted to take the things that they left [their properties]. Therefore, [Maung H---] stepped on this Burma military regime landmine. The victim, Maung H---, said: “They [the PDF and KNLA] said: ‘It is not clear yet.’ They were not allowing the villagers to enter [into the village]. However, because the villagers were very hurried, they allowed [them] to enter and unfortunately, I got hit [by a landmine]. I stepped on [the landmine] after two people passed ahead [of me]. There were four people in total who went back [to the village]. […] [When the landmine exploded,] I went up into the air and the bag that I took with me flew away. After that, [the other people] phoned a village tract administrator. Then, he contacted the organisations [the KNLA and PDF] to rescue [me]. They also called a mine clearance team and they cleared [the landmines]. It took 30 minutes [to clear the landmines].”

After Maung H--- stepped on the landmine, his friends transported him to Bb--- clinic, which is located in Bb--- village, Kyaung Pyan village tract, Moo special area. Because he sustained a severe injury on his left leg, it was amputated at Bb--- clinic. He didn’t have to pay anything for the treatment or transportation costs. Regarding the other injured villager, he received treatment from a CDM [Civil Disobedience Movement][12] doctor in Ba--- village, because he sustained only minor injuries. After this incident, Ba--- villagers dared not to go back and take their possessions from the village anymore. Regarding Maung H---, he lost his left leg, and he could not work as before to earn a livelihood for his family members. At the time of the interview, Maung H--- had not been discharged from the clinic yet, but his leg injury was getting better. He hoped to get a prosthetic leg once his injury healed so that he could work to earn a livelihood for his family members.

The villagers in Moo special area must face livelihood, healthcare, and education challenges because the Burma military regime violated the [human rights of the] villagers by conducting shelling, drone strikes, and air strikes and entering the villages.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Nepal Floods (10 - 30 September 2026)
content:
More than a month after the flash flood on 26 August, communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts continue to face displacement and disrupted access to essential health and protection services. Approximately 352,000 people have been affected, including an estimated 98,560 women of reproductive age. To date, 1,453 deaths have been reported, while 5,285 people remain unaccounted for.

Between 10 and 30 September, UNFPA and its partners reached 2,722 people across seven municipalities with life-saving sexual and reproductive health services, as well as gender-based violence prevention and response services.

UNFPA requires US$3.5 million to implement its six-month flood response in Nepal. As of the end of September, US$1.64 million had been received, leaving a gap of US$1.86 million. This funding is urgently needed to ensure the continuity and restoration of essential sexual and reproductive health services, gender-based violence prevention and response, psychosocial support, and assistance to meet the dignity needs of affected women and girls.

title: UNFPA Sudan Situation Report (1 to 31 August 2026)
content:
Throughout August, women and girls in Sudan continued to face significant humanitarian and protection challenges amid ongoing conflict, displacement and deteriorating economic conditions.

Renewed fighting in Blue Nile State displaced approximately 21,000 people, adding to existing humanitarian needs and placing further strain on already overstretched health and protection services.

Across Greater Kordofan, continued hostilities and insecurity are driving further displacement, while heavy rains and flooding are worsening living conditions and restricting access to essential services in displacement sites and makeshift settlements. The humanitarian situation is further compounded by a cholera outbreak, with more than 2,200 cases and 160 deaths reported.

During August, UNFPA and its partners reached nearly 121,700 people with sexual and reproductive health services and more than 71,000 people with gender-based violence prevention and response services. However, UNFPA’s appeal remains significantly underfunded, with only 37 per cent received of the US$129.2 million required. This funding shortfall is limiting UNFPA’s ability to sustain and scale up life-saving services for women and girls across Sudan.

title: Nepal Flash Flood 2026 Situation Report 6 (1 October 2026)
content:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at approximately 9:00 AM on 26 August 2026, causing significant loss and damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi are among the worst affected areas, with impacts reported on communities, markets, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure.

The cause of the flood remains under investigation, with authorities assessing the possibility of a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or another upstream hydrological event. The Government of Nepal has mobilised security forces for search, rescue and relief operations and issued alerts for communities downstream along the Trishuli River corridor.

title: Africa CDC Epidemic Intelligence Weekly Report, September 2026
content:
Welcome to our Epidemic Intelligence Weekly Report, your trusted source for real-time updates on priority events of concern on the continent. The narrative brought to you focuses on three main areas: the epidemiological situation, event assessment (risk assessment and geoscope) and public health interventions by the affected Member State, partners, and Africa CDC. Every week we highlight events reported to Africa CDC that rank from moderate to very high risk as per the Africa CDC risk assessment tool.

Geographic Focus: Reports could either focus on events affecting single country or multiple countries.

Inclusion criteria: While Africa CDC continues to track all public health events on the continent, this report highlights only moderate to very high-risk events (with new updates in the reporting week).

Events: We focus on a range of health threats, ranging from emerging infectious diseases to endemic conditions, and natural disasters. We follow a one-health multisectoral approach highlighting events across all relevant sectors: animal, environmental and human.

This Event-Based Surveillance Weekly Report is your compass for navigating Africa’s public health landscape. We empower you with the latest information and insights, for informed decisions and effective interventions to attain a healthy and prosperous Africa.

title: VNM: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy Rainfall caused flooding #2 (2026-10-01)
content:
Description

According to Viet Nam authorities, flooding from the earlier heavy-rain episode in northern and north-central Viet Nam continues to recede. Subsequent heavy rainfall affected parts of central and southern Viet Nam, with impacts generally remaining localized.

  • Lam Dong: Government assessments recorded 2,848 houses flooded and approximately 7,540 ha of rice, vegetables and other crops affected during 20–24 September. Floodwaters have since receded, with no houses remaining flooded and relocated households returning home.
  • Dong Nai: The person previously reported missing after being swept away was confirmed dead. On 29 September, heavy rainfall caused localized flooding of 70 houses in Long Thanh, with flood depths of approximately 0.5–1.2 m. Around 2.4 km of local roads were flooded or affected by erosion. Water had largely receded by 30 September.
  • Ho Chi Minh City: Heavy rainfall on 30 September caused widespread urban flooding, disrupting transport and daily activities. Water had largely receded by the evening. No casualty or displacement figures were reported.
  • Ca Mau: Prolonged rainfall and high tides affected agricultural and aquaculture production, including approximately 6,866 ha of summer-autumn rice, more than 11,000 ha of newly planted rice-shrimp areas and more than 5,450 ha of aquaculture. A thunderstorm on 28 September damaged or unroofed 11 houses.
  • Vinh Long: A localized embankment breach in Cai Ga, Cho Lach, flooded 20 households and more than 20 ha of fruit trees. Local authorities mobilized personnel and equipment to reinforce the embankment and support affected households.

Current Weather and Hydrological Situation

The broader heavy-rain episode has eased. Monitoring is currently focused on localized rainfall in southern Viet Nam, Mekong/Cuu Long River levels and high-tide conditions. The National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting (NCHMF) continues to monitor rainfall, river levels and tidal conditions. Current forecasts indicate mainly localized afternoon and evening thunderstorms, rather than another widespread heavy-rain event.

title: Hostilities in Yemen | UNFPA Flash Update (15 – 28 September 2026)
content:
Rapidly escalating hostilities along Yemen’s western coast and the southern Taiz frontlines have continued since early September, resulting in the displacement of more than 145,000 people, with numbers doubling over the past two weeks.

Displaced women and girls are among the most vulnerable and face serious health and protection risks. UNFPA estimates that approximately 35,000 women of childbearing age and more than 3,200 pregnant women are among those displaced. UNFPA partners have reported several instances of pregnant women giving birth on the roadside while fleeing hostilities, without skilled assistance and amid life-threatening delays in reaching comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care.

The intensifying violence has disrupted reproductive health services in affected governorates. Nine health facilities have reportedly been destroyed or rendered non-functional, while eight have suspended services. The reduced access to antenatal care and safe delivery services is increasing the risks of miscarriage, premature and obstructed labour, and hypertensive complications for pregnant women.

Repeated displacement is also increasing the exposure of women and girls to gender-based violence. Whilst three UNFPA-supported women and girls’ shelters remain operational, other UNFPA-supported gender-based violence services are being disrupted by intensifying hostilities along the West Coast. Women and girls’ safe spaces in Al Mukha, Hays and Al Khukhah remained closed, and the displacement of over 20 key technical and service-delivery personnel due to ongoing hostilities is further affecting service continuity.

UNFPA continues to lead the coordination of reproductive health and women’s protection services within the humanitarian response. The UNFPA-led UN Inter-Agency Rapid Response Mechanism remains a first-line humanitarian response, delivering emergency relief to nearly 92,000 individuals as of 28 September.

However, funding constraints are severely limiting UNFPA’s ability to respond. UNFPA requires US$22.7 million to support its humanitarian response in Yemen through December 2026, yet only 6 per cent of the required funding has been received to date.

title: Bosnia & Herzegovina — Migrant Mobility Situation Report (August 2026)

title: Haiti: Nationwide Humanitarian Response | 1 July to 31 August 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 10,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been registered in the commune of Kenscoff, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
  • At least 47 people were killed and 22 injured during armed attacks on 23 and 24 August in Kenscoff, according to the United Nations.
  • Some 11,364 people have been displaced in the Artibonite department as a result of violence.
  • The World Food Programme (WFP) assisted 482,112 people in August, distributing 2,376.55 metric tons of food and US$5.7 million in cash transfers to vulnerable households.
  • Nutrition sector partners, supporting the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP), screened 43,679 children under five, enabling the treatment of 5,864 cases of severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
  • The Pan American Health Organization / World Health Organization (PAHO/WHO) distributed 31.7 metric tons of medicines, equipment and medical supplies to health institutions and health directorates in the Ouest department.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

During July and August 2026, the humanitarian situation in Haiti deteriorated sharply due to escalating armed violence and successive population displacements in several departments.

The commune of Kenscoff (Ouest department) was hit by two major waves of attacks by armed groups. Attacks carried out from 4 to 8 July in Téléco, Le Refuge, Viard and the 5th communal section of Grand Fond led to houses being set on fire, loss of life, the hostage-taking of more than 50 people and the displacement of 5,840 people (1,836 households) (ETT 100.1) according to IOM.

A new series of attacks during the night of 23 to 24 August left at least 47 dead and 22 injured, displacing further 4,238 people (ETT 105.1) and confirming the continued deterioration of security conditions in the area.

Armed violence has also triggered several waves of forced displacement in Artibonite department. Clashes in Dessalines and Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite between 6 and 23 July displaced some 6,254 people (ETT 101.2), followed by renewed clashes in Saint-Michel de l’Attalaye between 28 and 31 July that displaced 4,216 people (ETT 103). Armed attacks on 29 August in the locality of Jean Denis forced a further 894 people (ETT 106) to flee. Most displaced people found refuge with host families, while a minority settled in existing displacement sites, highlighting the precarious protection conditions in the department.

At the same time, as the hurricane season approaches its peak, WFP estimates that some 1.1 million people are exposed to the impacts of El Niño, including 700,000 highly vulnerable people who may require emergency assistance due to vegetation water stress and high levels of food insecurity.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 87, as of 29 September 2026

title: UNAMA confirms Civilian Casualties in Afghanistan | United Nations Peace Operations
content:
KABUL - UNAMA has confirmed that at least 10 civilians were killed, most of them children, and nine people injured in airstrikes carried out in Afghanistan’s Kunar and Helmand provinces earlier today.

Civilians continue to be affected by cross-border hostilities. Just a week ago, on September 21, UNAMA confirmed the killing of at least three civilians with four others injured in another airstrike in Kunar province.

So far in 2026, UNAMA has documented over 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries in Afghanistan from cross-border armed violence.

UNAMA reiterates its call for de-escalation, dialogue, respect for international law and prevention of further civilian harm.

title: Yemen - Displacement Caused by Escalation in the West Coast — Update #12 (30 September 2026)
content:

On 29 September 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded an increase of 18,306 individual IDPs compared to the previous report, making the displacement between 1 August to 29 September reach an approximate of 151,794 individuals (approximately 25,299 households1). title: Ukraine Crisis Response Situation | July 2026 Fact Sheet
content:
World Vision started working in Ukraine in March 2022 through 6 and now 3 active offices in Ukraine (Kyiv, Dnipro, Mykolaiv), which currently support aid efforts reaching conflict-affected people. While also supported Ukrainian refugees and host communities in Moldova, Romania, and Georgia. title: Colombia: Flash Update 015- Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - September 30, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia based on inputs from humanitarian partners and official reports (as of 30 September, 18:00 local time). This document concludes the weekly update, with resources available for reference regarding the situation and response.

  1. Nearly two months after the earthquake, the Government is moving into the recovery phase through the Specific Action Plan for Recovery (PAE in spanish). However, it remains important to address the impacts in remote rural areas facing multiple challenges, where the effects of the earthquake, armed conflict, and other emergencies converge.
  2. Gaps persist in the identification of affected populations, damage assessments, and access to essential services. Rural, ethnic, refugee, and migrant communities face greater risks of exclusion, insufficient protection, and limited recovery opportunities.
  3. Complementing the government response, at least 35 humanitarian organizations have assisted 239,000 people across 90 municipalities through interventions in health, food assistance, shelter, WASH, protection, education, and cash transfers, as well as technical and legal assistance.
  4. Recovery efforts face challenges in ensuring safe returns from temporary shelters, strengthening local capacities, and guaranteeing equitable access to institutional assistance, particularly in areas with limited state presence and multiple impacts.

With this document, the weekly publication comes to an end. Resources for consultation and reporting on the situation and response will remain available. These products were made possible through continued partner reporting, which should be maintained, and the support of 3iS in developing visual resources.

title: THA: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding #2 (2026-10-01)
content:
Description

According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), Ministry of Interior, Thailand has experienced prolonged heavy rainfall since mid-September, resulting in widespread flooding across the country. The flooding has been driven by intense rainfall, river overflows and increased water discharge, with water levels continuing to rise in several central and eastern provinces. The situation remains dynamic, with water levels rising, stabilising or receding depending on the location.

Water levels continued to rise in several provinces, including Nakhon Sawan, Uthai Thani, Lop Buri, Chai Nat, Sing Buri, Suphan Buri, Kanchanaburi, Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya, Samut Prakan, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, Ratchaburi, Nakhon Nayok, Prachin Buri, Chachoengsao, Sa Kaeo, Chon Buri and parts of northeastern Thailand. In other affected areas, floodwaters remained stable or gradually receded. Bangkok was also significantly affected, with approximately 329,000 households impacted.

As of 1 October 2026, flooding remained ongoing in 30 provinces, affecting 191 districts, 1,228 sub-districts and 8,714 villages. An estimated 1,177,404 households (3,352,395 people), including those in Bangkok, were affected.

title: Nepal: Flash Floods - LTC Telecoms Situation Report #4 [Final] (Reporting period: 26 August - 30 September 2026)
content:
This consolidated Situation Report summarizes the telecommunications impacts of the flash floods that struck Nepal on 26 August 2026 and the resulting response. Following activation of the Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) on 02 September, LTC Telecoms supported humanitarian partners through telecommunications coordination, assessments, connectivity services and information management. The report highlights the evolving operational context, telecommunications recovery, response activities and transition to longer-term recovery and preparedness efforts.

Summary Points

• One month after the flash floods of 26 August, government-led response efforts under the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) had begun transitioning from life-saving activities towards rehabilitation, early recovery and longer-term support.

• Telecommunications services were largely restored across the most affected districts through operatorled repairs, temporary microwave backhaul, adjacenttower coverage and backup power solutions. However, sustaining reliable services in remote and difficult-to-access locations remained a challenge.

• Following activation of the LTC on 02 September, LTC Telecoms supported humanitarian partners through coordination, assessments, shared connectivity services and information management. The LTC Telecoms Coordinator completed a two-week mission from 05 to 18 September before handing over responsibilities to the Inter-Agency IT Operations Officer to support continuity and recovery.

title: Colombia Earthquake response Situation Report # 12 | 29 September 2026
content:
Situation Overview

According to the latest information from the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD), as of September 28, 335 people have been reported dead, 105 missing, 364 rescued, 4,516 injured, and 486,917 affected following the earthquake of August 10, 2026. In addition, 206,931 homes were damaged, 36,478 homes destroyed, 402 health facilities affected, 4,431 educational institutions affected, and 6,094 community centers affected, across 16 departments and 500 municipalities. According to information from the Single Registry of Affected Persons (RUD), as of September 26, 364,668 families and 778,274 people have been registered, including 84,855 habitable homes, 104,038 uninhabitable homes, 19,142 destroyed homes, and 119,752 damaged homes. More than six weeks after the earthquake, the needs of the affected population have evolved from immediate assistance toward requirements related to durable housing solutions, livelihood recovery, infrastructure rehabilitation, and sustained access to essential services. In Cali, Valle del Cauca, approximately 20,000 families are still reported to be displaced from their homes, while structural assessments and demolitions continue. The institutional and international cooperation response continues to include humanitarian assistance and financial support, while increasing attention is being placed on evacuated families, housing assessments, subsidies, educational infrastructure, and continuity of services. Over the past week, the World Bank approved an additional US$200 million in financing to support the response and recovery following the earthquake, including reconstruction needs and the strengthening of disaster risk management and financing mechanisms. This new financing adds to the US$200 million previously disbursed, bringing the total resources mobilized by the institution for the emergency to US$400 million.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 313: Week 4 - September 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

During the 4th week of September, prices show limited week-on-week volatility, although underlying pressures remained evident. The higher cost of imports through longer and alternate routes and the rise in fuel prices continue to increase transportation and supply-chain costs and exert upward pressure on market prices. Meanwhile, rice, wheat flour, cooking oil, sugar and salt prices remained elevated compared with last year, while weak labour availability and subdued purchasing power continued to constrain household food access.

Food Categories: National average food prices recorded mixed but generally modest movements during the week, although provincial disparities persisted. While several commodities experienced minor price adjustments, the year-on-year comparison highlights a significant increase in rice, wheat flour, cooking oil, sugar, salt and potato prices.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and flour prices recorded negligible weekly fluctuations, however compared to last year, wheat grain and low-price wheat flour remained 14% higher.

• Rice: Rice prices edged down during the week, with Palawi declining by 0.4% and Sholae by 0.5%. Nevertheless, both varieties continued to register substantial annual increases of 20% and 35%, respectively, and both remained significantly above their three-year average levels.

• Other Staples: Weekly price movements across cooking oil, sugar, pulses, salt and bread remained limited. Cooking oil, sugar and salt continued to trade above last year's levels, by 13%, 9% and 7%, respectively, whereas pulses and bread remained 12% and 3% below their corresponding annual levels.

• Vegetables: Potato prices fell by 3.6% during the week, while tomato and onion prices declined only marginally by 1.2% and 0.4%, respectively. Despite the weekly decline, potato remained 30% above last year and 22% above its three-year average. Tomato and onion prices were 31% and 5% lower year-on-year, respectively.

Non-Food Categories: Terms of Trade (ToT): The ToT, which reflects purchasing power, remained constraint for both labourdependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Unskilled Labour ToT: The nominal casual labour ToT declined slightly to 9.9 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 16% decline from last year and 13% decline against the three-year average. The sustained decline in purchasing power reflects continued pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 15% below last year and 19% below the three-year average. Consequently, the real unskilled labour ToT shows a 29% decline YoY.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 260 kg of low-price wheat flour, which is 15% below last year and 8% below the three-year average. This indicates continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and Agricultural Inputs: DAP and Urea prices recorded marginal weekly changes. Despite minor weekly fluctuations, annual prices remained elevated, with DAP 13% and urea 26% higher than last year. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices remained broadly stable due to low market demand and standing 7% and 6% below last year, respectively.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #2 (28 September 2026)

title: Djibouti Population movement: Yemen Influx 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRDJ011)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

09-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

As a result of the deteriorating security and humanitarian situation in Yemen, a significant influx of population movement has been observed towards Djibouti. Since 10 September 2026, the Obock region has been experiencing a sudden and massive arrival of people from Yemen, mainly women and children. According to preliminary figures shared by ONARS, approximately 1,600 Yemeni people on the move had arrived in the Obock region by Saturday, 13 September 2026. This number increased to 2,935 people on the move by Thursday, 17 September 2026, and is expected to continue increasing. Approximately 50% of the arrived population are minors. The arrivals have been reported at several locations along the coast, including Obock Port and the coastal areas of Khor Angar, Moulhoul and Siâm. Some groups of population movement reportedly arrived after experiencing difficulties at sea, with Djiboutian Coast Guard authorities conducting search and rescue operations and assisting people whose boats had run out of fuel. Arrived population on the move are currently located in the coastal areas are awaiting arrangements for their transfer to Obock town for registration, next transition and referral to appropriate services.

title: Mozambique | Floods 2026 - Six-Month Operation Update (MDRMZ027)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Mozambique continues to face a significant humanitarian crisis following intense and prolonged flooding that began in late December 2025. According to the latest cumulative data from the National Institute of Disaster Management (INGD), approximately 724,131 people (170,877 families) have been affected nationwide, including 27 fatalities, 147 injuries and nine people reported missing1 . Although the heavy rainfall has slowed, the humanitarian impact remains severe.

Flooding has damaged or destroyed 201,411 houses (183,866 flooded, 12,279 partially destroyed and 5,266 completely destroyed), and critical infrastructure has been extensively affected, including more than 880 kilometres of roads, 228 bridges and 44 water supply systems. A total of 257 health facilities have also been impacted, significantly restricting access to essential services, markets and hard-to-reach communities.

Agricultural losses are substantial, with over 440,000 hectares of crops damaged and more than 412,000 livestock lost, undermining livelihoods and exacerbating food insecurity during a crucial agricultural period1 . While displacement has declined from the peak of the emergency, 39 accommodation centres remain operational, currently hosting approximately 32,030 people in overcrowded conditions1 . These sites continue to face critical gaps in shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health services, food assistance and protection support, alongside heightened risks of cholera and malaria linked to stagnant water and damaged infrastructure.

Some areas remain flooded, and access constraints persist due to damaged infrastructure. As Mozambique remains within the 2025–2026 cyclone season, affected communities continue to face heightened vulnerability to further shocks, underscoring the need for sustained humanitarian assistance and early recovery support.

title: Afghanistan | Earthquake - DREF Final Report (MDRAF019)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

01-09-2025

What happened, where and when?

On 31 August 2025, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck southeastern Afghanistan near Jalalabad, approximately 30 km from Momand Dara (Nangarhar) and Nurgal (Kunar). The earthquake caused strong shaking across Kunar and Nangarhar, with effects also felt in Laghman and Nuristan. Aftershocks of magnitude 5.2, 4.5, and 5.6 followed immediately after the initial quake and again on 5 September, adding to the damage and complicating the early response. On 23 September 2025, a 4.9-magnitude earthquake struck eastern Afghanistan at a depth of 10 km, approximately 23 km from Jalalabad, the capital of Nangarhar province. It damaged key infrastructure, including water sources, and losses of livestock and farmland were reported.

A Federation-wide Emergency Appeal of CHF 25 million with timeframe until 31 December 2027 was launched on 3 September 2025 to support ARCS' relief and early recovery efforts. As a part of the Appeal, a DREF allocation of CHF 1 million was released to support the response to the southeastern earthquake. The Appeal and the total Federation-wide funding requirement was later revised to CHF 30 million following the second earthquake in northern Afghanistan in November 2026. As of 30 June 2026, the Emergency Appeal is approximately 35 per cent funded with CHF 9,130,312 mobilized against the 27 million Secretariat funding requirement.

title: Ukraine - Conflict: LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #63 - Reporting period: September 2026
content:
The WFP-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) on 03 March 2022 in response to the crisis in Ukraine. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC Telecoms activities.

title: Venezuela: Earthquakes - LTC (Telecoms Area) Final Situation Report #08 (Reporting period: 24 June - 30 September 2026)

title: Democratic Republic of the Congo: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu and Tanganyika provinces - DIEM-Monitoring emergency agriculture support brief, May 2026 (round 11)

Synopsis (short abstract)

This emergency agriculture support brief presents the results of the latest Data in Emergencies Monitoring (DIEM-Monitoring) round conducted in the Democratic Republic of the Congo from January to March 2026. A total of 867 477 agricultural households are in need of emergency agricultural assistance in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This DIEM-Monitoring brief provides humanitarian actors with an in-depth analysis focused on the agricultural households in need to target interventions aimed at supporting livelihoods and strengthening resilience to future shocks, protecting the food security of rural populations. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) established DIEM-Monitoring in June 2020. title: UNRWA Situation Report #235 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
content:
Highlights

The Gaza Strip

  • UNRWA started the 2026/2027 school year on 19 September across the Gaza Strip through a combination of in-person and distance learning. A launch event was held in Nuseirat Camp at an UNRWA school that has fully returned to education use, after having been used previously as an emergency shelter. During the first week of the school year, nearly 97,000 students attended UNRWA learning spaces across the Gaza Strip.
  • Students also returned to in-person learning at both campuses of the UNRWA Rehabilitation Centre for the Visually Impaired (RCVI), with classes resuming in Deir El Balah on 19 September and in Gaza City on 20 September.
  • UNRWA opened two additional carpentry workshops, bringing the total to three facilities operating in Khan Younis, Deir El Balah and Gaza City. Together, the workshops can produce approximately 450 school desks and chairs per week to support the expansion of learning spaces.
  • Multiple war-damaged residential buildings collapsed in the Gaza Strip during the reporting period, highlighting the risks faced by families sheltering in unsafe structures. UN Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov warned that people live in “hundreds of damaged structures assessed as unsafe, for lack of better options”. These include some families sheltering in non-operational UNRWA installations, which are no longer managed by UNRWA, for safety reasons. With winter approaching, risks are expected to increase as rainfall further weakens already compromised structures. UNRWA remains engaged in inter-agency efforts to address the issue and encourage families to relocate to safer shelter options where available.
  • Over the reporting period, Israeli authorities issued multiple evacuation orders and shelter-in-place alerts affecting UNRWA installations across the Gaza Strip. Separately, hostilities in the vicinity of UNRWA facilities resulted in injuries to six displaced persons sheltering at UNRWA schools, including four children. One cash-for-work beneficiary supporting UNRWA operations was killed and one UNRWA staff member seriously injured in separate incidents linked to strikes by Israeli forces in their vicinity.

Key points

The Gaza Strip

Fatalities and injuries

  • Between 7 October 2023 and 20 September 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the Health Cluster, 73,914 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 174,952 were injured. This includes 1,394 fatalities and 4,991 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 20 September 2026.
  • UNRWA has recorded 394 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 83 persons who were supporting UNRWA[2], as of 22 September.

Health crisis

  • The worsening fuel and engine oil shortage is increasingly disrupting health services across the Gaza Strip. The UN warned that reduced fuel support to hospitals, driven by funding shortfalls and high procurement costs, could affect most hospitals and lead to cuts in primary and secondary healthcare services.
  • Over the reporting period, several UNRWA health centres also experienced temporary disruptions due to generator overload, highlighting the growing operational impact of the shortage of fuel, lubricant oil and spare parts on the delivery of healthcare.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs

  • According to the WASH Cluster’s Light Touch Monitoring Survey, completed in early July 2026, 90 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene – an increase from 84 per cent the previous month.

Shelter needs

  • According to the Shelter Cluster’s classification, based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks.

Protection needs

  • According to UN Women, the number of women-headed households in the Gaza Strip has doubled since October 2023, reaching about 86,000 households – or almost one in every four families. This includes widows and women whose husbands are missing, detained, severely injured, or forcibly disappeared, or whose fate simply remains unknown.

Operational implications and humanitarian response

  • Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with over 4,000 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, health, and other services to Palestine Refugees.
  • All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[3] that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact between Israeli officials and UNRWA. Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including the Gaza Strip, since the end of January 2025.
  • Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 12 – 18 September 2026
content:
Ukraine’s strikes knock out refining capacity at Moscow refinery, while Russia targets Ukrainian communications

Author Tetiana Gaviuk

Key trends

  • Russia has expanded its front line campaign of disabling Ukrainian logistics and transport infrastructure to key logistical routes linking the Ukrainian capital with the west of the country. It has done so using jet-powered drones that are remotely controlled using mesh networks in Belarus. Between 10 and 17 September, Russian drone strikes affected at least 10 gas stations and transport infrastructure, including locomotives, in Kyiv, as well as in communities in the Zhytomyr, Rivne, Volyn, and Odesa regions. While the 13 September strike on the Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train raised concerns due to its proximity to Poland, strikes on gas stations in the northwest and a key pontoon crossing on the Dniester River in the southwest suggest a broader effort to disrupt road traffic to Ukraine’s western borders. In doing so, Russia is likely aiming to hinder the movement of civilian goods and people in and out of the country and between key economic centers, increasing pressure on Ukraine’s economy.
  • Despite United States President Donald Trump’s claims that Russia and Ukraine agreed to a ceasefire on striking each other’s oil facilities, Ukraine continued striking key oil refineries and depots in at least five regions. After at least 12 strikes in the past year, a 16 September strike on a major oil refinery in Yaroslavl prompted its operator to suspend crude processing due to damage and fires slowing down repairs on previously hit units. Once sustained, Kyiv’s drone campaign on Russian oil has gradually reduced oil and gas budget revenues, strained Russia’s internal consumer market for oil products, caused queues at gas stations beyond the front line regions, and forced fuel imports. After talks between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on 22 September ended with no sign of a unilateral ceasefire of Ukrainian attacks, only unlikely negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv on a reciprocal ban on strikes targeting all energy infrastructure, including Ukraine’s heating and electricity plants, could halt sustained damage to Russia’s oil refining.
