title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, October 01, 2026 – October 07, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño is strengthening. Abnormal heat continues to threaten parts of northern and eastern Africa, Hispaniola, and northern South America. Previously dry parts of Central America received heavy rain. Southern Africa sees flooding.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is forecast over northwestern Africa, the eastern Sahel, and much of Eastern Africa, while high flood risk persists in far western West Africa and parts of Southern Africa.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Following 90 days of severe rainfall deficits across Chad and East Africa, abnormal dryness has intensified into drought over western Sudan, southern and southeastern South Sudan, northern Uganda, and portions of northern, eastern, and central Ethiopia.
3) Abnormal dryness persists over southeastern Mali and central and eastern Liberia due to consistently below-average rainfall.
4) Recent heavy rainfall has triggered flooding across Nigeria's Anambra and Delta States, Ghana's North East Gonja District, and northern Libya.
5) Forecast heavy rainfall during the next week raises flood risk across parts of West Africa (southern Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea-Conakry, Sierra Leone, and western Liberia) and Southern Africa (central Angola, southern Zambia, much of Zimbabwe, southern Mozambique, South Africa’s northern, eastern, and southern regions, and southern Madagascar).
6) In the coming week, abnormal heat is expected in southern Morocco, Western Sahara, eastern Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, northern Uganda, northwestern Kenya, and northeastern Ethiopia.

title: Global Price Watch August 2026 Prices (September 30, 2026)
content:
Key Messages

  • In West Africa, cereal prices were below last year and the five-year average across the Sahel and coastal countries, except for conflict-affected and refugee-hosting areas. In Nigeria, local cereal prices were mostly declining or stable, while rice and cowpea prices remained high. Prices in Cameroon were mixed, with atypical declines in the north, and elevated prices for imported rice in urban areas. In the Central African Republic (CAR), fuel shortages and supply constraints kept prices high. Regional livestock prices broadly remained above the average (Page 3).
  • In East Africa, staple food prices remained elevated but broadly stable. Prices declined seasonally in Somalia with increasing gu harvest availability, while stronger increases persisted in Sudan, South Sudan, and parts of Uganda amid tight supplies, high transport costs, currency depreciation, and conflict-related disruptions. In Kenya and Tanzania, domestic and cross-border supplies continued to moderate maize prices despite below-average production in some areas. Livestock prices generally remained stable at above-average levels (Page 5).
  • In Southern Africa, August maize prices were mixed. Prices continued to decline in Zambia and Lesotho and were stable or decreasing across most of Tanzania and Mozambique. Malawi and South Africa recorded increasing prices due to concerns over El Niño-related weather risks. Prices trended upward in Madagascar and Angola, driven by an early lean season and production constraints. Maize prices were lower than last year in Zambia, Mozambique, and South Africa, but remained under upward pressure in several deficit markets across the region (Page 7).
  • In Central America, staple prices remained stable across the region with the start of the primera harvest but showed mixed trends compared to average levels. Black bean prices were below average in Guatemala, driven by expanded import quotas, and above average in Honduras due to tighter domestic supply and low imports. In Haiti, local food prices were stable due to post-harvest supply. In Venezuela, monthly inflation eased, and food prices increased in USD and VED. In Colombia, staple food supply was near average, and cereal prices remained stable (Page 9).
  • In the Middle East and Europe, staple price trends remained mixed. In Lebanon, wheat flour prices were stable, and prices increased for animal-source foods and produce. In Syria, staple prices remained high, while high fuel costs and shortages disrupted milling and bakeries. In Gaza, markets remained functional with continued inflows; in the West Bank, staple prices were broadly stable, but higher fuel, gas, egg, and chicken prices increased the CPI. In Yemen, staples were mostly stable, but intensified conflict, LPG shortages, and liquidity constraints continued to affect market functioning. In Ukraine, bread prices declined, but conflict and input costs continued to shape markets (Page 11).
  • In Asia, staple food prices were mixed but largely stable. Stable wheat and rice prices in Afghanistan and Sri Lanka reflected adequate domestic and imported supplies, while wheat flour remained elevated in Pakistan despite little monthly change. Stronger pressures were concentrated in Burma, where palm oil and diesel prices rose amid fuel and foreign exchange constraints, and Kathmandu, where coarse rice and black bean prices increased sharply due to monsoon-related road disruptions and higher transport costs (Page 13).
  • International markets: Maize prices rose 5.3 percent driven by decreased U.S. yields and the smallest EU crop since 2007/08. Wheat prices increased 4.6 percent, and Black Sea shipping remained at a standstill. Rice prices were mixed. Brent averaged 91 USD/bbl with 6.7 million barrels per day of Middle East production shut in, and the fertilizer index fell 1.9 percent as nitrogen eased while phosphate rose. No grain faces a global shortfall, but importers face grain freight costs 18.5 percent above a year ago (Page 2).

title: Nepal | Flood - Simplified Early Action Protocol Final Report (sEAP №: sEAP2024NP01 | Operation №: MDRNP017) - 30 September 2026
content:
SUMMARY OF THE SIMPLIFIED EARLY ACTION PROTOCOL

The IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) allocated CHF 199,964 for the implementation of anticipatory actions to reduce and mitigate the impact of flood in Karnali, Babai, and West Rapti rivers, covering selected municipalities in Kailali and Bardiya districts, Nepal. The simplified Early Action Protocol (sEAP) allocated CHF 71, 485 for Readiness, CHF 58,229 for pre-positioning stock and CHF 70,250 for Early Action. The readiness and pre-positioning stockrelated activities ensured the Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) was prepared to implement timely and effective implementation of early actions if the established trigger thresholds were reached during the sEAP timeframe. The early actions and activities planned for 2024 and 2025 were pre-agreed with and oriented to the National Society and are described in the sEAP summary.

This report summarizes the annual readiness and prepositioning activities done during June 2024 to June 2026.

The sEAP for floods was approved in June 2024, just before the beginning of Nepal’s monsoon season. The sEAP was funded by IFRC’s DREF, where the Danish Red Cross, Finnish Red Cross and the IFRC Red Cross Climate Centre also provided technical engagement. The programme started in June 2024 and was implemented for two years (until June 2026), covering 22 high flood-risk communities in 12 municipalities in the Banke, Bardiya, and Kailali districts across the West Rapti, Babai, and Karnali River basins, respectively. Being the first approved early action protocol of NRCS, the sEAP is focused on safeguarding lives, household items, and livestock, while also ensuring access to safe water and hygiene. Key activities include early warning dissemination, evacuation to safer shelters, and advance preparedness measures carried out in collaboration with local governments.

Following its approval, NRCS conducted an orientation for national headquarters staff, volunteers, and staff from the targeted district chapters, with active participation from all 12 targeted local authorities. Based on this orientation, municipalities worked with district chapters to jointly select the communities for sEAP interventions and endorse the implementation of readiness, pre-positioning, and early action activities in the agreed locations. The NRCS engaged in the overall implementation of field activities, while the IFRC Country Delegation team provided operational and financial support to implement sEAP for floods in western Nepal. Under the shared leadership modality, the Danish Red Cross provided technical support to NRCS for the implementation on behalf of IFRC.

During the implementation period of the sEAP from June 2024 to June 2026, the NRCS, with the support of IFRC, Danish Red Cross, Finnish Red Cross, and the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, implemented readiness and early action activities under the sEAP for Floods in the targeted flood-prone areas. The operation focused on strengthening forecast-based preparedness, early warning, pre-positioning, community readiness, coordination, and timely early action.

During the initial reporting period from June to December 2024, most of the planned readiness activities were completed, although some activities remained pending because the sEAP plan was approved just one month before the monsoon started, and the time available to start readiness activities was short. A major achievement was the establishment of the sEAP Advisory Team at NRCS Headquarters, comprising representatives from NRCS, IFRC Country Delegation, the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, Danish Red Cross, and Finnish Red Cross. The Advisory Team provided strategic, technical, and managerial guidance continuously to support timely decision-making and effective implementation of readiness, pre-positioning, and early action activities.

Forecast monitoring mechanisms were also strengthened through the establishment of forecast monitoring teams at both NRCS Headquarters and the three targeted district chapters. These teams monitored weather and flood forecasts throughout the monsoon period, regularly updated forecast conditions, and compared forecast information against the agreed trigger statements to assess the need for activation.

The sEAP was partially activated in September 2024 (and later de-activated), providing an important opportunity to test the established systems and identify operational lessons. The experience contributed to strengthening subsequent readiness planning, coordination, trigger monitoring, and early action arrangements.

In 2025, NRCS continued and completed the remaining readiness activities, strengthening the systems established during the first year. The year-2 implementation began with a joint planning meeting involving NRCS Headquarters, district chapters, and targeted municipalities, followed by a refresher orientation on the flood sEAP. These activities helped align stakeholders on priorities, timelines, roles, responsibilities, activation triggers, early actions, coordination mechanisms, and reporting requirements, while incorporating lessons learned from the 2024 partial activation. During the activation, eight volunteers in Banke district were mobilized to manage two pre-identified evacuation sites and 32 volunteers (12 from Banke and 20 from Bardiya Districts) were mobilized to inform communities about the heavy rains and possible flooding. A total of 3,600 people were reached in Banke (2,000) and Bardiya (1,600) through awareness messages on SGBV and child protection, as well as early warning messages to alert communities to possible evacuation.

Key readiness activities undertaken during 2025 included the establishment and strengthening of early warning task forces, completion of household-level WASH assessments, simulation exercises on early warning dissemination and evacuation, strengthening of community engagement and accountability mechanisms, development and dissemination of early warning communication channels, and regular coordination with government authorities and other stakeholders.

Significant progress was also made in pre-positioning essential non-food items (NFIs) at strategic locations within the targeted district chapters. Shelter toolkits, NFIs, waterproof bags, dignity and hygiene kits, and equipment for early warning communication were strategically stored to facilitate rapid deployment to at-risk communities in the event that the sEAP trigger thresholds were reached.

Throughout the 2025 monsoon season, national and district-level forecast monitoring teams remained operational and regularly reviewed forecasts from the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) against the established flood trigger thresholds. Although the monitored forecasts did not meet the predefined thresholds required for activation of the sEAP during the 2025 monsoon, the continued monitoring and coordination helped maintain operational readiness and ensured that NRCS remained prepared to act if the situation deteriorated.

Overall, the sEAP operation contributed to strengthening NRCS's institutional capacity for anticipatory action, particularly in forecast monitoring, early warning, community preparedness, coordination, pre-positioning and decision-making, while also strengthening collaboration with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) on anticipatory action. The implementation also generated valuable operational learning from the 2024 partial activation and the subsequent readiness activities undertaken in 2025.

As the sEAP timeframe ended in June 2026, before the next monsoon season, NRCS completed the operation and its activities in December 2025. As the existing sEAP could not be activated beyond the 2025 monsoon season, NRCS, with technical support from the IFRC country delegation team and the Red Cross Climate Centre, developed an sEAP for next two years (2026-2028) – MDRNP021, targeting to start from coming monsoon season to ensure continued anticipatory action preparedness and to further incorporate the lessons, operational experience, and improvements identified during the 2024–2025 implementation period.

title: Mongolia: Snow Storm - DREF Final Report (MDRMN021)
content:
Description of the Event

Date of event

24-02-2026

What happened, where and when?

The snowstorm event started on 21 February 2026 across multiple provinces in Mongolia, particularly affecting eastern, northern, southern, and western regions, including Bayanhongor, Darkhan-Uul, Orkhon, Dornod, Dornogovi, Dundgovi, Govi-Altai, Khentii, Khuvsgul, Selenge, Sukhbaatar, Umnugovi, Tuv, Khovd, Uvs, and Zavkhan provinces. The storm brought sustained winds of up to 31 m/s, heavy snowfall, drifting snow, and extreme cold reaching -48°C. These conditions resulted in blocked roads and mountain passes, widespread mobility disruption, and life-threatening exposure risks. While immediate impacts were recorded during the storm period, 24 February marked a critical escalation in humanitarian consequences.

Livelihood impacts were particularly severe for herder households. By 24 February, authorities had reported that 89,934 livestock had strayed during the storm, while 52,199 were reported missing. Of these, 24,017 had been recovered at that stage, while 28,182 remained unaccounted for. Preliminary reports initially recorded more than 4,900 livestock deaths directly associated with the snowstorm. Subsequent national data indicated that approximately 28,000 livestock died across Mongolia during February as a result of adverse weather conditions, including blizzards, extreme cold, snow, and pasture icing. The scale of livestock mortality and displacement placed significant economic pressure on pastoral households, particularly those that had already entered the winter season with reduced coping capacity.

During the height of the emergency, authorities introduced road and transportation restrictions in affected provinces as hazardous weather and snow accumulation made travel unsafe. The closures further constrained access to markets, health services and emergency assistance and complicated search-and-rescue and livestock recovery operations. The combination of human casualties and injuries, stranded and missing people, transportation disruptions, livestock losses and the isolation of vulnerable herder households constituted the operational trigger for Red Cross action and informed the subsequent humanitarian response.

Five fatalities due to exposure and hypothermia were confirmed in connection with the snowstorm, including herders who became lost during severe weather conditions. More than 100 people, including adults and children, were rescued after becoming stranded, lost, or trapped in snow, and numerous emergency calls were received in relation to snow entrapment, missing persons, and vehicle breakdowns. A total of 56 people were reported injured in relation to the event.

Emergency response operations also addressed a serious ice-related accident on Buir Lake in Dornod Province on 24 February 2026, when a vehicle carrying six people broke through the lake ice. Two occupants survived, while four people lost their lives. Search-and-recovery teams subsequently located the vehicle using underwater surveillance, recovered it from approximately six metres below the surface, retrieved the bodies of all four victims, and transferred them to the relevant authorities, bringing the search-and-recovery operation to a close.

By the end of the DREF operation on 30 June 2026, the situation had shifted from an acute snowstorm emergency toward recovery and seasonal preparedness. Immediate risks related to extreme cold, snow blockage, and isolation had reduced compared with the initial emergency period. However, the effects of livestock losses and the depletion of household resources continued to affect the recovery capacity of some herder households, particularly those with limited livestock holdings and few alternative sources of income. The operational focus therefore increasingly moved toward supporting livelihood recovery, strengthening household and community preparedness, and reducing vulnerability ahead of the next winter season. The DREF operation concluded on 30 June 2026 after four months of implementation.

title: Ecuador | Floods and Environmental Contamination - Operation update #6 | Annual Report (MDREC027)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Situation Overview: Esmeraldas Province

During 2025, the province of Esmeraldas experienced a sequence of overlapping emergencies that significantly affected both the population and the ecosystem. Since February 2025, the province has faced multiple shocks, including severe flooding, landslides, a crude oil spill, a 6.1 MLv earthquake, and repeated disruptions to water supply, generating a complex and evolving humanitarian context.

Between 1 January and 13 March 2025, a total of 1,682 adverse events associated with the rainy season were recorded nationwide, affecting 23 provinces, 189 cantons, and 611 parishes. The most recurrent events included landslides (40.78%), floods (38.35%), structural collapses (5.59%), erosion (5.35%), strong winds (4.34%), and mudflows (3.03%). The provinces with the highest population impact were Manabí, Guayas, Los Ríos, El Oro, Esmeraldas, Santa Elena, Loja, Pichincha, Chimborazo, and Cotopaxi. According to National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR) Situation Report No. 591 , these incidents resulted in 19 deaths, 94 injured people, 98,071 people affected, and 11,968 displaced, corresponding to 28,004 affected families and 4,889 displaced families.

Crude Oil Spill and Environmental Emergency (March 2025)

On 13 March 2025, landslides caused damage to the Trans-Ecuadorian Pipeline System (SOTE), resulting in a crude oil spill that contaminated key water sources in the cantons of Atacames, Esmeraldas, Muisne, Quinindé, and Rioverde. Environmental remediation efforts were led primarily by the state-owned company EP Petroecuador in coordination with the Ministry of Environment and Water. More than 500,000 people were estimated to be affected, mainly due to the loss of livelihoods and disruption of access to safe water. Emergency Operations Committees (EOCs) at national, provincial, and cantonal levels were activated to coordinate the response, including environmental monitoring in the Esmeraldas River Estuary Mangrove Wildlife Refuge, humanitarian assistance delivery, and clean-up operations such as hydrocarbon suction. Drinking water supply was progressively restored until July 2025, complemented by water trucking operations in areas without network access, coordinated by EP Petroecuador and other entities.

Earthquake (25 April 2025)

On 25 April 2025, a 6.1 MLv magnitude earthquake struck the province, affecting 8,241 people, including 2,391 displaced people who experienced partial or total housing loss, and 49 injured people. The Esmeraldas Cantonal Emergency Operations Committee declared Emergency No. 016-GADMCE-2025 to facilitate humanitarian assistance, restoration of basic services, and psychosocial support. At the same time, Esmeraldas was one of the provinces most severely affected by hydrometeorological events, with 7,057 people impacted by flooding. In response, the SNGR declared a provincial red alert between February and May 2025.

Water Supply Disruption (September 2025)

On 12 September 2025, the province faced another major water supply emergency affecting approximately 300,000 people in the cantons of Esmeraldas, Atacames, and Rioverde. The emergency was caused by severe damage to a transformer at the San Mateo Drinking Water Treatment Plant, which interrupted water pumping operations. The activated Provincial EOC ordered the temporary suspension of classes and requested support from the Ecuadorian Red Cross (ERC) for the installation of water treatment plants while the system was being restored. The total service interruption affected 211,848 people in Esmeraldas, 51,204 in Atacames, and 32,885 in Rioverde. The Public Water Utility Association (EPMAPSE) estimated that the emergency would last at least 10 days until the transformer replacement was completed. By 25 September 2025, the San Mateo plant resumed normal operations, restoring drinking water supply to the affected cantons.

Following the resolution of the water supply crisis in September, the province entered a preventive monitoring phase during October and November 2025 under a national yellow alert. Institutional efforts focused on drainage cleaning and community preparedness in critical areas of Esmeraldas and Quinindé. However, the beginning of the rainy season towards the end of the year, combined with the intensification of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, progressively saturated urban drainage systems that already presented structural vulnerabilities.

By January 2026, the emergency intensified as high-intensity rainfall caused the collapse of stormwater drainage systems in low-lying areas of Esmeraldas city, prompting the declaration of an orange alert in the province to reinforce response actions. As of 25 March 2026, situation reports highlighted severe flooding caused by water accumulation, resulting in mud and wastewater entering homes and significantly affecting household assets and living conditions. This situation required the full activation of Emergency Operations Committees to coordinate water pumping operations in flooded neighborhoods and the delivery of urgent humanitarian assistance to populations in areas where water remained stagnant for several days.

title: ZMB: Epidemic - 08-2026 - Cholera outbreak (2026-09-30)
content:
Description

The cholera outbreak is placing significant pressure on the health system and affected populations. The outbreak has increased the demand for cholera case management, surveillance, laboratory testing, emergency response and WASH services. As of 29 September 2026, seven districts across five provinces had reported 304 cases, including 62 laboratory-confirmed cases, with 35 patients receiving treatment and 11 reported deaths. The response has therefore required health workers and emergency teams to strengthen active case finding, laboratory testing, rapid response and treatment services in affected districts. The affected population is experiencing increased illness and mortality, while communities remain exposed to risks associated with unsafe water, sanitation and possible contamination of water sources. The response has required the provision of safe water and household chlorine, water-quality monitoring, super-chlorination of shallow wells, disinfection and establishment of oral rehydration and treatment points. Secondary effects include delays in seeking treatment, which are contributing to community deaths. Of the 11 deaths reported, eight (8) occurred in the community and three in health facilities, with the Ministry identifying the community deaths as an indication of delayed treatment-seeking. The outbreak also creates additional demands on health workers, facilities, logistics and response resources, potentially affecting the capacity to maintain routine health services while responding to the outbreak. At household level, affected families may face additional burdens associated with illness, caregiving, accessing treatment and obtaining safe water and sanitation supplies. The outbreak also has social and behavioural effects, including the potential for stigma and discrimination against affected individuals and families. Continued transmission increases the need for sustained risk communication, community engagement and health education to promote safe water use, handwashing, sanitation, early treatment and prompt reporting of suspected cases. The Ministry has emphasised the involvement of community leaders, churches, civil society, media and other influencers in ensuring consistent and accurate information reaches affected communities.

title: Mozambique Health Cluster Bulletin
content:
1 Context Overview
Mozambique continues to face a complex humanitarian situation driven by the combined impacts of climate-related shocks and protracted conflict, with significant consequences for the health and well-being of vulnerable populations. In 2026, severe flooding in the central and southern provinces caused widespread displacement, damaged health infrastructure, and heightened the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, disrupting access to and continuity of essential health services.
At the same time, insecurity in Cabo Delgado continues to trigger displacement and place additional pressure on already fragile health systems. Humanitarian needs remain acute, particularly among displaced populations, returnees, and host communities, requiring sustained support for primary health care, emergency medical services, mental health and psychosocial support, and outbreak prevention and response.
In response, Health Cluster partners have maintained a coordinated humanitarian effort to ensure the delivery of life-saving and essential health services. Interventions have focused on integrated approaches, including mobile health services, disease surveillance and outbreak response, sexual and reproductive health care, mental health support, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities. Despite these efforts, considerable challenges remain, particularly related to humanitarian access, funding constraints, shortages of critical resources, and the need to further strengthen health information management, monitoring, and reporting systems.

title: Humanitarian Response Forum (HRF) - Situation Report No. 1 – Floods in Cambodia (2026)
content:
Over the past three weeks, Cambodia has experienced moderate to heavy rainfall, resulting in localized flash floods across 10 provinces. As of 30 September 2026, an estimated 73,922 families have been affected, including 6,344 families evacuated, with the most significant impacts reported in Battambang and Siem Reap Provinces. Flooding has also affected 62,801 houses, 184 schools, 29 health facilities, more than 1.19 million meters of roads, and 160,427 hectares of agricultural land.

The Royal Government of Cambodia, through the National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM) and Provincial Committees for Disaster Management (PCDM), is leading response efforts, while humanitarian partners continue to provide support to affected communities. Relief activities include the distribution of food, non-food items, shelter kits, and WASH supplies, with more than 3,500 households targeted for immediate assistance in Banteay Meanchey Province.

Current forecasts indicate generally stable river levels and low to moderate rainfall over the coming days, with no active flood warnings currently in place. Nonetheless, authorities and humanitarian organizations remain on standby and continue to monitor the situation closely.

The Humanitarian Response Forum (HRF) continues to coordinate information sharing and response planning among humanitarian partners in close collaboration with the Government to ensure timely assistance reaches communities most affected by the floods.

title: Lebanon Health Sector Emergency Situation Report Issue #24 - September 28, 2026
content:
Situation Overview

Continued insecurity, access restrictions, damage to health infrastructure and limited resources are constraining the health system’s capacity to sustain essential
services across aected areas. No new attacks on healthcare have been reported through the Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA) since 14 September.
Since 2 March 2026, 215 attacks have been recorded, resulting in 135 deaths and 416 injuries. Continued adherence to International Humanitarian Law is critical to
safeguarding healthcare workers, facilities, ambulances and patients.
While most health facilities are maintaining services through permanent or temporary arrangements, insecurity and access constraints continue to delay rehabilitation
of some conict-aected facilities in South Lebanon and strain referral pathways. Primary Health Care Satellite Unit (PSU) operations and healthcare access, particularly
in Nabatieh, remain vulnerable to security-related disruptions, requiring ongoing adjustments to service delivery. Funding constraints, transportation barriers, population
movements, and referral challenges also risk disrupting outreach services and continuity of care, especially for patients requiring specialized maternal health,
Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), rehabilitation services.
The dispersal of displaced families across collective shelters and private households continues to complicate outreach, needs identication and coordinated service
coverage. Inconsistent arrangements for covering the PHC costs of returnees are also creating uncertainty, particularly in southern areas. Clearer guidance is needed on
eligibility, geographic vulnerability and socioeconomic assessment.
Population movements and changing demand are further contributing to uneven availability of psychotropic and chronic disease medications. Redistribution of
psychotropic medicines between PHCCs is ongoing, while increased demand from newly registered patients and returnees is placing additional pressure on chronic
disease medication supplies, particularly in Nabatieh.

title: WFP Syria Country Brief, September 2026
content:
IN NUMBERS

619,338 people assisted in August

3,550 mt food dispatched in August

USD 4.62 M cash transferred in August

USD 201.7 M required (September 2026 – February 2027)

3.65 M returnees have arrived in Syria since December 2024 (UNHCR, 2025)

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • Syria remains at a critical juncture, with 7.1 million people facing acute food insecurity, including 700,000 experiencing severe food insecurity.
  • Rising return movements are placing additional strain on basic services, livelihoods, and social protection systems, highlighting the urgent need for sustained investment in nationally led systems to preserve social cohesion, and facilitate a stable transition.
  • Funding shortfalls have already forced a reduction in food assistance from 1.3 million to 650,000 people, limiting assistance to those with the greatest needs.
  • WFP urgently requires USD 201.7 million over the next six months to restore vital food assistance to 1.3 million vulnerable people affected by food insecurity, displacement, and economic hardship. These funds would also be critical to sustain nutrition programmes, protect livelihoods and continue supporting national social protection interventions.

title: Ukraine Health Cluster Bulletin #8 (August 2026)
content:
Key Highlights

• In August, the number of civilian casualties remained at near record levels, and most of them
occurred far from the frontline. The UN HRMMU verified at least 373 civilians killed and 2,349 injured,
second only to the number of casualties recorded in July. Long-range weapons caused 47 per cent
of casualties, mostly in densely populated urban centers.
• Attacks on Kyiv and its surrounding region escalated in July, continuing throughout August, with
deadly attacks on 1, 5, 20, and 28 August. Kherson, Kryvyi Rih, and Zaporizhzhia recorded the nexthighest
casualty numbers. Among the deadliest incidents was a double-tap attack on a shopping
mall in Kryvyi Rih that killed at least 16 people, with more than 150 civilian casualties overall. By
August 2026, Health Cluster partners provided 1,305 post-strike primary health care and mental
health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) consultations, prepositioned supplies to receiving health
facilities to cover for the treatment of 3,599 people.
• The pace of displacement nearly doubled in the second half of August, rising by 85 per cent
compared to the first half (from 11,150 to 20,620 people, according to IOM DTM Frontline Flow
Monitoring). As hostilities intensified, drone attacks and shelling on civilian areas and infrastructure
continued, and mandatory evacuations expanded to additional settlements. According to the
Ukraine Protection Cluster, 18,088 people were registered at transit centers in August. Health Cluster
partners provided partners provided 4,390 consultations at seven Transit centers across Ukraine.
• As frontline communities rely on humanitarian support for access to health care, timely evidence
on service gaps is critical to guide the response. In August, the Health Cluster led a pilot Rapid
Health Analysis in frontline communities in Kherson, under the oversight and guidance of the
Kherson oblast health authorities and 14 health partners to analyze where service gaps are most
acute, strengthen coordination of the response and prioritize assistance for the most affected and
underserved populations.
• The growing number of attacks on warehouses is threatening the continuity of emergency health
operations by damaging essential medical supplies. WHO SSA verified 15 attacks on health care
affecting warehouses in 2026, and more warehouses were hit in August alone than in the entire first
quarter. A Health Cluster survey revealed that at least 8 partners were impacted by these attacks
this year, most of them in July and August. Frontline service delivery has been the hardest hit.

title: UNICEF Burundi Humanitarian Situation Report No. 23, 31 August 2026
content:
Situation Overview & Humanitarian Needs

In August 2026, Burundi continued to face complex humanitarian challenges driven by the crisis in eastern DRC, population movements, public health risks and climate-related threats. Humanitarian actors, in coordination with the Government, are accelerating preparedness and response efforts to address risks related to the continuing threat of the Ebola outbreak in neighbouring DRC.

Population movements remained significant. Following the launch of voluntary repatriation from Busuma refugee site in April 2026, the refugee population continued to decline. By the end of August, Busuma hosted over 45,000 Congolese refugees, while approximately 21,000 refugees remained in Musenyi and more than 3,000 asylum seekers were registered in Cishemere. Concurrently, the repatriation of Burundian refugees from Tanzania was nearing completion, with 98,617 returnees recorded in 2026. These movements continued to strain basic services, particularly in health, education, WASH and child protection in key return areas.

Public health risks remained elevated. Burundi strengthened preparedness measures in response to the Ebola outbreak in DRC, supported by UNICEF’s US$3.39 million contribution to the national preparedness plan. Cholera transmission persisted while a measles outbreak affected eight health districts with 1,661 suspected cases.

Climate-related risks also remained a concern, with preparedness measures underway for a forecasted El Niño likely to increase flooding, displacement, disease outbreaks and food insecurity among vulnerable communities.

title: Indonesia Drought 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRID030)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

08-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Indonesia has experienced progressively worsening drought conditions during 2026, with prolonged rainfall deficits reducing groundwater, surface-water and household water availability across parts of Java, Bali, Nusa Tenggara, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi. Household wells, community springs, small reservoirs and other traditional water sources have declined or dried up in affected locations, increasing dependence on emergency water assistance.

Government drought alerts and emergency declarations issued from May to July 2026 provided early indications of the evolving situation. These earlier declarations are not considered the operational trigger for this DREF.

The DREF trigger date is 8 September 2026, when consolidated PMI operational reporting demonstrated that the response had expanded substantially and that continued humanitarian needs required additional support to sustain and strengthen the response. At that point, PMI reported drought-response activities across 16 provinces and 126 districts/municipalities, including approximately 35.97 million liters of safe water distributed through 7,195 water-trucking trips, supported by 129 water tankers and more than 700 personnel.

PMI had already been responding with its own resources since 30 June 2026. The DREF is therefore not requested because the drought only emerged in September, but because accumulated operational evidence demonstrated continuing humanitarian water needs, expanding geographical demand and increasing pressure on PMI and locally available response resources.

The situation continued to evolve after the trigger. PMI's consolidated assessment as of 23 September records 8,135 water-distribution trips and approximately 44.97 million liters of safe water delivered across 133 districts/municipalities, 721 subdistricts and 1,776 villages. Based on beneficiary records consolidated by PMI, at least 764,171 estimated unique people had received emergency water assistance.

Approximately 2.43 million service contacts were also recorded, reflecting repeated services and not additional unique people.

These operational figures demonstrate a sustained humanitarian water-access problem. They should not be interpreted as the total population affected nationally, as a consolidated national estimate remains under verification.

Reduced access to safe water is the primary documented humanitarian impact. Affected households may have to travel longer distances, wait for emergency deliveries, rely on reduced quantities of water or spend additional household resources to obtain water. These pressures particularly affect low-income and underserved households and people who face barriers to collecting, transporting or safely storing water.

Prolonged dry conditions also contribute to secondary public-health risks, including dehydration, heat-related illness, reduced hygiene and, in selected locations, deteriorating air quality associated with smoke and haze. The DREF will address these humanitarian consequences only where needs are verified. Firefighting and fire suppression remain the responsibility of government authorities and are outside the scope of this operation.

The proposed DREF will therefore support immediate humanitarian assistance in locations where needs and response gaps are demonstrated, while targeted assessment, monitoring and community feedback continue to refine geographical targeting, sectoral priorities and the transition from repeated emergency assistance toward more sustainable solutions

title: Syria Operational update, August 2026
content:
August 2026

Syria has entered a phase marked by large-scale refugee and IDP returns alongside persistent humanitarian vulnerability and reintegration needs. While around 1.8 million refugees and over 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) have returned since December 2024, 15.6 million people still require humanitarian assistance. As return movements continue, ensuring sustainable reintegration through access to documentation, housing, essential services, livelihoods and community support is critical to helping returnees rebuild their lives and is central to Syria’s recovery. In line with Syria’s National Recovery Priorities and the Government’s “No Tents, No Camps” vision, UNHCR supports this transition while maintaining protection and humanitarian assistance for vulnerable populations.

  • Malnutrition remains alarmingly high, with nearly 2 million children projected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026, including 433,000 children facing severe acute malnutrition and requiring urgent treatment.

From reaching over 4 million people per month during the 2022–2023 drought response, current resources allow WFP to support less than five percent of people facing emergency levels of hunger from October, with nutrition treatment running out of resources after September.

title: UNICEF Latin America and Caribbean Region Humanitarian Situation Report No.1 (El Niño Multi-Country Preparedness and Response), 11 June - 18 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • On 11 June 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared El Niño conditions, which are expected to reach very strong intensity between November 2026 and January 2027. Across Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), impacts will vary considerably by location. Drought and extreme heat are anticipated across the Central American Dry Corridor, the Caribbean and parts of South America, while the Pacific coasts of Mexico, Central America and South America, face heavy rainfall, flooding and landslides during an above-normal hurricane season.
  • UNICEF’s preliminary regional estimates indicate that 86 million people, including 25.8 million children, are exposed to El Niño-related hazards across LAC. Of these, up to 30 million people, including 9 million children, are at risk of humanitarian need, with an estimated 5 million children at heightened risk across 11 high-priority countries.
  • UNICEF and partners continue to prepare and respond accordingly. In Central America, CERF-funded Anticipatory Action is delivering nutrition and WASH support in the Dry Corridor, and offices in Guatemala, Nicaragua and Mexico are scaling up drought response. In South America, Country Offices have activated emergency teams, updated contingency plans and pre-positioned supplies ahead of the rainy season, while Caribbean countries are strengthening water management, early warning and community preparedness.
  • El Niño requirements are being consolidated under UNICEF’s 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal for LAC. UNICEF is seeking early, predictable funding to sustain access to essential services and reach children before the worst impacts arrive, when acting will cost more and the window to prevent harm will have closed.

title: Documento de Advocacia — Cadeia de Abastecimento de Produtos Médicos em Moçambique - Setembro de 2026
content:
Este documento analisa a situação atual da cadeia de abastecimento de produtos médicos de Moçambique, com contributos dos parceiros do Cluster de Saúde, e identifica onde a continuidade do investimento poderá melhor proteger os doentes.

As organizações parceiras que trabalham diretamente com os doentes descrevem um quotidiano sob pressão: 79% destas organizações referiram ruturas frequentes ou constantes de artigos essenciais, e algumas indicaram que as faltas duravam habitualmente mais de um mês. Luvas, antibióticos, compressas para tratamento de feridas, analgésicos e contracetivos foram os artigos mais frequentemente afetados. Os parceiros humanitários continuam a complementar os esforços do Governo com donativos próprios para ajudar a colmatar estas lacunas; como muitas organizações de saúde também são afetadas pela crise de financiamento humanitário, várias salientaram que um financiamento mais previsível ajudaria a manter este apoio ao longo do tempo.

title: WFP Guinea Country Brief, July 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

  • Guinea continues to face persistent food insecurity, poverty and malnutrition, compounded by climate-related shocks.
    According to the latest Global Analysis of Vulnerability, Food Security and Nutrition (AGVSAN – 2024), 35.8 percent of households (4.8 million people) are food insecure compared to 21.8 percent in 2018, reflecting growing vulnerability across the country.

  • Despite the country’s rich natural resources and agricultural potential, 43.7 percent of the population and 80 percent of those in rural areas live below the poverty line.

  • Nutrition remains a concern, with the 2025 Fill the Nutrient Gap (FNG) survey indicating that over 50 percent of households cannot afford a nutritious diet, while acute malnutrition affects 4 percent of children aged 6-59 months.

  • Since 1964 and through its Country Strategic Plan (2024-2029), WFP Guinea continues supporting the Government to strengthen emergency preparedness and response, school feeding, nutrition, resilience and technical capacities, while providing logistics and supply chain services to facilitate humanitarian assistance delivery.

  • Seasonal risks intensified in June with the onset of the rainy season. Localized emergencies, market pressures, and food security concerns continued to affect vulnerable households, highlighting the importance of preparedness and resilience-building interventions.

title: UNHCR Afghanistan Situation Regional Update August 2026
content:
Operational Context

In Afghanistan, pressure on reception and reintegration services remained high in August, despite lower return numbers than in July. Nearly a year after the nationwide ban on national female UN staff accessing UN premises was introduced, the restriction remained in place, while tighter restrictions in Herat disrupted protection and community activities. At Torkham, customs checks delayed the movement of families’ belongings until the suspension was lifted on 24 August. Renewed border tensions on 28 August prompted humanitarian teams to temporarily relocate to Omari camp, with operations resuming the following day. These restrictions and disruptions constrained humanitarian access and required sustained engagement with the de facto authorities to maintain support for people in need. In Iran, renewed conflict and heightened security measures in August raised concerns over wider regional escalation. Economic pressures, including disrupted trade, currency depreciation and rising food prices, further reduced household purchasing power and livelihoods. UNHCR and partners continued to monitor emerging protection and assistance needs and adapt responses as required. In Pakistan, insecurity, access restrictions and monsoon-related flooding affected operations in August, particularly in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, alongside continued Afghan returns. Conditions varied across the country, with security constraints and localized disruptions affecting access and requiring operational flexibility. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, localized disruptions affected movement and access in some areas. In Islamabad and Punjab, refugees and asylum-seekers continued to face protection concerns, including mobility restrictions, arrest and detention, police harassment, extortion, limited access to livelihoods and basic services and landlord evictions. In Sindh, reported arrests and deportations of Afghan nationals decreased although enforcement actions against undocumented Afghans continued. In Balochistan, security and movement restrictions also continued to limit humanitarian access to the former Mohammad Khail refugee village and refugee settlements in Chaghi. ¹ As of end-December 2025 ² As of 31 August 2026 ³ 3.2 million IDPs as of 2025, and 69,000 new IDPs in 2026 from areas reached with assessments. For the latest figures and updates on UNHCR’s broader response in sub-region, visit the Afghanistan Situation page on UNHCR’s Operational Data Portal.

For any queries, please contact: RBAPEXT@unhcr.org

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 25 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Demolitions displaced 147 Palestinians across the West Bank in one week, more than three times the 2026 weekly average, including 58 people in South ‘Anata Bedouins, near the area designated for the E1 settlement expansion plan.
  • Israeli forces’ operations and movement restrictions disrupted access to essential services for thousands of Palestinians in Ramallah governorate, while operations by Israeli forces in Nablus temporarily displaced families and closed schools and a health clinic.
  • Funding shortfalls threaten mobile health services in Area C: 20 locations are at risk of losing mobile-clinic coverage without continued funding, while 17 locations are already without services.
  • In Gaza, shortages of cancer medications, chemotherapy and radiotherapy supplies, dialysis materials, insulin and engine oil – caused by underfunding and lack of clearance for limited available medicines to enter Gaza – are disrupting life-saving services.
  • The new academic year in Gaza began on 19 September with an estimated 200,000 children remaining out of school, amid funding shortfalls. Partners had prepared by removing rubble, cleaning some classrooms and providing bags and stationery. In the Strip, approximately 495,000 preschool and school-aged children are enrolled in learning spaces supported through the UN and partners’ humanitarian response.
  • Funding shortfalls and restrictions are severely constraining preparations for the rainy season, with very limited available stocks covering only a fraction of the needs; hundreds of child-friendly spaces and protection services face disruptions.
  • Across the Gaza Strip, 451 displacement sites identified as being at high risk of flooding are hosting an estimated 464,402 people.

Overview

Violence and restrictions continue to drive humanitarian needs in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, while shortfalls in humanitarian funding are further holding back relief efforts. Addressing Member States as part of the General Assembly High-level Week, the United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said that "we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory."

Regarding Gaza, he said that “the resumption of assistance since the ceasefire was announced last October has brough some relief – but conditions remain intolerable... International law, including international humanitarian law, is brazenly violated. Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and the level of human suffering is still off the charts.” He reiterated the need to allow the UN to perform its mandates in Gaza and for UN and humanitarian personnel to be protected, stressing that all parties must comply with international law and the orders of the International Court of Justice.

Regarding the West Bank, he said that "record levels of settler attacks and relentless efforts to expand settlements are pushing Palestinian communities to the breaking point. Such actions are unlawful and unjust." The Secretary-General further said that violence, displacement and settlement expansion by Israel "are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing."

title: THA: Flood - 09-2026 - Heavy rainfall caused flooding (2026-09-29)
content:
[...]

Sources for data marked as Other

1)Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitiagaion (DDPM) 1784 : กรมป้องกันและบรรเทาสาธารณภัย กระทรวงมหาดไทย 2).Thai Red Cross Society สำนักงานบรรเทาทุกข์และประชานามัยพิทักษ์ https://www.facebook.com/buntaotook

Description

Thailand has experienced widespread flooding following heavy rainfall during 16–28 September 2026. According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation(DDPM) report, flooding affected 41 provinces, covering 214 districts, 1,017 sub-districts and 5,164 vilages, with approximately 927,400 households (2,561,569 people) affected. A total of 23 deaths were reported, with no injuries recorded.

As of 28 September, flooding remained ongoing in 28 provinces, covering 160 districts, 849 sub-districts and 4,685 villages, affecting approximately 921,488 households (2,547,117 people). Bangkok was also affected, with approximately 329,000 households reported affected.

The most significant impacts were reported in the Central, Eastern and Bangkok metropolitan areas, including Samut Prakan, Pathum Thani, Bangkok, Chon Buri, Nakhon Pathom, Ayutthaya, Suphan Buri and Nakhon Nayok. Several areas continued to experience rising or stagnant water levels.

Particularly significant impacts included:

  • Samut Prakan: 260,784 households affected; 8 deaths.
  • Pathum Thani: 113,323 households affected; 1 death.
  • Bangkok: approximately 329,000 households affected and 4 deaths.
  • Chon Buri: 118,723 households affected.
  • Ayutthaya: 28,176 households affected; 1 death.
  • Suphan Buri: 9,985 households affected.
  • Sa Kaeo: 8,719 households affected; 6 deaths.

The situation was driven by heavy and accumulated rainfall, river overflow and increased discharge from the Chao Phraya Dam. The DDPM warned that further rainfall could result in flash flooding, accumulated flooding, river overflow and landslides, particularly in low-lying areas and areas near waterways.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance

No

NS Requests International Assistance

No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by National Society

Summary

The Thai Red Cross Society (TRCS) has activated its disaster relief mechanisms through the Relief and Community Health Bureau (RCHB), Red Cross Stations, provincial Red Cross chapters and volunteers. Bangkok. On 28 September, RCHB operated the Thai Red Cross Mobile Kitchen to prepare and distribute 8,000 cooked meals to flood-affected communities and shelters in six areas: • Khlong Sam Wa shelter – 1,500 meals • Rom Klao Housing Estate, Lat Krabang – 800 meals • Suan Luang shelter – 200 meals • Riverside community, Wang Thonglang – 1,500 meals • Saphan Sung – 2,000 meals • Bang Kapi – 2,000 meals An additional 100 ready-to-eat meal sets were provided at Amornphan Condominium, Khan Na Yao. Thai Red Cross volunteers supported food preparation and distribution. On 27 September, the Thai Red Cross also distributed 1,000 cooked meals in Bangkok, including 200 meals at Ban Bang Kapi School temporary shelter and 800 meals at Khlong Chan flats. Due to high flood levels in Khlong Chan, where normal vehicles could not access affected communities, RCHB used a high-clearance Unimog vehicle to transport cooked food and essential supplies to affected residents. Provinces outside Bangkok The Thai Red Cross has mobilised provincial Red Cross chapters, the Office of Provincial Red Cross Affairs, RCHB and 12 Red Cross Stations outside Bangkok to support affected communities, particularly in: • Nakhon Nayok • Samut Prakan • Pathum Thani • Chachoengsao Where widespread flooding or access constraints made it difficult to establish mobile kitchens or transport dry food, provincial Red Cross chapters were authorised to contract local/private food providers to prepare cooked meals for affected communities. The Thai Red Cross has also authorised the use of high-clearance vehicles and larger boats to support transportation and delivery of cooked meals to areas affected by high flood levels.

Actions taken by Federation

Summary

IFRC is maintaining close coordination with TRCS and monitoring the evolving humanitarian situation.

Actions taken by others

The Government and local authorities have activated multi-agency response measures, including: • Search, rescue and immediate assistance: Provincial DDPM offices, district authorities, police, military units, local authorities, volunteers and foundations have been deployed to assist affected communities, move household belongings to higher ground and accelerate drainage. • Evacuation and temporary shelters: Temporary evacuation centres have been established in several provinces. For example, 27 shelters were opened in Sa Kaeo, while shelters were also established in Chanthaburi and Nakhon Ratchasima. • Flood drainage and emergency equipment: Authorities have deployed pumps, boats and other equipment to support drainage and rescue operations. In Nakhon Sawan, for example, the regional DDPM centre provided 5 flat-bottom boats, 2 rescue boats and 10 paddle boats. • Government monitoring and coordination: The Government established a Joint Information and Communication Center (JICC) to consolidate and communicate flood, rainfall and risk information. The Government also instructed provinces to provide daily situation and assistance updates. • Water management: As of 28 September, the Chao Phraya Dam was discharging approximately 1,900 m³/s. Authorities warned that discharge could be increased to 1,500–2,000 m³/s depending on conditions, potentially increasing downstream water levels. • Health and hospital preparedness: The Ministry of Public Health instructed hospitals in high-risk areas to maintain 24-hour preparedness, secure essential medicines, oxygen, electricity, water, communications and referral systems, with contingency stocks for at least 72 hours. • Bangkok response: Bangkok authorities have supported drainage, traffic management, emergency assistance and temporary shelters. The DDPM reported 233 temporary shelters opened in Bangkok.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #5 (Reporting period: 19–26 September 2026 | Issued: 27 September 2026)
content:
4,481 Cumulative casualties since 6 Aug (HEOC, 26 Sep)

838 Cumulative deaths 18.7% of casualties

809 New casualties this period 19–26 Sep: 645 injured, 164 deaths

180,513 People displaced 27,413 families, 10 governorates (Exec. Unit, 23 Sep)

20+ Mobile medical teams deployed in 4 priority governorates

59.3 MT WHO supplies dispatched Aden warehouse, 13–23 Sep (US$ 656k)

Highlights

• Casualties continue to rise at roughly 100 per day. The HEOC register recorded 809 new casualties between 19 and 26 September (645 injuries, 164 deaths), bringing the cumulative total since 6 August to 4,481, including 838 deaths. Deaths represented 20% of newly reported casualties this period, compared with 24% in the previous period and 17% before that.

• Lahj remains the heaviest front. Al-Madharibah wa Ras Al-Arah and the Bab Al-Mandab coast accounted for the largest daily burden on both days for which detailed field reports are available (47 casualties on 21 Sep, including 18 deaths; 34 on 26 Sep), followed by Marib (Al-Jubah, Sirwah) and Taiz (At-Turbah, Maqbanah, Al-Ma'afer, AlMudhaffar).

• Registered displacement has grown by more than half in eight days. The Executive Unit for IDPs consolidated report of 24 September registers 27,413 displaced families (180,513 people) across ten governorates, up from 17,852 families (122,297 people) on 15 September. Marib and Al-Dhale'e have been added as governorates of arrival; Aden has more than tripled its caseload to 3,741 families.

• A complex emergency, not only a trauma response. Displaced families face rising risks of cholera, measles, malaria and dengue, and disrupted maternal, mental health and chronic care.

• RRM registrations reached their highest daily levels of the crisis (1,315 households on 21 Sep and 1,470 on 23 Sep). The mechanism has reached 15,197 households (81,140 people) since 1 August, but kit stock-outs meant no households could be assisted in Taiz or Lahj on 24 September.

• Cholera alerts in two IDP sites in Aden. WHO and MoPHP have activated rapid response teams for active surveillance. Suspected cholera cases reached 7,784 by week 38. Around 40% of newly displaced households on the West Coast draw drinking water from unprotected wells or surface water, and nearly one third have no lockable latrine.

• Trauma load is displacing maternal care. Comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care (CEmONC) has been temporarily suspended in two hospitals in Marib and Ras Al-Arah as theatres and staff are redirected to warwounded; patients are being referred to the nearest functioning hospitals.

• Early warning signs. Fewer facilities are reporting in Marib, Taiz, Ad Dali' and Aden, where only about 60% were fully functional before the escalation. Verification is under way.

• WHO pipeline strengthened. Two trucks carrying 258 IEHK and TESK kits (US$ 184,082; 8.9 MT) left the WHO Dubai hub on 22 September. Between 13 and 23 September the Aden warehouse dispatched US$ 655,891 of supplies (59.3 MT) to 40 facilities in 10 governorates. Eight Starlink kits were distributed to PHEOCs to secure reporting connectivity for six months.

• Outbreak preparedness supplies secured through CERF. A US$ 517,109 CERF-funded procurement package has been planned covering case-management supplies and 200 oxygen cylinders, 216 rapid response team kits, WASH/IPC supplies and laboratory diagnostics for cholera, measles, dengue and diphtheria. WHO has also secured a further US$ 1 million from CERF and EUR 600,000 from ECHO for surgical and trauma supplies.

• Joint advocacy brief. MoPHP, WHO and the Health Cluster will present a joint Health Response Advocacy Brief and Call to Action, setting out the response plan and the resources required to sustain it, at a joint MoPHP–WHO highlevel meeting with donors and partners on 28 September, convened by H.E. Dr Qasem Buhebeih, Minister of Public Health and Population, and Dr Jaffar Hussien, WHO Representative in Yemen.

Situation overview

Fighting continued through the reporting period along three main axes: the Lahj coastal front (Al-Madharibah wa Ras Al-Arah, Bab Al-Mandab and the Kahbub approach towards Aden), the Marib fronts (Al-Jubah, Sirwah, Harib and Marib Al-Wadi) and the Taiz fronts (Ash Shamayatayn/At-Turbah, Maqbanah, Al-Ma'afer, Al-Mudhaffar and Al-Misrakh). Open-source monitoring by the Civilian Impact Monitoring Project (CIMP) also recorded airstrikes and shelling affecting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Taiz, Al-Hodeidah, Al-Dhale'e, Ibb, Al-Jawf, Hajjah and Sa'dah, including incidents in which displaced people were injured. Independent monitoring is not real-time; the Ministry's daily register remains the basis for casualty figures in this report.

Displacement is now the dominant driver of health need. Movement remains overwhelmingly short-range and circular: two thirds of RRM-registered households moved within their own governorate, and contested Taiz districts such as AlMa'afer and Jabal Habashi are simultaneously among the largest areas of origin and of arrival. A second, longer-range stream from the Al-Hodeidah coast disperses into Aden, Abyan, Lahj, Hadramout and Al-Mahra. Newly displaced families are settling largely in host families, tents and makeshift shelter, in conditions that favour the transmission of cholera, measles, malaria and dengue as the El Niño season approaches. This is therefore a complex emergency, not only a trauma response. Alongside trauma care, displaced families and host communities need access to basic and lifesaving health services, including through mobile teams, and public health measures such as mass vaccination and vector control to prevent outbreaks of epidemic-prone diseases. Meeting these needs requires stronger basic public health functions and a response coordinated among partners, guided by an inter-agency rapid health needs assessment.

title: Eastern Chad: Sudan Situation – Flash Updates #57
content:
Context

The security situation along Chad’s borders remains a concern, while conditions inside the country remain generally stable. The eastern provinces of Sila, Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira and Ennedi Est continue to be affected by the spillover of the conflict in neighbouring Sudan. In addition to the continued arrival of refugees fleeing violence in Sudan, several security incidents linked to the conflict have been reported in Chad since late August, including drone strikes in Wadi Fira and Ennedi Est. On 11 September, a Chadian national was reportedly killed near Kulbus in Wadi Fira by members of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and reports of kidnappings have also emerged from the border area.

At the same time, worsening climatic conditions and the impact of drought, described by the World Food Programme (WFP) as one of the most severe in the region since 1984, continue to undermine livelihoods, reduce agricultural production and drive additional population movements towards eastern Chad. In response, the Chadian Government recently conducted an assessment mission in the eastern provinces to evaluate the extent of the rainfall deficit and identify appropriate mitigation measures. Proposed actions include the exemption of customs duties on selected essential food commodities and the targeted distribution of cereals to the most affected households.

The drought situation was also discussed during meetings between provincial authorities in Ouaddaï and the UNHCR Regional Director for East and Horn of Africa and the Great Lakes, who also serves as Regional Coordinator for the Sudan Refugee Situation, during his mission to Chad from 17 to 21 September 2026. Chadian authorities expressed concern over the humanitarian and socio-economic consequences of the climate crisis, which are compounding pressures arising from the continued influx of Sudanese refugees.

Within the country, incidents of criminality and petty crime, including armed robberies, assaults and explosions caused by explosive devices, continue to be reported in some refugee-hosting areas. Meanwhile, heavy seasonal rains and rising wadi water levels are restricting access to several locations in eastern Chad, creating additional challenges for humanitarian operations.

Two Safe and Secure Approaches in Field Environments (SSAFE) training sessions were conducted for 61 participants, and two additional sessions, organized in collaboration with WFP, are planned for October.

title: World Vision International Nepal Rasuwa – Nuwakot Flash Flood Emergency Response - Situation update 7 | 23 September, 2026
content:
Devastating flash floods triggered by a glacier-related ice-rock avalanche on 26 August have left communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Gorkha and Dhading facing immense loss and destruction. At least 1,415 people have lost their lives, while 5,786 remain missing or unaccounted for. The disaster has affected around 20,000 households, with 84,000 people, including 22,000 children, now in need of humanitarian assistance.

Homes, markets, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure have been damaged or destroyed, disrupting access to essential services and livelihoods. Around 20,000 households require food assistance, while 65,000 people need emergency water, sanitation and hygiene assistance. Some 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support. Families also need safe shelter, livelihood support and psychosocial care as they begin their journey towards recovery.

World Vision’s response

World Vision International Nepal, together with local partners KIRDARC Nepal and Good Neighbors Nepal (GNN), is supporting children and families affected by the floods. As of 23 September, the response has reached 8,684 people, including 3,521 children and 258 people with disabilities.

The response so far includes:

  • 3,750 people supported with emergency food packages
  • 2,325 people, including 930 children, provided with hygiene kits
  • 455 people, including 182 children, supported with shelter kits
  • 860 people supported with bedding sets
  • 559 women and girls supported with dignity kits
  • 116 children supported through two Child Friendly Spaces
  • Water purification supplies, water tanks and other support provided to improve access to safe drinking water
  • Equipment provided to four local institutions to help restart essential services

title: Syria Protection Sector 2026 Mid-Year Report
content:
Syria Protection Sector Mid-Year Report

January - June 2026

  • Humanitarian Reset initiated: The Sector initiated implementation of the consolidation of the Sector, beginning with a streamlined chapter in the 2026 HNRP. The Sector also began mapping and reviewing existing working groups, coordination mechanisms, tools and information products as part of the humanitarian reset. The process aims to streamline and consolidate the coordination architecture, reduce duplication, improve efficiency, and strengthen the leadership and participation of national and local NGOs. Additionally, and as part of the humanitarian coordination reset, the Protection Sector launched calls for expressions of interest from national NGOs to support sub-national co-coordination and participate in the consolidated Strategic Advisory Group. These calls initiated the process of strengthening national NGO leadership and ensuring more inclusive representation within the revised coordination structure.
  • Strengthened engagement and coordination with MoSAL: In February 2026, the Protection Sector consulted with MoSAL on the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, presenting its proposed response strategy, priorities, activity portfolio and financial requirements. The discussion covered 2025 achievements and operational challenges and the planned focus for 2026, including specialized protection services, safe and dignified returns, community-based protection, protection monitoring, national capacity strengthening and protection risk mitigation across sectors.
  • Mine Action formally recognized within the NGO registration framework: MoSAL introduced Mine Action as a distinct activity category within the NGO registration framework, providing greater administrative clarity and recognition for organizations implementing mine-action activities in Syria.
  • Country-wide protection response maintained: Between January and June 2026, Protection Sector partners reported reaching approximately 1.4 million people across 253 sub-districts in all 14 governorates, demonstrating sustained country-wide coverage despite a challenging and evolving operational environment.
  • Harmonized 5Ws reporting strengthened: The Sector completed the development of the unified country-wide consolidated response framework and dashboard by end of Q1. An online orientation on harmonized 5Ws reporting was delivered to partners on 15 April 2026, supporting more consistent data collection, reporting and analysis across the unified response.
  • Inter-Agency Referral mechanisms strengthened: On 19–20 May 2026, the Sector conducted a Training of Trainers on the Inter-Agency Referral SOPs, preparing partners to pilot the referral mechanism at sub-national level and promoting safer information sharing, more consistent referral practices and stronger linkages between protection services.
  • Engagement with the Transitional Justice Commission: Initial engagement with the Transitional Justice Commission progressed to explore opportunities for coordination and information-sharing, as well as potential linkages between transitional justice processes, protection actors and relevant services.
  • Donor engagement informed through partner consultation: In June, the Sector convened an ECHO consultation with approximately 25 protection partners to discuss access to people facing heightened protection risks, geographic and thematic prioritization, returns, the no-camp approach and social cohesion. The consultation helped consolidate operational perspectives and inform key protection messages for subsequent donor engagement.

title: Yemen-Conflict Escalation, Mass Displacement | Disaster Brief (OT-2026-000172-YEM) - 25 September 2026
content:
Yemen is experiencing a renewed escalation of conflict, with a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions since early September 2026. Intensified hostilities have resulted in civilian casualties, large-scale internal displacement and increased pressure on essential services and communities hosting displaced families. The most significant displacement has been recorded in Ta’iz and Lahj, with additional displacement reported in Aden, Al Hodeidah, Abyan, Hadramawt and Ma’rib, with many families experiencing secondary or repeated displacement, further increasing protection risks and reducing household coping capacity.

As of 23 September 2026, IOM Yemen’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) had recorded 134,550 internally displaced people, representing 22,425 households, cumulatively since the escalation began in June 2026. The largest concentration was reported in Ta’iz Governorate, hosting 75,180 people (56%), followed by Lahj with 34,446 (26%) and Aden with 10,920 (8%). Additional displacement was recorded in Al Hodeidah (8,244), Abyan (3,888), Hadramawt (1,254) and Ma’rib (618). IOM notes that its monitoring has partial geographic coverage and therefore represents recorded displacement rather than a comprehensive estimate of all displacement associated with the escalation.

The escalation is compounding long-standing humanitarian vulnerabilities in Yemen, including high levels of food insecurity, weakened basic services, protracted displacement and constrained household coping capacity. The Yemen Red Crescent Society (YRCS) has activated its Emergency Operations Centre and is responding through its branches, volunteers and emergency medical services, supporting first aid, casualty transport and referrals, rapid assessments and relief assistance in affected areas.

title: Nepal Flood 2026 - DREF Operation Update #01 (MDRNP022)
content:
As of 18 September 2026, CHF 5.682 million in confirmed multilateral hard pledges recorded against the CHF 18 million IFRC Secretariat Emergency Appeal (approximately 32 per cent). Continued funding is required to sustain the response and scale up early recovery interventions.

A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

On 26 August, a major avalanche occurred in the upper Bhote Koshi watershed near the China–Nepal border triggered a highly destructive debris flow and flash flood along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river corridor. The event caused extensive damage across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, affecting settlements, roads, bridges, schools, health facilities, water systems, telecommunications, markets and hydropower infrastructure. About 41 bridges along the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system was damaged, significantly constraining access to affected communities and disrupting essential services and livelihoods. The flood devastated infrastructure eroding the main road to Rasuwa district, rendering many communities inaccessible for territorial access.

According to the updated data from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)1 dated 21 September 2026, 1,411 people have lost their lives, 5,875 remain missing, and 13,784 have been rescued. To date, authorities have identified and handed over bodies to their families. NDRRMA cautioned that the number of people reported missing was still being verified and could include unidentified deceased persons or individuals who had subsequently been rescued. Search and recovery operations remained ongoing, particularly around affected hydropower facilities and along the river corridor.

Displacement remains a major humanitarian concern. As of 14 September, 2,418 people were staying in 33 government holding centres, including 1,499 people in Nuwakot, 825 in Rasuwa, and 94 in Dhading. The movement of people from holding centres to alternative places like host families or their own abandoned homes continues. As of 21 September, 1,342 people are taking shelter in holding centers across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts2. Assessments of potential sites for temporary shelter were completed in several locations, while food, household items, and other relief supplies continued to be transported by road and helicopter to affected and difficult-to-reach areas. The Government has also initiated arrangements for temporary accommodation, including cash support for households opting for self-arranged accommodation.

The response is progressively shifting from immediate search, rescue and lifesaving relief towards restoration of essential services, temporary and transitional shelter, and early recovery. Significant needs remain in shelter, safe water and sanitation, health and MHPSS, protection, cash assistance and livelihood recovery, while damaged transport and communication infrastructure continues to affect humanitarian access and information flows. The situation also remains dynamic due to continued exposure to flooding, landslides and unstable terrain, requiring ongoing assessment, monitoring and adjustment of the response as access improves and more detailed information becomes available.

International assistance is supporting Nepal’s response through specialized search-and-rescue, forensic identification, health and humanitarian assistance. Teams from India, China, the Republic of Korea, United Arab Emirates, Malaysia, and Australia are supporting rescue operations, while forensic teams from India, China, Japan, Singapore and the Republic of Korea are assisting with DNA collection and identification of deceased persons. Nepal continues to request additional specialized equipment, including drones, LiDAR systems, Bailey bridges, DNA testing kits, underwater drones, pumps and tunnel-rescue equipment.
