title: WHO Situation Report No.3: Health emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (August 2026)
content:
EXECUTIVE SMMARY

SITUATION UPDATE

• In Yemen, the escalation that began on 6 August generated mass casualties across several governorates. Between 6 August and 18 September, the Ministry of Health and Population recorded 3,672 casualties: 674 deaths and 2,998 injuries. Of these, 680 were recorded between 13 and 18 September. Casualty influxes exceeded local stabilization and surgical capacity.

• More than 130 000 people were internally displaced across eight governorates in Yemen as a result of the hostilities. The escalation also drove cross-border displacement, with an additional 3 500 people arriving in Obock, Djibouti.

• In the occupied Palestinian territory (oPt), more than half of health facilities in Gaza remained partially functional and 47% of essential medicines were out of stock.

• In Lebanon, 334 353 people remained internally displaced as of 26 August, while three hospitals and 22 primary health care centres remained closed.

• In Sudan, conflict, displacement and disease outbreaks continued to place severe pressure on the health system. Funding cuts affected 335 health facilities across 13 states, with 153 suspended and 182 operating at reduced capacity. Cholera remained a major concern, with 2 730 cases and 246 deaths reported through 31 August, while dengue transmission continued across 15 states.

• Multiple disease outbreaks remained active, although declining trends were reported for several diseases. In Afghanistan, acute watery diarrhoea decreased by 23.6% compared with July, suspected measles by 44.5%, dengue by 41.0% and CCHF by 36.8%. In Somalia, measles, diphtheria and dengue remained active but declined during the latest reporting weeks. In Iraq, CCHF cases declined by 44% compared with July, while confirmed measles cases increased from 29 to 42.

• Food insecurity and malnutrition remained major health concerns, particularly in Somalia, Yemen and Sudan. In Somalia, an estimated 1.88 million children under five were acutely malnourished, including 493 000 with severe acute malnutrition. In Yemen, an estimated 2.2 million children were acutely malnourished, including 520 000 with severe acute malnutrition.

• Population movements continued to increase demand for health services. Afghanistan recorded 109 305 returnees during August, bringing the total since January to 1 186 755. In Sudan, displacement from North and West Kordofan increased pressure on services in El Obeid, while returns to Khartoum and Al Jazirah increased demand for restored health services.

title: Shelter Cluster - Palestine Situation Report, July - August 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

GAZA

• Shelter Cluster partners continued delivering life-saving Shelter and NFI assistance across the Gaza Strip throughout July and August, responding to urgent needs among affected households through in-kind assistance and voucher modalities.

• In July, partners reached 52,940 households with emergency Shelter/NFI assistance, including 32,666 kitchen sets, 7,073 tarpaulins, 4,611 bedding kits, 3,790 blankets, 11,547 mattresses, 1,087 tents, 4,429 solar lights and 1,178 clothing kits. In addition, 405 households received clothing assistance through vouchers.

• The response remained predominantly NFI-focused, particularly kitchen sets, while the provision of core emergency shelter items remained limited due to shortages and constrained availability of shelter materials.

• Shelter Cluster partners completed sealing-off works for 2,860 housing units across Gaza governorates, improving protection from exposure and living conditions for affected households.

• In August, partners supported 28,631 households with in-kind Shelter/NFI assistance, representing a reduction of approximately 46 per cent compared with July. Distributions included 6,071 tents, 4,897 tarpaulins, 3,676 sealing-off kits, 1,436 tool kits, 74 RHUs, 21,305 mattresses, 18,049 blankets, 18,130 kitchen sets, 12,843 bedding kits, 10,718 clothing kits, 4,376 sleeping mats and 5,173 solar lights.

• Separately, in August, partners improved 4,226 makeshift shelters and completed emergency repairs to 627 partially damaged housing units.

• The Shelter Severity and Household Needs Across Accessible Areas of Gaza assessment was published by the Shelter Cluster and widely amplified. It received strong feedback and visibility, including through presentations to the HCT, NICCG, ECHO consultation, GHD donors and other humanitarian policymakers. Findings were also shared with Palestinian authorities and NGAC, referenced in UN Security Council discussions and presented at the UN Palestinian Rights Committee, and reflected in OCHA reporting. The assessment was also picked up by media outlets, including Haaretz, Ahram Online, Al Jazeera English, The Brussels Times, Common Dreams and DevelopmentAid.

• The SSC found that 1.98 million people—94 per cent of Gaza’s population—require shelter or household assistance. Around two thirds of households are living in tents, makeshift shelters or damaged housing, while 54 per cent of assessed shelters were in poor or very poor condition. More than half of households had been using the same emergency tent for over one year, underlining the urgent need to facilitate the entry of shelter materials and enable more durable improvements ahead of winter.

• Shelter partners continue to face significant access, supply-chain and funding constraints. Most core Shelter/NFI items—including tents, tarpaulins, kitchen sets, solar items, ropes and tapes, timber, tools and other essential shelter materials—remain classified as dual-use.

title: NRC Somalia: Monthly Programme Update (August 2026)
content:
Highlights

  • Somalia shifted towards a compound emergency driven by drought, hunger, conflict, displacement and imminent El-Nino flood risk.

  • PSMN recorded 774,923 displacements between January and 11 September, including 17,800 in August—42% caused by conflict and 36% by drought. Children represented 71% of those displaced and women and children nearly 87%.

  • About 6.5 million people faced acute food insecurity, while 1.9 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition, including nearly 500,000 severe cases. The national basket cost USD 213, up 8% annually, while wages fell 28% and livestock prices 16%.

  • Protection risks intensified, including fighting in Baidoa and the eviction of 310 households—1,860 people—from 10 Kismayo sites. Only 26% of specialized protection services remained operational; 54 facilities closed or scaled down and 295 staff were laid off.

  • Only 25% of health requirements were funded, leaving more than 380 facilities operating at reduced capacity. With risk of AWD/cholera outbreak due to Elnino projected.

  • NRC is implementing El Niño Anticipatory Action (AA) and preparedness initiatives through community-led Group Cash Transfers (GCTs), with 41 communities across five districts—Kismayo, Jowhar, Galkacyo, Dhusamareeb and Adado—submitting GCT applications totaling USD 258,000 following community engagement and contingency planning. Proposed actions reflect locally identified priorities, including drainage and flood-channel clearing, reinforcement of flood protection structures, rehabilitation of access routes, protection of communal infrastructure and preparation of evacuation areas, linked to localized early warning and contingency planning.

title: Syria Field Office - Mid-Year, 2026 Protection Case Update As of 30 June 2026: Protection Case Trends - (January – June), 2026
content:
Executive Summary – Mid-Year 2026 Protection Case Trends, UNRWA Syria

During the first half of 2026, UNRWA recorded 587 protection cases affecting Palestine refugees across Syria. Reported cases increased from 266 in Q1 to 321 in Q2, reflecting strengthened case identification and referral pathways, expanded implementation of the Protection Case Referral SOP, and continued engagement of frontline personnel across programmes. As with previous reporting periods, reported case numbers should be interpreted in the context of reporting capacity, programme access and referral mechanisms, and not as a direct measure of the prevalence of protection risks.

Key Protection Trends

  • Gender-Based Violence (GBV) accounted for the largest share of reported cases (381 cases; 65%), with psychological and emotional abuse remaining the most frequently reported GBV concern (149 cases).
  • General Protection (GP) represented 164 cases (28%), with psychological/emotional abuse and neglect continuing to dominate reporting. Increases were also observed in barriers to services, civil documentation concerns and physical violence, reflecting evolving protection risks affecting vulnerable households and returnees.
  • Child Protection (CP) accounted for 42 cases (7%) of reported cases. Child abuse and neglect remained the principal concern, while reduced reporting during Q2 may partly reflect fewer identification opportunities during school closures and holiday periods rather than reduced protection risks.

Geographical Concentration of Needs

Protection concerns remained concentrated in a limited number of locations:

  • Rural Damascus accounted for 289 cases (49.2%), representing nearly half of all reported protection cases.
  • The North Area recorded 92 cases (15.7%), followed by the Central Area with 87 cases (14.8%) and the South Area with 74 cases (12.6%).
  • Increasing return movements are generating additional protection concerns related to housing, civil documentation, access to services and psychosocial wellbeing, particularly in areas of return.

Emerging and High-Risk Protection Patterns

  • Psychological and emotional abuse remained the most prominent protection concern across both GBV and GP categories, highlighting persistent psychosocial distress among Palestine refugees.
  • Civil documentation and barriers to services increased during the reporting period, raising concerns regarding access to rights, assistance and reintegration support.
  • Complex cases requiring coordinated responses across multiple programmes continue to highlight the importance of integrated protection interventions and strengthened referral mechanisms. During H1 2026, 119 cases required multi-service referrals within UNRWA.

Programme Contributions and Service Response

  • The Health Programme remained the primary entry point for case identification (81% of reported cases), reflecting the critical role of health and MHPSS personnel in detecting and responding to protection concerns.
  • UNRWA continued to provide a range of protection-related services, with health and hospitalization services (40%) and PSS/MHPSS support (34%) accounting for the largest share of responses.

Why Support Remains Critical

Protection risks affecting Palestine refugees in Syria remain acute and increasingly complex. Sustained support is needed to:

  • Strengthen PSS/MHPSS and GBV prevention and response services, given the continued predominance of psychological and emotional harm.
  • Support integrated responses for complex and high-risk cases, including survivors of GBV, children at risk and vulnerable returnee households.
  • Expand legal assistance and civil documentation support to address growing administrative and access-related barriers.
  • Strengthen community-based protection mechanisms and referral systems to improve early identification and response.
  • Maintain emergency protection assistance and multi-programme service delivery for individuals and families facing heightened protection vulnerabilities.

Overall, H1 2026 demonstrates both the continued protection needs facing Palestine refugees in Syria and the importance of sustained investment in integrated protection systems, referral pathways and frontline services to ensure timely identification, referral and response to those most at risk.

title: Syrian Arab Republic: Humanitarian Update No. 7 | July - August 2026 [EN/AR]
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • Camp departures accelerated during July and August, with 38,836 IDPs leaving displacement sites, including 19,600 people supported through facilitated return mechanisms. During the same period, 130 IDP sites were inactivated.
  • More than 60,000 IDPs have been supported to return from displacement sites since January 2026, reflecting continued progress under Syria’s No Camps Vision while increasing pressure on services and infrastructure in communities of return.
  • Humanitarian needs are increasingly shifting from camps to communities of return, where inadequate housing, damaged infrastructure, limited services and constrained livelihoods continue to undermine sustainable reintegration and increase the risk of secondary displacement.
  • Infrastructure and service restoration are helping create conditions for return and recovery across Syria, including through rehabilitation of bakeries, water and electricity networks, hospitals, schools, roads, bridges and housing in return-affected communities.
  • Humanitarian partners reached an average of 2.53 million people per month between January and July 2026, with 314 organizations delivering assistance across 4,765 communities. More than US$123 million was provided through cash and voucher assistance.
  • Ar-Raqqa continues to show some of the strongest signs of recovery in north-east Syria, with improvements in water, electricity and protection conditions; however, economic vulnerability remains a major obstacle to sustainable recovery and durable solutions.

title: Venezuela Situation Report, July - August 2026
content:
This report has been prepared by OCHA Venezuela in collaboration with humanitarian clusters and partners, and covers the humanitarian response both in the context of the 24 June earthquakes and the implementation of the Humanitarian Response Plan across the rest of the country.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • Between January and August 2026, the humanitarian response reached 1,901,213 people, of whom 1,463,890 were reached under the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and 437,323 through the response to the 24 June earthquakes.
  • As of 22 September, the humanitarian response in Venezuela had mobilized US$490.7 million, of which US$402.2 million (43.2%) was allocated to the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP).
  • The Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) estimated US$21 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs following the June earthquakes.

HUMANITARIAN RESPONSE PLAN

6,2M Target population
$931M Funding requirements
$402,2M Financed (43,2%)

SITUATION OVERVIEW
Venezuela continues to face the consequences of the two major earthquakes (magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5) that struck the country's north-central region on 24 June at 18:00 local time, causing significant humanitarian impacts and infrastructure damage. The first earthquake, with a magnitude of 7.2, had its epicenter along the San Felipe–Yumare–Montalbán corridor (Yaracuy/Carabobo). According to a recent update from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the second earthquake, with a magnitude of 7.5, had its epicenter 17 kilometers west of Catia La Mar, off the coast of La Guaira State.

As of 24 August, authorities had reported 6,509 deaths resulting from the earthquakes. In addition, they indicated that 60,785 housing units had been assessed, of which 11,001 were classified as high risk.

Three months after the earthquakes, the humanitarian response continues to expand across the affected states. As of 22 September, approximately 1.9 million people (59% women and girls) had gained access to essential services and humanitarian assistance through the joint efforts of communities, humanitarian organizations, United Nations entities, donor partners, and government authorities. Of this total, 1,463,890 people received assistance under the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) (62% women and girls), while 437,323 people were reached through the response to the 24 June earthquakes (54% women and girls).

Prior to the earthquakes, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) for Venezuela aimed to assist 5.5 million people, in coordination with national authorities, with a financial requirement of US$632 million. Following the 24 June earthquakes, an HRP addendum expanded the response to reach 1.3 million earthquake-affected people, requiring an additional US$299 million. This figure includes 596,000 people already covered under the 2026 HRP who reside in affected municipalities, as well as an additional 751,000 people incorporated to address humanitarian needs arising from the impact of the earthquakes. With this expansion, the plan is expected to assist a total of 6.2 million people and requires US$931 million.

On 15 September, the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) was presented, estimating recovery and reconstruction needs at US$21 billion. The assessment also estimated US$14.831 billion in damages and losses across the seven states affected by the earthquakes: La Guaira, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, Falcón, and Yaracuy. This exercise, led by the authorities with the support of the European Union and the World Bank, and with technical assistance from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), and CAF-Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, will serve as a basis for identifying priorities and coordinating recovery efforts.

title: IOM Nepal Flood Response Situation Report #6 | 23 September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

The 26 August flash floods in central Nepal have caused significant loss of life, displacement and widespread damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services. Government-led search and rescue operations are on their twenty-eighth day, while access constraints and ongoing verification of displacement and housing impacts remain key challenges.

As of 23 September, the Government of Nepal reports 1,453 bodies recovered, 5,644 people missing and 13,795 people rescued following the 26 August floods, with figures expected to change as access improves. Preliminary humanitarian analysis estimates 84,270 people affected across 17 municipalities in six districts.

The Government-led Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) indicates approximately 7,570 houses affected, impacting around 32,963 people, alongside damage to roads, bridges, agricultural land and critical infrastructure. Priority needs include shelter and essential household items, WASH, food, health and MHPSS services, protection and access to affected communities. Longer-term support requirements include private housing and settlement, economic activities and livelihood rebuilding, repair and replacement of damaged household energy systems, telecommunications, debris and sediment management, and disaster and climate risk management as the damage to infrastructure continues to constrain humanitarian access and delivery. A Rapid Damage Needs Assessment (RDNA) has also been published by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), which further elaborates on the post-disaster needs.

IOM is supporting the Government-led response through site assessments, coordination, health, protection, non-food items (NFI), recovery and Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).

title: IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 19 (14 - 20 September 2026)
location: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Burundi
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 20 September 2026, the Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) outbreak had resulted in 7,733 confirmed cases, 3,732 deaths and 1,902 recoveries, representing a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 63 of 167 health zones (37.7%) across seven provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, while 55 health zones across five provinces remain classified as active transmission zones.

Although several health zones have reported extended periods without detecting new cases, transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC. A total of 61 newly confirmed cases were reported in Ituri (34), North Kivu (23) and Haut-Uélé (4), with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for 93.4 per cent of all newly reported cases. The continued concentration of transmission in these areas underscores the need to sustain disease surveillance, response and preparedness capacities within affected provinces, while maintaining readiness in neighbouring countries connected through cross-border mobility corridors.

While localized progress has been observed in parts of the response, mortality remains a significant concern. Community deaths continue to account for the majority of newly reported deaths, highlighting ongoing challenges related to early detection, timely referral and access to care. These challenges are particularly relevant in settings affected by displacement, insecurity and population movement, where delays in seeking or accessing care may contribute to continued transmission.

title: Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of): Earthquake Response Situation Report #30 (17 to 23 September 2026)
content:
The Situation Report #30 provides an update on IOM’s response to the earthquakes that struck the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela on 24 June 2026, covering the period from 17 to 23 September 2026. During the reporting period, IOM maintained management and co-management of four planned camps in La Guaira, strengthened inter-agency coordination, expanded health and mental health services, and continued supporting housing solutions, protection services and population monitoring for affected communities. Official figures indicate that 107 transitory camps remain operational, accommodating 23,901 people, while recovery and relocation efforts continue nationwide.

Highlights

IOM completed a comprehensive Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) needs assessment across the four camps under its management and co-management through 32 focus group discussions involving 224 participants. The findings will guide future interventions aimed at strengthening psychological well-being, community resilience and access to mental health services. IOM also launched mhGAP training for first-line responders, health workers and partners to strengthen the identification and management of mental health conditions in humanitarian settings.

IOM significantly expanded health service coverage through mobile outreach teams, field hospital services and new deployments in La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo and Yaracuy. During the reporting period, 531 health consultations were delivered through five mobile activities, strengthening access to primary health care, sexual and reproductive health services, mental health support and referrals for specialized care.

At Polideportivo José María Vargas, IOM continued preparedness measures for potential population movements by improving infrastructure, installing rain protection curtains, expanding service areas and delivering 7 bunk beds and 14 mattresses. In parallel, IOM continued supporting housing solutions through the housing repair pilot in areas adjacent to César Nieves and strengthened coordination around possible relocation processes.

IOM Activities

IOM maintained direct management of Polideportivo José María Vargas and continued co-managing César Nieves, Campo de Golf and Mare Abajo II with its implementing partner NRC. Activities focused on camp management, population monitoring, infrastructure improvements, community participation, relocation preparedness and support for housing solutions. Population verification exercises and household assessments continued to support evidence-based planning and decision-making.

In shelter and basic assistance, IOM distributed essential household items to more than 116 families in camps and affected communities. During the reporting period, the Organization delivered 906 collapsible jerry cans and 454 hygiene items. Since the beginning of the response, IOM has distributed more than 10,893 plastic tarpaulins, 9,163 collapsible jerry cans, 6,813 kitchen sets, 5,922 toolkits, 4,563 solar lamps and 5,622 hygiene items, contributing to improved living conditions for affected households.

In WASH, IOM continued monitoring water supply, sanitation systems, drainage networks and hygiene services across camps. Together with sector partners, IOM coordinated the delivery of 90,000 litres of water to 575 households in Mare Abajo II. Since the start of the response, partners have distributed 3,183,000 litres of water, 3,769 family hygiene kits and 3,702 menstrual hygiene kits, while IOM continued supporting technical coordination and service monitoring.

IOM also maintained protection programming and community-based services. Between 15 and 22 September, IOM and its partners provided protection assistance to 108 individuals, including legal counselling, case management, psychological support and referrals to specialized institutions. The Organization continued monitoring protection risks, supporting survivors, facilitating humanitarian transfers and strengthening child protection and community protection mechanisms.

IOM Planned Response

IOM will continue monitoring accommodation conditions, population movements and temporary accommodation arrangements, while strengthening preparedness in camps that may receive populations in the event of relocations. The Organization will also continue advancing the housing repair pilot in César Nieves and maintaining updated population data to support operational planning and durable solutions processes.

IOM will maintain mobile health and mental health services, strengthen referral pathways and access to specialized care, continue WASH monitoring and infrastructure follow-up, and sustain protection activities for vulnerable populations. Inter-agency coordination with authorities, partners and communities will remain a priority to support safe, dignified and sustainable solutions for people affected by the earthquakes.

title: PAHO Regional Situation Report No.12: Measles in the Region of the Americas (24 September 2026)
content:
Summary of the Situation

Between epidemiological week (EW) 1 and EW 37 of 2026 (which ended on 19 September 2026), the Region of the Americas reported 53,957 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories, representing a 3.8- foldincrease compared with the same period in 2025. Guatemala (33,866), Mexico (12,943), the United States (3,471), Peru (2,292), and Canada (1,120) account for the vast majority (99.5%) of confirmed cases (Map 1). A total of 68 deaths have been reported, including 45 in Guatemala, 22 in Mexico, and one in Bolivia (1).

During EW 35 andEW 36 of 2026, the Region of the Americas reported 709 new confirmed cases of measles in seven countries and territories, representing a 43% decrease compared with the previous two-week period (EW 33–34; 1,244 new cases, of which 333were retrospectively accounted for since the lastregional situation report was published) (Figure 1). Of the 709 new confirmed cases reported during EW 35–36, the United States accounted for 290, followed by Peru with 190, Guatemala with 176, Mexico with 46, and Bolivia with 5, while Canada and Colombia reported one case each.

title: UNHCR Nigeria Benue Protection Update - August 2026
content:
Situation Update

Coordinated armed attacks on the communities of Ayaba, Ukpen, Bom, Aboajio and Yina in Mbazun Ward, Ukum LGA, killed 58 people in August, in the deadliest single episode recorded in Benue this year. A joint assessment by the Benue State Emergency Management Agency, the Nigerian Red Cross Society and UNHCR profiled more than 440 displaced families, with total household displacement estimated at around 500 and verification continuing. four more residents were killed in a night attack on Abaushwa community in Guma, and further deaths were recorded in Logo, Okpokwu and Otukpo. Civilians remained at the centre of the crisis in August, with 92% of reported security incidents involving direct protection violations. Benue is facing a widening protection crisis. Kidnappings reached their highest level of 2026 in August, with 14 incidents recorded across nine LGAs, while escalating attacks continue to kill, displace and terrorize rural communities. The impact extends far beyond immediate casualties: families are being cut off from farmland during a critical agricultural period, displacement into host communities is increasing pressure on already scarce resources, and women and children face heightened protection risks. Despite the growing severity of the crisis, some of the most affected LGAs remain outside structured community-based protection monitoring systems, limiting early warning and timely humanitarian response.

title: Escalation in the Middle East and Beyond — Mobility Report (08 – 21 September 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

On 17 June 2026, the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran reached an agreement on a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) concerning the cessation of hostilities. The escalation in the Middle East and beyond had triggered a humanitarian crisis affecting multiple regions in an already fragile context. A resurgence of hostilities in recent weeks is placing pressure on humanitarian access and threatens civilian and essential services. Mobility dynamics across the region and beyond due to renewed escalation remains uncertain. The situation continues to be highly fragile, requiring sustained monitoring and operational preparedness.1 In the Islamic Republic of Iran, some families have begun returning to their homes amid signs of de-escalation. However, thousands continue to shelter in hotels due to damage to housing and civilian infrastructure. As of 01 June, approximately 9,000 individuals remain displaced, unable to return to their homes due to the extent of the damage. Overall, population movements remain localized, temporary, and economically driven, with no signs of mass displacement. In Yemen, displacement increased significantly following the escalation of conflict along the West Coast in early September 2026. Between 07 June and 21 September 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded approximately 132,330 displaced individuals, the majority of whom were hosted in Ta’iz and Lahj governorates. Displacement accelerated sharply in early September, with many families experiencing repeated movements and seeking refuge in already overstretched displacement sites and host communities. In addition, 3,506 Yemeni nationals arrived in Djibouti between 10 and 21 September, reportedly fleeing the deteriorating security situation.2 In Lebanon, displacement nationwide remains significant despite continuing returns. As of 15 September 2026, 341,228 people remain internally displaced across 626 cadasters, a 2 per cent increase compared to the previous reporting period (as of 09 September 2026). Of the total IDPs in Lebanon, 16,536 individuals remained displaced in 166 collective shelters. Returns have continued, with 864,680 returned IDPs reported as of 15 September 2026, marking a 6 per cent increase from the previous round (as of 09 September 2026).3 Humanitarian and protection needs remain acute, driven by the destruction of homes and services, prolonged displacement, explosive ordnance risks, protection concerns, and declining coping capacities. Meanwhile, cross-border flows into the Syrian Arab Republic are continuing, with a total of 813,000 movements recorded as of 21 September 2026.

title: Humanitarian Access Snapshot 14: Palestinian Communities at Risk of Erasure Amid Escalating Settler Violence and Access Restrictions across the West Bank (23 September 2026)
content:
Executive summary

This snapshot is based on a survey of 29 international and national NGOs conducted in the first week of September and covering the previous six months, from March through August 2026. While the results do not capture every NGO operating in the West Bank, they reflect the persistently constrained operating environment and impact on Palestinian communities.

Israeli policies in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are pushing Palestinians deeper into humanitarian crisis. State-backed settler violence is escalating sharply, targeting Palestinians in their homes, on the roads and on their land.

Combined with military raids, settlement expansion, demolitions and movement restrictions, these policies and practices are further consolidating annexation of the occupied West Bank, forcibly displacing communities and making it increasingly difficult for Palestinians to remain on their land.

For humanitarian organisations, the consequences are immediate. Needs are rising while the space to respond is shrinking. Staff and partners face attacks and threats, routes are closed or too dangerous to use, and communities are increasingly cut off from essential assistance and services. National and international NGOs are consistently being forced to delay, relocate, scale back or suspend services, while adopting alternative ways of working to maintain operations

wherever possible. Despite reducing their visibility to mitigate risk, they continue to face attacks. At the same time, many of these organisations are facing shrinking budgets as donors reduce funding, forcing cuts to essential services for families in need.

As Israeli elections approach, the government is not restraining these dynamics, and instead is allowing them to accelerate. Political measures and increasingly extreme rhetoric are emboldening settlers and entrenching impunity, leaving already displaced and isolated communities to face even greater danger.

title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 86, as of 22 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

  • One person killed and dozens abducted by armed men in Haut-Mbomou.
  • Approximately 2,000 households receive cash assistance in Mbomou and Haut-Mbomou.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture - South-East

  • On 17 September, armed men prevented humanitarian organizations travelling from Zémio to Djéma, where they had planned to resume activities suspended for an extended period due to insecurity. The armed men demanded money in exchange for freedom of movement and threatened members of the humanitarian mission. Despite efforts to continue the mission, humanitarian actors were forced to turn back at Kitessa because of security constraints. On 21 September, the same humanitarian workers were again ambushed by armed men while returning to Zémio along the Mboki-Zémio road. As a result, more than 20,000 vulnerable people in Djéma and along the Zémio-Djéma, Zémio-Dembia and Zémio-Mboki corridors continue to face disruptions in humanitarian assistance. These incidents occurred after more than two months of humanitarian activity suspensions since July 2026 amid a continued deterioration of the security situation in Haut-Mbomou. Protection risks remain high, with killings, gender-based violence and abductions continuing to be reported. Haut-Mbomou remains the second most affected prefecture by incidents impacting humanitarian actors.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

WASH

Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture - North-East

  • From 15 to 17 September, Plan International distributed hygiene and dignity kits, as well as goats, in Ndélé town, Aliou-Lemena and Bangbali. Six girls aged 12 to 17 received kits containing wraps, buckets, cooking utensils and personal hygiene items. In addition, 61 households each received two goats, for a total of 122 animals, to strengthen their livelihoods. Monitoring of livelihood recovery and economic empowerment activities was also conducted.

title: Afghanistan: Weekly Market Report: Issue 312: Week 3 - September 2026
content:
Key Highlights

Market Overview

Markets continued to show limited week-on-week volatility in the third week of September, although underlying price pressures remained evident. Rising fuel prices and higher import costs continued to increase transportation and supply-chain costs and exert upward pressure on market prices. Meanwhile, rice, wheat flour, cooking oil, sugar, salt and potato prices remained elevated compared with last year, while weak labour availability and subdued purchasing power continued to constrain household food access.

Food Categories:

Food markets recorded mixed but generally modest movements during the week. While several commodities experienced minor price adjustments, the year-on-year comparison highlights persistent increases in rice, wheat flour, cooking oil, sugar, salt and potato prices.

• Wheat and Wheat Flour: Wheat grain and flour prices recorded negligible weekly increases, however compared to last year, wheat grain, wheat flour (low-price and high-price) remained 15%, 13% and 8% higher, respectively.

• Rice: Rice prices edged down during the week, with Palawi declining by 0.5% and Sholae by 0.2%. Nevertheless, both varieties continued to register substantial annual increases of 21% and 35%, respectively, and both remained 21% above their three-year averages.

• Other Staples: Weekly price movements across cooking oil, sugar, pulses, salt and bread remained limited. Cooking oil and sugar continued to trade above last year's levels, by 13% and 8%, respectively, whereas pulses and bread remained 12% and 3% below their corresponding annual levels.

• Vegetables: Potato prices fell by 2.3% during the week, while onion prices rose by 3.2% and tomato prices increased marginally by 0.2%. Despite the weekly decline, potato remained 35% above last year and 27% above its three-year average. Tomato and onion prices were 30% and 5% lower year-on-year, respectively.

Non-Food Categories:

Terms of Trade (ToT): The ToT, which reflects purchasing power, remained constraint for both labour-dependent households and pastoralists, as declining income and higher prices limit their access to food.

• Casual Labour ToT: The nominal casual labour ToT declined slightly to 10.1 kg of low-price wheat flour, representing a 15% decline from last year and an 11% decline against the three-year average. The sustained decline in purchasing power reflects continued pressure on labour income relative to food prices.

• Labour Availability and Wages: Unskilled labour availability remained at 2.0 days per week, 15% below last year and 19% below the three-year average. Unskilled wages were 4% lower year-on-year, while skilled wages showed no annual change.

• Pastoralist ToT: A pastoralist could exchange a one-year-old female sheep for 262 kg of low-price wheat flour, which is 15% below last year and 7% below the three-year average. This indicates continued pressure on the purchasing power of livestock-dependent households.

• Fertilizers and Agricultural Inputs: DAP and urea prices recorded marginal weekly changes. Despite minor weekly fluctuations, annual prices remained elevated, with DAP 13% and urea 26% higher than last year. Meanwhile, improved seed and animal feed prices remained broadly stable due to low market demand and standing 7% and 6% below last year, respectively.

title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 31 August
content:
Highlights

  • UNICEF is scaling up its response from 49 to 60 affected and high-risk health zones, supporting Government-led efforts across community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, PSEA and continuity of essential services.
  • In August, 11,723 community actors, including 6,546 community mobilizers (RECOs), were trained and mobilized on RCCE and community-based surveillance. Since the beginning of the response, a total of 24,750 frontline workers, including 12,555 community mobilizers (RECOs), have been mobilized.
  • UNICEF-supported community surveillance networks generated 29,689 alerts in August, representing an 186 per cent increase from the previous reporting period. Contact tracing coverage reached 88 per cent, with 22,499 of 25,560 contacts followed, strengthening outbreak detection and monitoring efforts.
  • UNICEF and partners continued to deliver lifesaving support despite operational constraints due to the Ebola outbreak. In August, 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health and nutrition assistance through the rapid response mechanism.
  • Ahead of the new school year, UNICEF and the Ministry of Education agreed on measures to ensure the safe reopening of schools in Ebola-affected provinces. UNICEF provided technical support to establish reopening standards based on risk assessments of the BVD spread in schools and will support 900 schools with WASH and IPC supplies, MHPSS services, and community awareness activities on Ebola prevention.
  • UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 31 August 2026, US$34.4 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$79 million funding gap, equivalent to 70 per cent of the requirement.

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL SITUATION UPDATE

Between 1 and 31 August 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,581 confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 1,420 deaths. As of 31 August, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 6,186, including 3,007 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%. The outbreak continued to expand geographically with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Bas-Uélé Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to six (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé,
Tshopo and Bas-Uélé). During August, an additional 12 health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 60 affected health zones, representing 39.7 per cent of the country's 151 health zones.

The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for 81.9 per cent of all confirmed cases (5,065) and 2,305 deaths followed by North Kivu (868 cases, 589 deaths) and Haut-Uélé (227 cases, 100 deaths). Transmission also continued in Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uélé. Women and girls represent 53 per cent of reported cases. Children under 17 account for approximately 30.2 per cent of cases and 21.8 per cent of reported deaths, with children under five bearing the greatest burden, representing nearly two-thirds of deaths among children under 18. During August, 42 health workers were affected, underscoring ongoing risks to frontline responders.

title: Malawi: Population Movement - DREF Final Report (MDRMW022)
content:
Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

29-01-2025

What happened, where and when?

1. Background

Following the post-election unrest in Mozambique, Malawi hosted 7,456 asylum seekers across Nsanje, Dedza, Chikwawa, Mwanza, Mulanje, and Dzaleka beginning in December 2024. The influx followed political instability and violence that forced Mozambican citizens to seek refuge in Malawi.

On 27 February 2025, Mozambique's Minister of Home Security led a delegation to Malawi to meet with government officials and discuss plans for a voluntary repatriation process. The two governments agreed that asylum seekers willing to return should be allowed to do so under a coordinated and safe process.

2. Repatriation Process

A joint registration exercise was conducted for asylum seekers who expressed willingness to return to Mozambique. The Mozambican government provided vehicles to transport voluntary returnees to the Shire River Dock, where they were ferried across the river by speedboats.

The repatriation process began on 28 February 2025 and concluded on 13 March, during which 7,076 registered Mozambicans were repatriated. Despite this achievement, the operation faced challenges, including high Shire River water levels caused by heavy rains and flooding, logistical constraints, and reluctance among some asylum seekers due to ongoing security concerns in Mozambique.

Between 13 March and 30 April 2025, the Government of Malawi undertook various activities to facilitate the closure of the Nyamithuthu Camp, marking the end of the repatriation phase.

3. Remaining Population and Refugee Status Determination

While a majority of asylum seekers returned to Mozambique, a number remained unwilling to do so. Many of those who stayed cited fears for their safety, particularly individuals with political affiliations who feared persecution upon return. Others reported trauma from earlier violence, including assaults, arson attacks, and property loss.

As of 26 April 2025, 336 households (671 individuals) remained registered as Mozambican asylum seekers at Nyamithuthu Camp. On 27 April, the Department for Refugees (DfR) conducted a Refugee Status Determination (RSD) exercise to assess eligibility for refugee status. Of the 268 individuals targeted for interviews, 221 participated, but their claims were found to lack credibility. Most applicants failed to provide consistent or verifiable information about their origins or experiences. Consequently, all 221 individuals were recommended for denial of refugee status. The Government of Malawi concluded that the remaining asylum seekers did not qualify as persons of concern requiring protection.

4. Camp Closure:

Following the RSD outcomes, Nyamithuthu Camp was officially closed by the Government of Malawi on 30 April 2025. During the process, it was observed that the Mozambican authorities repatriated not only asylum seekers linked to the 2024 unrest but also other Mozambican nationals who opted to return. Despite ongoing reconciliation efforts, reports of insecurity and violent protests in Mozambique persisted, suggesting that new asylum inflows into Malawi could continue in the future.

5. Post-Closure Humanitarian Response

In response to the camp closure and its effects on host communities, the Malawi Red Cross Society (MRCS), with support from the IFRC Harare Cluster, submitted an operations update in May 2025. The update requested approval for additional activities aimed at rehabilitating affected host communities, focusing on Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) interventions in schools and nearby villages. Following the approval, a WASH assessment was carried out between 20 and 25 June 2025. The assessment found that key sanitation activities such as solarization of water systems, desludging, and latrine maintenance could not be completed before the DREF operation's official closure in August 2025. This revealed a gap between the planned interventions and the achievable implementation timeframe.

6. Impact on Host Communities

The arrival and temporary settlement of asylum seekers placed significant strain on host communities and public infrastructure. Local villages lacked sufficient capacity to provide essential health services such as first aid, mental health support, and epidemic prevention awareness. This increased vulnerability to potential health crises. Access to safe water remained limited, as asylum seekers relied heavily on boreholes in host communities. These boreholes were later damaged when tensions escalated after the announcement that none of the remaining asylum seekers qualified for refugee protection. Pipes, roads, and pedestals were destroyed or filled with mud, further disrupting water access. In the education sector, children of asylum seekers were integrated into three nearby schools, which became overcrowded. The heavy use of school latrines resulted in deterioration and filling of sanitation facilities, with two schools now requiring urgent rehabilitation. Despite repeated requests from the Department for Refugees, these sanitation challenges remained unresolved due to competing priorities among humanitarian actors.

7. Key Observations and Outstanding Needs

• The repatriation process demonstrated strong collaboration between the Governments of Malawi and Mozambique, but logistical challenges hindered efficiency.

• The lack of sustainable WASH infrastructure in host communities highlighted the need for longer-term recovery support beyond camp closure.

• Health and sanitation systems in affected areas remained overstretched, increasing the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly cholera.

• Rehabilitation of damaged boreholes and latrines, along with continued hygiene promotion, was urgently required to restore community resilience.

title: UNFPA Situation Report: Crisis in Mali - April 2026
content:
Highlights

These escalating risks are critically compounded by severe response deficits, leaving 79 percent of safe shelter needs and 87 percent of economic empowerment support unmet.
  • Forced Displacements: An armed ultimatum by non-state armed groups (NSAGs) in Zouera is causing continuous population movements in the Northern Circle (Gourma Rharous, Goundam, Niafunké).
  • Armed Blockades and Social Control: Ongoing blockade on Léré armed groups severely hindering access to emergency sexual and reproductive health (SRH) care, combined with targeted restrictions against women including mandatory head coverings, limited movements and extortion.
  • In August, UNFPA deployed 49 midwives and 2 mobile teams across eight regions, reaching 7,500 women and girls with SRH and GBV prevention, mitigation and response support. UNFPA also distributed 170 dignity and menstrual hygiene kits to women and adolescent girls.

title: El Niño Phenomenon in the Americas Region: Situation Report #1, 14 September 2026
content:
HIGHLIGHTS

• On 24 June, the Public Health Situation Analysis: El Niño in the Americas, 2026–2027, was published, highlighting the main hydrometeorological and environmental hazards associated with the El Niño phenomenon and their implications for public health (1).

• El Niño continues to strengthen: the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) raised the probability of a “very strong” event during the fall and winter of 2026–2027 to over 90%. Sea surface temperature anomalies in the eastern equatorial Pacific exceeded +2 °C (2).

• These conditions create a regional public health risk scenario, with varying manifestations across different subregions. Eight countries/territories in the Region have issued official emergency or alert declarations, at the national and/or subnational levels, due to hazards associated with El Niño.

• In Central America, the most clearly documented health impact of the period continues to be food insecurity in the Central American Dry Corridor (Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador), consistent with the expected pattern of drought (1,3–5).

• In the Andean Region, Colombia presents one of the most complex risk profiles in the Region: forest fires declared a public disaster in Tolima, a spreading dengue outbreak, and heavy rains – all occurring alongside the response to the August 10 earthquake (6–8). Peru is experiencing one of the most prolonged and severe impact scenarios of 2026: a coastal El Niño episode with rains and flooding since February, with 70 reported deaths and 633 health facilities affected (9–11, 12–15).

• In the Brazil and Southern Cone Subregion, Brazil accounts for the region’s most significant impact, with reduced water levels in the Amazon basin and air quality affected by wildfires, leading to public health emergencies declared at the municipal and state levels.

• PAHO/WHO is providing support for preparedness and response efforts in various countries of the Region, primarily in the Central American Dry Corridor, the Andean Region, Brazil, and the Caribbean, with an emphasis on the resilience of health services in the Dry Corridor of Honduras (16).

title: UNHCR-IOM Pakistan Flash update # 112 on Arrest and Detention/Flow Monitoring, 15 Sep 2023 to 19 Sep 2026
content:
INTRODUCTION

In response to the Ministry of Interior's (MoI) decision of 26 September 2023 to enact an “Illegal Foreigners' Repatriation Plan”, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency and IOM, the UN Migration Agency, have collated their data on the arrest, detention, and deportation of Proof of Registration (PoR) holders, Afghan Citizen Card (ACC) holders, and undocumented Afghan nationals as well as on the outflows of Afghan nationals at the Torkham, Ghulam Khan, Chaman, Badini and Bahramcha border crossing points, to better understand the protection environment and movements of Afghan nationals returning to Afghanistan from Pakistan.

In 2025, the Government of Pakistan (GoP) issued several directives impacting Afghan nationals. In January, the GoP announced that Afghan nationals should relocate from Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) and Rawalpindi, or else face deportation. In April, further announcements indicated the implementation of the second phase of the “IFRP”, targeting ACC holders, in addition to undocumented Afghans. In July, the GoP issued a Statutory Regulation Order (SRO) directing the repatriation/deportation of PoR card holders following the expiry of PoR card validity on 30 June. The GoP later indicated a deadline of 1 September for PoR holders to leave Pakistan, before the start of the repatriation/deportation process. UNHCR issued a press briefing expressing concern regarding the decision and urging the GoP to exempt Afghans with international protection needs, as well as those with particular circumstances or vulnerabilities, from involuntary return.

title: Haiti Protection Analysis Update - September 2026
content:
Haiti has been experiencing a deepening political, security, and humanitarian protection crisis since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, with escalating armed violence and civil unrest, particularly in the West, Artibonite, and Centre departments. Weak rule of law institutions, constrained resources, and endemic corruption hinder the State’s ability to protect and promote human rights. Armed violence exacerbates pre-existing humanitarian needs and vulnerabilities stemming from socio-economic inequalities and frequent natural disasters.

The Haitian population faces serious protection risks arising from the actions of armed groups, self-defence groups, and security forces. From 1 January to 31 July 2026, the Human Rights Service (HRS) of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH) and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) documented 3,373 killings and 1,494 injuries. During the same period, 176 people were kidnapped for ransom by armed groups, compared with 433 in 2025.

These patterns of violence intersect with other protection risks and disproportionately affect people facing heightened vulnerabilities. Gender-based violence (GBV) remains alarmingly high and underreported, with 6,337 incidents, primarily affecting women and girls, reported between January and 31 July 2026. Children are exposed to violence, family separation and trafficking, including recruitment by armed groups, increasing their vulnerability to abuse and exploitation. Restrictions on freedom of movement further compound these risks, limiting access to food, safe drinking water, healthcare and education, disrupting the transportation of goods and constraining humanitarian access.

Continued violence and restrictions on movement have also contributed to more than 1.47 million people being internally displaced since 2022. Many live in increasingly overstretched host communities, while others remain in overcrowded and unsafe displacement sites with limited access to basic services. Repeated displacement has disrupted family and community networks, education, livelihoods and access to social protection, eroding existing coping capacities.

These internal displacement dynamics are compounded by forced returns of Haitians from countries of destination. Haitians returning from the Dominican Republic and other countries may face return without adequate safeguards or due process, often into areas where insecurity, limited services and weak institutional capacity constrain opportunities for safe and sustainable reintegration. The termination of U.S. Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians on 27 July 2026, which had protected 350,000 Haitian nationals and the arrival of the first deportation flight in Cap-Haïtien on 20 August, further underscore the potential for increased return-related protection pressures.

Mass displacement forced returns and weakened State presence in areas affected by violence are aggravating barriers to legal identity and access to justice. Loss of documentation limited civil registration services and restricted access to legal assistance and remedies particularly affect internally displaced persons and forcibly returned Haitians. These barriers undermine fundamental rights and compound risks, including restrictions on freedom of movement, exposure to violence and exclusion from essential services.

Against this backdrop, the Humanitarian Reset provides an opportunity to move beyond responding to incidents and delivering assistance to address the underlying drivers of protection risks – by reducing threats, mitigating vulnerabilities and strengthening the capacities of affected populations, through prevention, community-based protection and multisectoral interventions. Such an approach is critical to strengthening community leadership and resilience, preserving social cohesion and ensuring that humanitarian interventions contribute measurably to reducing protection risks.

The priority protection risks requiring immediate attention in the period covered by this analysis are:
1. Attacks on members of the population and other unlawful killings, and attacks on public and private objects
2. Unlawful impediments or restrictions to freedom of movement, and forced displacement
3. Gender-based violence
4. Forced recruitment and association of children in armed forces and groups
5. Impediments and/or restrictions to access to legal identity, remedies and justice

title: Colombia: Flash Update 014 - Update on the Impact of the Earthquake in Colombia - September 23, 2026
content:
This Flash Update is produced by OCHA Colombia with inputs from humanitarian partners and official reports. Information is current as of 23 September at 6:30 p.m. This document will continue to be issued on a weekly basis through the end of September.

  • More than one month after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake, approximately 487,000 people have been affected across 500 municipalities in 16 departments, with the most severe impacts reported in Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Chocó, Quindío and Caldas. The potential onset of a severe El Niño event could further exacerbate humanitarian and recovery needs.
  • Communities are facing multiple, simultaneous crises. In addition to the impact of the earthquake, people continue to experience pre-existing effects of the armed conflict, including displacement, confinement and restricted access to essential services. These factors increase population vulnerability and place additional strain on institutional response capacities.
  • The Government and international partners continue to deliver a coordinated response. Institutions within the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD) are providing sectoral assistance in coordination with territorial authorities. United Nations agencies and humanitarian partners continue to work together to deliver health care, water, sanitation and hygiene services, food security support, shelter, protection and early recovery assistance. To date, 31 organizations have supported more than 137,000 people in 53 prioritized municipalities.
  • Significant needs and funding gaps persist. While recovery efforts are advancing through the development of the Specific Action Plan for Recovery (PAE), the humanitarian response still faces a 52 per cent funding gap against the US$619 million required to address the multisectoral needs of affected populations through the end of 2026.

title: Eswatini | Drought - Early Action Protocol Activation, 9th September 2026 (EAP2023SZ01/MDRSZ005)
content:
Early action protocol Activation

Activation Overview

Baphalali Eswatini Red Cross Society (BERCS) has activated its Early Action Protocol for drought following National forecasts indicating a high probability of an El Niño-induced drought season in Eswatini. Seasonal outlooks and forecast monitoring conducted through the Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG), National Meteorological Services and Regional climate information systems indicated an elevated likelihood of below-normal rainfall in the October to December season (Figure 1). This is expected to lead to reduced water availability and worsening food insecurity conditions across drought-prone areas, particularly in the Lubombo, parts of Lowveld, parts of the Highveld and Middleveld.

The trigger threshold in the Drought Early Action Protocol was reached when the OND forecast issued in early September indicated below normal rainfall was expected. Early actions will be implemented before peak drought impacts occur during the January-March lean season.

Implementation will focus on vulnerable households who will potentially be exposed to food insecurity, loss of livelihoods and reduced access to water. Priority will be given to households headed by women, older persons, persons with disabilities, child-headed households, smallholder farmers, and households dependent on rain-fed agriculture.

Target geographical areas include drought-prone chiefdoms across the Lubombo and Shiselweni identified through EAP risk analysis, vulnerability assessments and drought monitoring systems.

title: Middle East Situation Lebanon - Operational Update (August 2026)
content:
Lebanon remains among the countries most affected by forced displacement globally, hosting one of the largest refugee populations per capita while almost 334,353 people remained internally displaced at the end of August. Despite ceasefire agreements, repeated violations and persistent insecurity continue to drive humanitarian needs and repeated displacement, hinder safe and sustainable returns and recovery of conflict-affected areas, and place additional stress and strain on families and affected local communities.

Around 136,000 refugees who had been living in areas directly impacted by the escalating hostilities became internally displaced and faced difficulties finding safe and dignified shelter and livelihoods in displacement. Nearly 29,700 displaced Syrian refugees were directly identified as being in need of protection and assistance and referrals to services. The volatile situation, repeated displacement and uncertainties continue to affect people’s safety, dignity and psychological well-being.

title: Lebanon Crisis Response Plan 2026 (update)
content:
In 2026, IOM aims to support and empower Lebanon’s most vulnerable populations, including migrants, refugees, internally displaced persons, and host communities, amid ongoing socioeconomic challenges and the lasting impact of the 2024 conflict escalation, and the renewed hostilities which started in March 2026. IOM will continue delivering essential humanitarian aid and protection services, while strengthening community recovery and resilience, reducing tensions, and promoting safe, dignified, and regular migration. Through integrated efforts across the humanitarian-development-peace nexus, IOM seeks to foster stability, inclusion, and renewed hope for all communities in Lebanon.

This plan has been updated to reflect renewed hostilities resulting in a fluid mix of active displacement, fragile returns, and secondary displacement. It outlines IOM's efforts to save lives and protect people on the move, drive solutions to displacement and facilitate pathways for regular migration. In 2026, IOM now requires USD88,564,750 to support 1,159,200 individuals, including internally displaced persons, local populations / communities, international
migrants and a range of stakeholders.

title: Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 19, Data as of 20 September 2026
content:
Event description
The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé Province, bordering South Sudan, being the latest affected, bringing the total number of health zones affected to 63 since the start of the outbreak. This latest geographic expansion heightens concern about further spread towards international borders, while transmission within the country remains increasingly heterogeneous across affected provinces and health zones. Since External Situation Report #18, a further 475 confirmed cases and 222 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 7733 confirmed cases, including 3732 deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR 48.3%)], as of 20 September 2026. Ituri remains the principal focus, although its relative contribution continues to decline, accounting for 76.9% of cumulative confirmed cases, while substantial transmission continues in Nord-Kivu and persists in Haut-Uélé.

At the national level, daily incidence remains high and fluctuating, with the seven-day moving average rebounding in early September before declining in the most recent days. This national pattern masks divergent provincial trajectories. Ituri continues a gradual decline from its late-July peak but remains at a high level, while Nord-Kivu experienced a marked increase, reaching its highest incidence in mid-September, followed by an apparent decline in recent days. Transmission in Haut-Uélé remains sustained but below its August peak, while Tshopo shows renewed activity from a low baseline. Bas-Uélé continues to report sporadic transmission, with no recent transmission evident in Sud-Kivu. Overall, the epidemic remains geographically heterogeneous, with recent declines in the principal transmission areas occurring alongside persistent low-level transmission and continued geographic expansion to new areas.

title: WFP Guinea Bissau Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Guinea-Bissau is one of the world's least developed countries, with a population of approximately 2.2 million people, nearly half of whom live below the national poverty line. Ranked 174th out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index, the country faces persistent development challenges that perpetuate intergenerational vulnerabilities.

• Food insecurity and malnutrition remain widespread, particularly in inland regions. An estimated 146,000 people face acute food insecurity, while nearly one in three children under five suffers from chronic malnutrition, with stunting rates surpassing the 30 percent threshold of a serious public health burden in the Oio, Gabú, and Bafatá regions.

• These outcomes are driven in large part by limited access to affordable and healthy food. While nearly 30 percent of the population cannot afford even an energy-only diet, almost 70 percent are unable to pay for a nutritious diet, estimated at USD 4 per day for an average household of seven people.

• In this context, since 1974 WFP has been supporting the Government of Guinea-Bissau in addressing immediate food and nutrition needs while strengthening resilience, livelihoods, and national capacities. Through an integrated food systems transformation approach, WFP contributes to improved food security and nutrition outcomes, enhanced resilience to shocks, and progress towards sustainable and inclusive development

title: IOM Yemen Dispatch August 2026: Updates on the humanitarian crisis, people on the move and IOM's response in Yemen
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security situation deteriorated markedly throughout August, with escalation in active conflict since the collapse of the 2022 truce in July. On August 6, deadly Ansar Allah (AA) strikes targeted the Government of Yemen (GoY) key positions in Hadramaut and facilities in Ma’rib, resulting in around 45 fatalities, marking one of the deadliest days on record. Over 119 operational incidents were reported in the first week of August alone as ballistic missiles, UAVs, and heavy artillery focused heavily on the Ma’rib, Hadramaut, and Red Sea coastal fronts. Ground fighting expanded toward the end of the month, as the AA forces launched concentrated offensives in western Ta’iz and southern Hodeidah, aimed at seizing strategic positions overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Maritime insecurity in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb has escalated freight costs and introduced critical supply delays for international relief goods. On the ground, flash floods have created additional challenges to road access, affecting emergency assistance delivery to displaced populations. Furthermore, the dual shock of conflict-driven displacements and extreme weather events has overwhelmed Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) and emergency stock pipelines, requiring an urgent, multisectoral scale-up to prevent further loss of life and mitigate acute food consumption gaps.

The severe cooking gas shortage in Aden and surrounding governorates like Abyan deepened in August, due to scheduled summer maintenance at Ma’rib Safer facility, which temporarily reduced gas production by 6,000 barrels per day. The supply disruption heavily impacted daily life by driving black-market prices for a 20-liter gas cylinder up to YR 18,000 (official rate is YR 8,500), rendering cooking gas unaffordable for poorer households and threatening already fragile food security. Beyond home kitchens, the crisis has paralyzed public transportation by stranding converted gas-powered buses, and brought local businesses, bakeries, and restaurants to the brink of shutdown.

Cholera transmission remains heavily concentrated in the same governorates that have consistently reported the highest caseloads since the beginning of the year. Abyan remained the epicenter of the outbreak, accounting for over 2,070 suspected cases, followed by Lahj with over 1,060 cases. Together with Ta’iz and Aden, these four governorates account for approximately 82 per cent of the national caseload.

UN Special Envoy Hand Grundberg and the USG for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, briefed the Security Council on 13 August, during which they underscored the dire situation that millions of Yemenis face and the heightened risk of Yemen getting entangled in complex regional confrontation. The humanitarian situation also has not improved, with the 73 UN staff still detained along with dozens of civil society staff. Despite the challenges, however, humanitarians reached 3.4 million people across Yemen with lifesaving assistance and protection in the first half of 2026.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 5 – 11 September 2026
content:
Russia increasingly targets border crossings in Ukraine, while Ukraine doubles down on striking Russian oil infrastructure.

Author

Tetiana Gaviuk

1863 conflict events

225 incidents of violence targeting civilians: 9% increase compared to last week

At least 92 civilians killed by targeted violence:19% increase compared to last week

1132 air- and drone strikes: 4% decrease compared to last week

276 shelling events: 48% increase compared to last week

444 armed clashe: 9% decrease compared to last week

221 Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure: 9% decrease compared to last week

Number of events and change compared to last week (per target):

Education: 15 events (21% decrease)

Healthcare: 12 events (9% increase)

Energy: 41 events (5% decrease)

Residential: 186 events (8% decrease)

Key trends

  • Russia has expanded its targeting of Ukraine’s transport infrastructure beyond passenger trains and railway hubs to drone attacks on or near border crossings in an attempt to further degrade Ukraine's connection to the outside world. Following a series of disruptive strikes on three Ukraine-Moldova border crossings in August and a ferry crossing to Romania on 6 September, Russia launched a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing on 8 September. This is significant as the border crossing connects Ukraine with Moldova and wider Europe. These kinds of attacks on border crossings risk hindering the movement of goods such as grain and military supplies and putting additional pressure on Ukraine’s economy.
  • In an attempt to further reduce Russia’s revenue sources and hinder its military production, Ukraine carried out its deepest strike inside Russia to date against two Arctic gas facilities on 9 September. Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces also resumed attacks on Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea, targeting 13 vessels on 8 September alone, including the Malta-flagged Seaviolet tanker at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s mooring point near Novorossiysk while it was loading Kazakh oil. Despite United States President Donald Trump’s claim on 14 September that Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, Ukraine is likely to maintain such strikes until a formal ceasefire is reached and Russia halts its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in turn

title: UNHCR Ecuador: Operational Update No. 8 | August 2026
content:
Operational context

UNHCR Ecuador operates in a complex and evolving environment shaped by security, humanitarian and environmental considerations. In August 2026, Ecuador received 1,441 new asylum applications, including 766 from Venezuelans and 675 from Colombians. Applications increased sharply compared to August 2025, rising by 72% and 239% respectively. Venezuelans accounted for 62% of all asylum claims processed in 2026, while Colombians represented 40%, underscoring the continued demand for international protection despite increased border restrictions and reduced mobility. Security-related incidents continued to affect several coastal areas, including Guayas, Manabí, Esmeraldas, and Santa Elena, including targeted killings in public spaces such as beaches during national holidays, reflecting the continued security challenges affecting the country. Also, the northern border remained an area of particular attention given developments involving transnational criminal and armed groups operating in the wider Colombia-Ecuador area. These dynamics continued to require close monitoring of protection risks and their effects on communities, including refugees, asylum-seekers and other people in need of international protection.

In light of these developments, national authorities maintained efforts to address organized crime and strengthen public security including the extension of the state of exception for 30 days across several provinces and cantons. In parallel, legislative developments further strengthened the framework for security operations through enhanced coordination between the Armed Forces and the National Police, and international cooperation.

Environmental risks added a further layer of complexity during the reporting period. National authorities maintained a high level of preparedness in anticipation of the potential impacts of the El Niño phenomenon, which is expected to affect the country over the coming months.

Rising sea levels and changing weather conditions have increased concerns of flooding, coastal erosion, and potential impacts on livelihoods and infrastructure, particularly in vulnerable coastal areas where forcibly displaced people reside. Authorities also expressed concern about the possible effects on energy production and essential services due to reduced water inflows affecting the country’s hydroelectric generation capacity. The 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia was felt across several Ecuadorian provinces. In a demonstration of regional solidarity, the Government of Ecuador established humanitarian aid collection points to support affected populations in Colombia.

Additionally, UNHCR continued to contribute to national and technical discussions on protection and internal displacement. UNHCR participated in the dialogue “Reflexiones sobre el desplazamiento interno en Ecuador” , organized by FLACSO Ecuador and 3iS, with the participation of the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights of Internally Displaced Persons. The exchange contributed evidence-based analysis and fostered academic reflections on internal displacement, supporting ongoing efforts to strengthen understanding of displacement dynamics and protection responses in Ecuador.

Overall, the August operational context required continued flexibility, risk monitoring and coordination with national and local authorities, partners and other humanitarian actors. UNHCR maintained its focus on ensuring access to protection and assistance for refugees, asylum-seekers and other people in need of international protection as well as host communities, while adapting its operational approach to the country’s evolving security and humanitarian environment.
